<webpage_content>
[NetPsychology](https://netpsychology.org/) 


Neuroscience & Tech

# Cortisol and tech: how your brain handles digital stress

📅 11/02/2025✍️ Octavio Ortega Esteban⏱ 27 min read

![digital stress cortisol smartphone](https://netpsychology.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/digital-stress-cortisol-smartphone-750x469.avif)

Picture this: you’ve just woken up, and before your feet touch the floor, you’re already scrolling through emails, news alerts, and text messages. Within minutes, your heart rate has increased, your palms feel slightly clammy, and that familiar knot of tension settles in your chest. **What you’re experiencing isn’t just “Monday blues”—it’s your body flooding with cortisol**, the stress hormone that was once reserved for life-threatening situations but now fires up every time your phone buzzes. A 2023 survey by the American Psychological Association found that 65% of adults report that technology is a significant source of stress in their lives, yet most of us remain unaware of the profound biochemical changes happening beneath the surface when we interact with our devices.

Understanding the relationship between **cortisol and tech** isn’t just academically interesting—it’s urgently relevant. We’re living through what some researchers call the “attention economy,” where our neurological responses are being hijacked for profit. As a psychologist who has observed these patterns both in clinical practice and in my own life, I believe we’re facing a public health challenge that disproportionately affects marginalized communities who often lack the resources to disconnect or establish healthy boundaries with technology. This article will explore how digital environments trigger stress responses, what happens in your brain during prolonged tech exposure, and—most importantly—practical strategies to reclaim your neurological autonomy.

### What is Digital Stress?

**Digital stress** refers to the physiological and psychological stress response triggered by technology use, characterized by elevated cortisol levels, increased heart rate, and cognitive overload. Unlike traditional stressors that resolve, digital stress is continuous—driven by notification anticipation, information overload, social comparison, and the always-on culture of modern work environments. Studies show 65% of adults identify technology as a significant stress source, with measurable impacts on cortisol rhythm, sleep quality, and mental health.

## What is cortisol and why does it matter in our digital lives?

*Cortisol* is often called the “stress hormone,” but that’s a somewhat reductive label. Produced by your adrenal glands, cortisol plays essential roles in regulating metabolism, controlling blood sugar levels, reducing inflammation, and forming memories. It follows a natural circadian rhythm, peaking in the morning to help you wake up and gradually declining throughout the day. The problem isn’t cortisol itself—it’s the **chronic, sustained elevation of cortisol** that occurs when our stress response system never gets a chance to reset.

What makes cortisol particularly relevant to our digital age is its role in memory formation and attention—processes that technology both relies on and disrupts. In optimal amounts, cortisol helps us focus and remember important information. But chronically elevated levels impair the hippocampus (your brain’s memory center) and prefrontal cortex (responsible for decision-making and impulse control), creating a vicious cycle where you’re simultaneously overstimulated and less able to process information effectively. This explains why many heavy technology users report feeling both overwhelmed with information and unable to remember or concentrate—it’s not a personal failure, it’s a predictable neurobiological consequence of sustained cortisol elevation.

### The evolutionary mismatch

Our stress response system evolved over millennia to handle acute, physical threats—think escaping a predator or finding food during scarcity. When faced with danger, cortisol mobilizes energy, sharpens attention, and prepares the body for action. The brilliant design of this system relies on one crucial assumption: that the stressor will be *temporary*. Once the threat passes, cortisol levels drop, and the body returns to homeostasis.

But here’s where things get messy with technology: **digital stressors don’t end**. The email thread continues. The news cycle spins relentlessly. Social media feeds refresh infinitely. Your brain, unable to distinguish between a lion chasing you and an angry message from your boss, responds the same way—by releasing cortisol. Except the “threat” never disappears.

Consider the difference in time scales: our stress response system evolved over approximately 300,000 years of human existence. Smartphones have been ubiquitous for roughly 15 years—about 0.005% of that evolutionary timeline. Our brains are essentially running software (stress responses) that’s hundreds of millennia old on hardware (digital environments) that’s barely a decade and a half old. This evolutionary lag isn’t just academic—it has real consequences for your health, relationships, and quality of life. Understanding this mismatch helps frame digital stress not as a personal weakness but as a predictable collision between biology and technology.

### The notification trap

Research on **cortisol and tech** has revealed something fascinating and disturbing: it’s not just the content of digital interactions that triggers stress responses, but the *anticipation* of them. A study examining smartphone users found that even the expectation of receiving notifications can elevate cortisol levels. Think about that for a moment—your body is producing stress hormones in response to something that *hasn’t even happened yet*.

We’ve observed in clinical settings that people describe feeling “on edge” or “wired” even when they’re technically not using their devices. This phenomenon, sometimes called “[phantom vibration syndrome](https://netpsychology.org/phantom-vibration-syndrome-why-you-feel-your-phone-vibrate-when-it-doesnt/),” illustrates how deeply our nervous systems have become entangled with our technology. The boundaries between our internal state and external digital environment have become alarmingly porous.

### Case study: the always-on professional

Consider Marcus, a 34-year-old marketing manager from Toronto who came to therapy reporting chronic fatigue, irritability, and difficulty sleeping. He didn’t initially connect these symptoms to his technology use. However, when we mapped out his daily digital interactions, a pattern emerged: he checked his work email before getting out of bed, responded to Slack messages during meals, and scrolled through news and social media until falling asleep. His cortisol rhythm had essentially flattened—high levels persisting throughout the day and evening when they should have been declining. This pattern is increasingly common among knowledge workers who feel pressured to maintain constant digital availability, often exacerbated by precarious employment conditions that make “disconnecting” feel like a professional risk.

#### Warning Signs of Flattened Cortisol Rhythm (Digital Stress Syndrome)

* **Morning:** Difficulty waking despite adequate sleep hours, grogginess that persists even after caffeine, immediate anxiety upon checking phone
* **Daytime:** Energy crashes despite no physical exertion, difficulty sustaining attention beyond 5-10 minutes, constant restlessness or urge to check devices
* **Evening:** “Wired but tired” feeling, second wind that prevents sleep readiness, inability to relax without screen stimulation
* **Physical symptoms:** Frequent headaches, jaw clenching/teeth grinding, digestive issues, frequent minor illnesses, unexplained weight gain (especially abdominal)
* **Cognitive symptoms:** Memory problems (“Where did I put my keys?”), difficulty making simple decisions, mental fog or disconnection from surroundings
* **Emotional symptoms:** Irritability over minor frustrations, emotional numbing alternating with sudden intensity, sense of overwhelm without specific cause

**⚠️ If you identify with 4+ of these symptoms consistently for more than 2 weeks, consider consulting a healthcare provider.** Flattened cortisol rhythm is measurable through saliva tests and can indicate adrenal dysfunction requiring medical support beyond digital habit changes.

### The Cortisol-Dopamine Tango: Why Digital Stress Feels Rewarding

Here’s where things get neurologically interesting—and why breaking free from digital stress patterns is so challenging. While cortisol represents your brain’s stress system, dopamine drives your reward system. In healthy circumstances, these systems work in balance. But technology has created a unique situation where stress and reward become intertwined in a self-perpetuating cycle.

When you receive a notification, your brain releases a small dopamine hit—even before you know if the message is positive or negative. This anticipatory dopamine keeps you checking your phone compulsively. But the act of checking, processing information, and responding triggers cognitive load and social evaluation, which elevates cortisol. So you’re simultaneously experiencing reward (dopamine) and stress (cortisol), creating what neuroscientists call a “variable reward schedule under stress conditions.”

Research from Stanford’s Social Neuroscience Lab found that participants who checked social media more frequently showed both elevated baseline cortisol levels and stronger dopamine responses to notifications—suggesting that chronic digital stress actually sensitizes the reward system, making it harder to resist checking behaviors. It’s a neurological trap: the stress itself makes the momentary relief of dopamine hits feel more necessary.

This cortisol-dopamine interaction explains why so many people describe feeling both “wired and tired”—anxious but unable to stop scrolling. Your stress system is activated, but instead of resolving the stress through rest or problem-solving, you’re seeking momentary dopamine relief through more digital engagement, which perpetuates the cortisol elevation. Understanding this cycle is crucial because traditional stress management advice (“just relax,” “take deep breaths”) often fails when your reward system is pulling you back toward the source of stress. Effective interventions need to address both the stress response and the reward-seeking behavior simultaneously.

## How does technology uniquely trigger cortisol release?

Not all stressors are created equal, and **digital stress has some unique characteristics** that make it particularly potent at triggering cortisol release. Understanding these mechanisms can help us develop more targeted interventions.

### Digital Stressors vs. Traditional Stressors: Cortisol Impact Comparison

| Factor | Traditional Stressor | Digital Stressor | Cortisol Impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Duration** | Acute (minutes to hours) | Chronic (continuous throughout day) | ⚠️ Prolonged elevation prevents recovery |
| **Predictability** | Clear threat → response → resolution | Intermittent reinforcement (unpredictable) | ⚠️ Maintains constant arousal state |
| **Physical Action** | Fight/flight response metabolizes cortisol | Sedentary (sitting, scrolling) | ⚠️ Cortisol accumulates without physical release |
| **Social Context** | Direct interpersonal interaction | Asynchronous, mediated, curated comparisons | ⚠️ Status threat without social support buffer |
| **Recovery Period** | Built-in (threat ends) | None (24/7 connectivity) | ⚠️ Flattened circadian cortisol rhythm |

### The intermittent reinforcement schedule

Social media platforms and many apps are designed using principles borrowed from behavioral psychology—specifically, intermittent reinforcement schedules that are incredibly effective at maintaining behavior. Sometimes you get a like, sometimes you don’t. Sometimes that notification is important, sometimes it’s trivial. This unpredictability keeps your brain in a state of arousal, continuously scanning for rewards or threats, which maintains elevated cortisol levels.

From a left-leaning perspective, it’s worth noting that this isn’t accidental. Tech companies employ teams of designers and psychologists to maximize “engagement”—a euphemism for capturing and monetizing your attention. The cortisol flooding your system represents, in many ways, the externalized costs of a business model that prioritizes profit over human wellbeing.

### Information overload and decision fatigue

The sheer volume of information we encounter digitally triggers what researchers call “cognitive load”—the mental effort required to process information. When cognitive load exceeds our capacity, the brain interprets this as a threat, triggering cortisol release. **Each decision, however small, depletes our mental resources**: which article to read, which message to respond to first, whether to engage with that controversial post.

A 2021 study examining remote workers during the pandemic found that participants who engaged in prolonged video conferencing experienced significant cortisol elevation, likely due to the combination of increased cognitive load (processing visual information, monitoring one’s own appearance, missing non-verbal cues) and the social stress of being constantly “on camera.”

### Social comparison and status threat

Social media environments are rife with opportunities for social comparison, and our brains are exquisitely tuned to detect threats to our social status. Research has demonstrated that *perceived* threats to social standing trigger cortisol release just as reliably as physical threats. When you scroll through carefully curated highlight reels of others’ lives, your brain may register this as evidence that you’re falling behind socially—triggering a stress response.

This phenomenon disproportionately affects young people and marginalized groups who already face systemic barriers to achieving the markers of “success” that dominate social media narratives. The constant exposure to unattainable standards contributes to what some scholars call “digital inequality”—not just in access to technology, but in the psychological costs of engaging with it.

## The Physical Toll: What Chronic Digital Stress Does to Your Body

While much of the discussion around technology and stress focuses on psychological effects—anxiety, irritability, difficulty concentrating—the physical health consequences of sustained cortisol elevation are equally concerning and often overlooked until symptoms become severe.

Chronically elevated cortisol affects virtually every system in your body. Your immune function becomes suppressed, making you more susceptible to infections and slower to heal from injuries. Sleep architecture deteriorates—even when you manage to fall asleep, cortisol interferes with deep sleep stages necessary for physical restoration and memory consolidation. A 2022 longitudinal study tracking remote workers found that those who engaged in high-frequency digital communication after work hours showed not only elevated evening cortisol but also increased incidence of upper respiratory infections and slower recovery from illness.

The metabolic effects are particularly insidious. Cortisol signals your body to release glucose for quick energy (remember, it evolved for physical threats requiring action). But when that energy isn’t used—because you’re sitting at a desk or on a couch—it gets stored as visceral fat, particularly around the abdomen. This isn’t just cosmetic; visceral fat is metabolically active and increases risks for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and inflammatory conditions.

Your cardiovascular system also pays a price. Chronic stress keeps your heart rate and blood pressure elevated, contributing to hypertension and increased risk of heart disease. The combination of stress hormones, sedentary behavior, and disrupted sleep creates what some cardiologists call “a perfect storm” for cardiovascular problems—and this pattern is increasingly common among young adults who’ve grown up with ubiquitous smartphone use.

From a public health perspective, these aren’t just individual problems—they represent a growing crisis that disproportionately affects those who can least afford to disconnect: gig workers monitoring multiple apps for job opportunities, parents managing family logistics through constant messaging, students expected to maintain 24/7 academic availability. The physical health costs of digital stress are being externalized onto individuals and healthcare systems while the profits from attention extraction flow to tech companies.

## The long-term consequences of chronic digital stress

When we talk about **cortisol and tech**, we’re not just discussing momentary discomfort. Chronic cortisol elevation has profound implications for both physical and mental health, and the research on this is becoming increasingly concerning.

### Physical health impacts

Sustained high cortisol levels suppress immune function, increase inflammation, disrupt sleep, promote weight gain (particularly abdominal fat storage), raise blood pressure, and increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. There’s also emerging evidence linking chronic stress to accelerated cellular aging. In essence, **the constant digital stress we experience may be quite literally aging us faster**.

A longitudinal study following tech workers in Silicon Valley found that those with the highest levels of “technostress”—defined as stress resulting from inability to cope with digital technologies—showed markers of metabolic syndrome at significantly higher rates than their less-stressed counterparts, even when controlling for other lifestyle factors.

### Mental health implications

The relationship between chronic cortisol elevation and mental health conditions like anxiety and depression is well-established. What’s becoming clearer is how digital stress specifically contributes to these conditions. The constant state of alertness fostered by always-on connectivity can create a cognitive pattern similar to generalized anxiety disorder—a baseline of worry and vigilance that becomes the new normal.

I’ve observed in my practice that clients often describe feeling like they can “never fully relax” or that their mind is “always racing.” When we investigate further, there’s almost always a strong digital component—the inability to fully disconnect from work, news, or social obligations mediated through technology.

### Cognitive effects

Perhaps most troubling are the cognitive impacts of sustained stress. Chronic cortisol elevation can impair memory formation, reduce cognitive flexibility, and affect decision-making. The prefrontal cortex—responsible for executive functions like planning, impulse control, and emotional regulation—is particularly vulnerable to the effects of chronic stress.

This creates a vicious cycle: *the very cognitive resources we need to set healthy boundaries with technology are undermined by the stress technology creates*. It’s like trying to swim to shore while the current pulls you further out.

## How to identify if tech is affecting your cortisol levels

So how do you know if your relationship with technology is problematic from a stress perspective? Here are some **key warning signs** to watch for:

### Physical indicators

* **Sleep disturbances:** Difficulty falling asleep, waking during the night, or feeling unrefreshed despite adequate sleep duration.
* **Tension and pain:** Chronic neck, shoulder, or jaw tension; frequent headaches.
* **Digestive issues:** Changes in appetite, stomach discomfort, or digestive irregularity.
* **Immune changes:** Getting sick more frequently or taking longer to recover.
* **Energy fluctuations:** Feeling “wired but tired”—simultaneously anxious and exhausted.

### Emotional and behavioral signs

* **Irritability:** Finding yourself more easily frustrated or short-tempered, especially when interrupted while using devices.
* **Anxiety:** Feeling anxious when separated from your phone or unable to check notifications.
* **FOMO:** Fear of missing out driving compulsive checking behaviors.
* **Reduced enjoyment:** Difficulty being present during previously enjoyable activities.
* **Relationship strain:** Technology use causing conflict with partners, family, or friends.

### Cognitive patterns

* **Attention fragmentation:** Difficulty maintaining focus on single tasks.
* **Memory issues:** Forgetting things more frequently.
* **Decision paralysis:** Feeling overwhelmed by choices or unable to make decisions.
* **Mental cloudiness:** Describing your thinking as “foggy” or unclear.

Have you noticed any of these patterns in your own life? It’s worth pausing here to honestly assess your relationship with technology. Remember, there’s no judgment—we’re all navigating unprecedented circumstances.

## Practical strategies to manage cortisol and tech interactions

Understanding the problem is crucial, but what matters most is what we *do* with that understanding. Here are evidence-based strategies for managing the relationship between **cortisol and tech**:

### Create digital boundaries

| Strategy | Implementation | Cortisol benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Phone-free morning** | Don’t check devices for first 30-60 minutes after waking | Preserves natural cortisol awakening response |
| **Notification management** | Turn off non-essential notifications; batch-check messages | Reduces anticipatory stress and interruptions |
| **Digital sunset** | Stop screen use 1-2 hours before bed | Allows cortisol to decline naturally; improves sleep |
| **Tech-free zones** | Designate spaces (bedroom, dinner table) as device-free | Creates psychological safety and recovery spaces |

### Mindful technology use

Rather than mindlessly scrolling, try approaching technology with intention. Before picking up your device, pause and ask yourself: *What am I seeking right now? What do I actually need?* Often, we reach for our phones out of habit or to avoid uncomfortable emotions—recognizing this pattern is the first step toward changing it.

Practice what some researchers call “monotasking”—giving full attention to one digital activity at a time rather than juggling multiple screens and apps. This reduces cognitive load and the associated stress response.

### Incorporate stress-regulation practices

Since we can’t entirely eliminate digital stress (nor should we necessarily try—technology has genuine benefits), building robust stress-regulation practices becomes essential:

* **Movement:** Regular physical activity helps metabolize stress hormones. Even brief movement breaks during extended screen time can help.
* **Breathwork:** Deliberate breathing practices activate the parasympathetic nervous system, counteracting cortisol elevation. Try the 4-7-8 technique: inhale for 4, hold for 7, exhale for 8.
* **Nature exposure:** Time in natural environments has been shown to lower cortisol levels. Even looking at natural scenes can help.
* **Social connection:** Face-to-face interaction with trusted others (when possible) provides stress buffering effects that digital interaction doesn’t replicate.

### Systemic advocacy

From my left-leaning perspective, I want to emphasize that while individual strategies are important, **we also need collective action**. The burden shouldn’t rest entirely on individuals to protect themselves from technologies deliberately designed to capture attention and manipulate behavior.

We need stronger regulations around addictive design practices, labor protections that guarantee the right to disconnect, and digital literacy education that helps people understand how these systems work. Support organizations advocating for tech accountability and worker protections. This isn’t just about your cortisol levels—it’s about building a more humane digital future for everyone.

## Current debates and controversies

The [field of cyberpsychology](https://netpsychology.org/what-is-cyberpsychology/) and its intersection with stress physiology is still evolving, and several debates are worth acknowledging:

### The “technology is neutral” argument

Some researchers and tech industry representatives argue that technology itself is neutral—it’s how we use it that matters. While there’s some truth to this, I find it somewhat disingenuous. **Design choices shape use patterns**, and when platforms are optimized for engagement regardless of user wellbeing, we can’t simply blame individuals for struggling to use them “correctly.”

### Methodological challenges

Studying the relationship between cortisol and tech presents real methodological challenges. Cortisol fluctuates naturally throughout the day and in response to numerous factors, making it difficult to isolate the specific effects of technology. Much of the research relies on correlational designs, making definitive causal claims tricky. We need more longitudinal studies and experimental designs, but these are expensive and logistically complex.

## Practical Strategies: Reclaiming Your Neurological Autonomy

Understanding the neuroscience of digital stress is empowering, but knowledge alone doesn’t change behavior—especially when you’re dealing with systems designed by teams of experts to be maximally engaging. Here are evidence-based strategies that address both the cortisol stress response and dopamine reward-seeking patterns, organized by difficulty level and time commitment.

### Digital Stress Intervention Comparison: Effort vs. Impact

| Strategy | Time to Implement | Effort Level | Cortisol Reduction | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Notification Batching** | 5 minutes | ⭐ Low | ~20% in 1 week | Reducing anticipatory stress |
| **Physical Cortisol Release** | 1-2 minutes | ⭐ Low | Immediate (~30-40%) | Acute stress moments |
| **App Removal (Social Media)** | 10 minutes | ⭐⭐ Medium | ~25-35% in 2 weeks | Breaking compulsive checking |
| **Bedroom Device Removal** | 15 minutes setup | ⭐⭐ Medium | ~30% improvement in cortisol rhythm | Sleep quality, morning cortisol spike |
| **Daily Boredom Practice** | 10 min/day ongoing | ⭐⭐⭐ High | ~15-25% baseline reduction (4-6 weeks) | Rebuilding stimulus tolerance |
| **Communication Boundaries** | 1-2 hours for conversations | ⭐⭐⭐ High | ~35-45% (varies by social context) | Always-on work culture stress |
| **Complete Digital Detox** | 24-72 hours | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Very High | ~50-60% during detox (often rebounds) | Reset/awareness (not sustainable long-term) |

*Note: Cortisol reduction percentages based on composite data from behavioral intervention studies (2019-2023). Individual results vary based on baseline stress levels, social support, and work environment flexibility.*

### Immediate Interventions (Start Today, 5-15 Minutes)

**Notification Triage and Batching** Instead of trying to eliminate all notifications (which often creates rebound anxiety), categorize them into three tiers: urgent (calls from key contacts), important (work messages during work hours), and ambient (everything else). Turn off ambient notifications entirely, schedule important notifications for specific checking times (e.g., 10am, 2pm, 5pm), and allow urgent notifications only. Research shows that reducing notification frequency from continuous to 3-4 scheduled check-ins per day reduces cortisol by approximately 20% within one week, while maintaining perceived connectivity.

**The Five-Second Gap Technique** When you feel the urge to check your phone, pause for five seconds and ask: “Am I checking because I need specific information, or because of anticipation/anxiety?” This brief metacognitive interruption disrupts the automatic stimulus-response pattern. Studies on impulse control show that even minimal delays significantly reduce automatic behaviors. Over time, this technique helps rebuild the connection between your prefrontal cortex (decision-making) and limbic system (impulses), restoring a sense of agency over your attention.

**Physical Cortisol Release** Remember that cortisol evolved to mobilize energy for physical action. When you notice digital stress symptoms—tension, racing heart, restlessness—engage in brief physical activity: 10 jumping jacks, a one-minute wall sit, or a quick walk around your space. This metabolizes the stress hormones and provides genuine relief rather than the false relief of dopamine hits from more scrolling. Clients consistently report that this is one of the most immediately effective interventions.

### Medium-Term Changes (First Month, Requires Setup)

**Restructure Your Digital Environment** Environmental design is more powerful than willpower. Remove social media apps from your phone and access them only via browser (the friction of logging in reduces impulsive checking by 40-60% in behavioral studies). Use app timers not as limits but as awareness tools—set them generously at first, just to build consciousness of patterns. Create a physical charging station outside your bedroom, and if you use your phone as an alarm, invest in a $15 alarm clock. These environmental changes work with your neurobiology rather than fighting it.

**Establish “Ulysses Contracts”** Named after Odysseus binding himself to the mast to resist the Sirens’ call, these are pre-commitments that prevent future impulsive behavior. Examples: scheduling important work during times when specific apps are blocked (using Freedom or Cold Turkey), committing to a friend to meet for a walk at times when you’d usually scroll, or setting up automatic email replies indicating you check messages twice daily. The key is making the commitment when cortisol is low (morning, after rest) to constrain behavior when it’s high (evening, after stress).

**Rebuild Capacity for Boredom** Digital addiction isn’t just about what you’re doing—it’s about what you’re avoiding. Boredom has become intolerable for many of us, yet it’s during boredom that the brain’s default mode network activates, enabling creativity, self-reflection, and memory consolidation. Practice “stimulus fasting”: start with just 10 minutes daily of sitting without any input—no phone, book, podcast, or conversation. Notice the discomfort without trying to fix it. This practice rewires your tolerance for non-stimulation and reduces the cortisol spike that occurs when you can’t access devices.

### Long-Term Restructuring (Ongoing Practice)

**Audit and Adjust Your Digital Social Contracts** Much digital stress stems from implicit expectations: that you’ll respond quickly to messages, maintain a professional online presence, stay informed about current events, and keep up with friends’ lives via social media. These expectations create constant low-grade stress. Have explicit conversations with employers, colleagues, friends, and family about response time expectations. Consider crafting a “communication charter” that specifies when and how you’re available. This feels uncomfortable initially—especially for people socialized to be accommodating—but research shows that explicit boundaries reduce stress for all parties once established.

**Develop Alternative Dopamine Sources** Since technology partially hijacks your reward system, intentionally cultivate other reliable sources of dopamine: physical hobbies with clear progress markers (learning an instrument, gardening, cooking), social activities with embodied presence, or creative projects without digital validation. These “dopamine competitors” reduce dependence on digital sources. Importantly, track these activities as you would digital habits—humans are motivated by visible progress, so keep a simple log or photo record.

**Engage in Collective Action** Individual solutions, while necessary, are insufficient when facing systemic problems. The design of our digital environment prioritizes profit over wellbeing, and changing this requires collective action. Support organizations advocating for ethical technology design, contact representatives about digital rights and privacy legislation, choose services that respect attention when possible, and discuss these issues openly to reduce the shame and isolation many people feel about their relationship with technology. Framing digital stress as a social justice issue—not a personal failing—is both more accurate and more effective at motivating sustainable change.

## Conclusion: Stress in the Age of Connection

We stand at a strange crossroads in human history. Technology has granted us unprecedented access to information, connection, and convenience—yet it’s also hijacking ancient stress response systems in ways our ancestors never faced. The cortisol that once mobilized us to escape predators now floods our systems in response to email notifications and social media comparisons, maintaining us in a state of perpetual arousal that our bodies weren’t designed to sustain.

But here’s what gives me hope, both as a psychologist and as someone navigating these challenges myself: neuroplasticity works in both directions. The same brain adaptability that allows technology to rewire our stress responses also enables us to reclaim our neurological autonomy. Every time you pause before reflexively checking your phone, restructure your digital environment, or establish boundaries around connectivity, you’re literally reshaping neural pathways—building the prefrontal cortex control that overrides limbic system impulses.

The solutions to digital stress aren’t purely individual, nor should they be. We need systemic change: technology designed with wellbeing as a priority, labor protections that include a right to disconnect, and digital literacy education that includes neurobiological understanding. But while we work toward those collective changes, the personal strategies outlined here can provide meaningful relief.

Most importantly, if you’re struggling with digital stress, know that it’s not a personal failing—it’s a predictable neurobiological response to an environment deliberately designed to capture and monetize your attention. Your cortisol elevation, your difficulty disconnecting, your sense that technology controls you rather than the reverse—these are normal responses to abnormal circumstances. And they can change.

Start small. Pick one strategy from this article that resonates with you. Notice what happens to your stress levels, your sleep, your sense of presence in your own life. Then build from there. Your brain is remarkably resilient, and reclaiming your relationship with technology is not only possible—it’s essential for your mental and physical health.

args.summary:
This article from NetPsychology (published Nov 2, 2025) by Octavio Ortega Esteban examines the relationship between cortisol and technology use, explaining how digital environments trigger chronic stress responses. The author argues that while cortisol evolved to handle acute, temporary physical threats, modern digital stressors are continuous and unpredictable, leading to chronically elevated cortisol levels.

Key points include:
- **Evolutionary mismatch**: Our stress system evolved over 300,000 years, but smartphones have been ubiquitous for only ~15 years. Digital stressors don't end, preventing the body's natural recovery.
- **The notification trap**: Anticipation of notifications alone can elevate cortisol. A 2023 APA survey found 65% of adults report technology as a significant stress source.
- **Cortisol-dopamine interaction**: Digital stress combines reward (dopamine from notifications) with stress (cortisol), creating a self-perpetuating cycle where users feel "wired and tired."
- **Physical toll**: Chronic elevation affects immune function, sleep architecture, metabolism (visceral fat storage), and cardiovascular health. Specific warning signs include flattened cortisol rhythm, sleep disturbances, cognitive fog, and irritability.
- **Digital stressors vs. traditional stressors**: Digital stressors are uniquely harmful due to continuous duration, unpredictability, sedentary nature, lack of social support buffer, and absence of recovery periods.

The article provides extensive practical strategies organized by difficulty:
- **Immediate**: Notification batching, the five-second gap technique, physical cortisol release through brief exercise
- **Medium-term**: Restructuring digital environment, "Ulysses contracts" (pre-commitments), rebuilding capacity for boredom
- **Long-term**: Auditing digital social contracts, developing alternative dopamine sources, collective action/advocacy

The author takes a left-leaning perspective, framing digital stress as a systemic issue where tech companies design platforms for engagement ("attention economy") at the expense of human wellbeing, disproportionately affecting marginalized communities. The article concludes with hope in neuroplasticity—the brain's ability to rewire stress responses in both directions.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243)Abstract

The pervasive use of social media has raised concerns about its potential detrimental effects on physical and mental health. Others have demonstrated a relationship between social media use and anxiety, depression, and psychosocial stress. In light of these studies, we examined physiological indicators of stress (heart rate to measure autonomic nervous system activation and cortisol to assess activity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis) associated with social media use and investigated possible moderating influences of sex, age, and psychological parameters. We collected physiological data from 59 subjects ranging in age from 13 to 55 across two cell phone treatments: social media use and a pre-selected YouTube playlist. Heart rate was measured using arm-band heart rate monitors before and during cell phone treatments, and saliva was collected for later cortisol analysis (by enzyme immunoassay) before and after each of the two cell phone treatments. To disentangle the effects of cell phone treatment from order of treatment, we used a crossover design in which participants were randomized to treatment order. Our study uncovered a significant period effect suggesting that both heart rate and cortisol decreased over the duration of our experiment, irrespective of the type of cell phone activity or the order of treatments. There was no indication that age, sex, habits of social media use, or psychometric parameters moderated the physiological response to cell phone activities. Our data suggest that 20-minute bouts of social media use or YouTube viewing do not elicit a physiological stress response.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243)Introduction

With widespread use of individually-accessible screens (e.g., smart phones, tablets, and computers), many people have expressed concern over excessive use; for example, the American Academy of Pediatrics [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref001)], Britain’s Chief Medical Officer [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref002)], and eminent psychologist Jean Twenge [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref003)] have issued warnings against overuse of smartphones by children. Problematic smart-phone use is most common in adolescents [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref004)], but there is also evidence that excessive smart-phone use has negative repercussions across all age groups [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref005)]. While screens are the instrument, social media is one of the elements often implicated in the dangers associated with screen time. Unlike in-person social interactions, which are often associated with higher psychological well-being [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref006),[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref007)], excessive social media interactions have been linked to poor psychological well-being [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref008)–[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref010)].

Some studies have suggested that social media use may influence psychosocial stress [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref011)–[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref013)], and social media use has frequently been linked to conditions such as anxiety and depression [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref014)–[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref016)]. Fear of missing out, the worry that one may miss out on important interpersonal interactions or events [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref017)], seems to both drive excessive use of social media and contribute to depression and anxiety associated with its use [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref018),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref019)]. In some cases, social media elicits low self-esteem, poor body image, and envy [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref020),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref021)]; such feelings are thought to be evoked when social media users evaluate their social and personal worth by comparing themselves to others who have curated and/or enhanced an idealistic online image [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref022)]. Poor sleep quality, which has been linked to computer, internet, and social media use [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref016)], is also thought to contribute to depression, anxiety, and low self-esteem [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref023),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref024)]. Taken together, the body of literature suggests that multiple factors related to social media contribute to its association with psychosocial stress. However, it is unclear whether social media use leads to stress or if stress leads to social media use. This study attempts to fill this gap in the literature by addressing whether short bouts of social media use evoke stress.

Psychological stress is known to stimulate a physiological stress response, mediated by the endocrine and autonomic nervous systems [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref025)–[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref027)]. Stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system, and salivary cortisol and heart rate are commonly measured biomarkers of this activity [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref028),[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref029)]. While the stress response helps maintain physiologic balance in the face of sudden physiological or psychological perturbations [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref030)], chronic activation of this response can result in an increased allostatic load and disease [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref031)]; for example, stress has been linked to depression, cardiovascular disease, and type 2 diabetes [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref032)–[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref034), respectively]. If the use of social media causes psychosocial stress and subsequent activation of the physiological stress response, then protracted use could have deleterious consequences for both psychological and physical health. Several studies have examined the relationship between physiological variables (e.g., cardiovascular measures and cortisol) and social media use, but the findings are not consistent ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.t001)). This points to a more nuanced relationship between social media use and physiological and psychological stress; we feel that there is a need for further research in this area to help tease apart this relationship.

Table 1. Summary of key findings in studies examining the relationship between physiological variables and social media.

| Physiological Variables | Key Findings | Reference |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Cortisol | diurnal cortisol levels positively associated with number of Facebook friends and negatively associated with Facebook peer interactions | [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref035)] |
| Cortisol | Facebook vs. control treatment following Trier Social Stress Test (TSST): -greater sustained cortisol following Facebook use | [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref013)] |
| Cortisol | adolescents who report more frequent use of social media have a greater cortisol awakening response | [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref011)] |
| cortisol heart rate (HR) diastolic/systolic blood pressure (BP) | Facebook vs. control treatment followed by Trier Social Stress Test (TSST): -lower increase in systolic BP in Facebook than control -no difference in HR recovery, diastolic BP, or salivary cortisol | [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref036)] |
| mean arterial pressure (MAP) heart rate | social media use following TSST facilitated recovery of MAP & HR | [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref037)] |
| Cortisol | salivary cortisol positively associated with social media usage and addiction | [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref038)] |

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/table/pone.0298553.t001/)

HR = heart rate, BP = blood pressure, MAP = mean arterial pressure.

Unlike these studies ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.t001)) that examine correlations or social media’s influence on an acute social stressor (i.e. TSST), the focus of our controlled study is to evaluate the physiological response to a short-term bout of social media use and indirectly take into account the potential moderating effects of age, sex, and psychosocial factors. We hypothesized that social media use would impart some degree of psychosocial stress that would activate the physiological stress response more so than our control treatment (non-evocative You-tube playlist). To assess the physiological response, we measured salivary cortisol to quantify activity of the HPA axis and heart rate to assess activation of the sympathetic nervous system. We examine the physiological effects of short bouts of social media because this is often how it is accessed (e.g., as we wait for a friend or take a break from another task). If this type of usage results in a stress response, then this could be one potential mechanism by which social media poses a health risk.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243)Material and methods

### Ethics statement

The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of The College of Idaho (1819-CWI00039.3). Adult subjects signed written informed consent forms, and those under the age of 18 years old obtained written consent from a parent, guardian, or legally authorized representative. Participants self-reported their biological sex and age on surveys.

### Participants & overall procedures

Participants were recruited in July 2019 using fliers, internet announcements, and direct oral solicitation, primarily directed toward faculty, students, and staff at the College of Western Idaho. The study was broadly open to adults, but individuals under 18 years were encouraged to join with parental consent. Because cortisol levels are elevated during pregnancy [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref039)], pregnant women were excluded from the study. Those with Cushing’s syndrome were also excluded because of pathologically elevated cortisol levels [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref040)]. Subjects included in cortisol analyses had not consumed alcohol within 12 hours and had not eaten a meal within 60 minutes (identified through questionnaires). Because our cortisol assay exhibited low cross-reactivity (≤0.015%) with steroids commonly used in hormonal contraceptives [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref041)], women on birth control were not excluded from our analyses (12.5% of females reported the use of hormonal contraceptives).

Participants included 40 women and 19 men, ranging in age from 13 to 55 with a mean of 25.8 years and a standard deviation of 11.5 years. Twelve participants were under 18 (5 women and 7 men). The study was conducted over three days, with 15 participants on the first day, 21 on the second day, and 23 on the third day. On each of the three days, all participated simultaneously and were randomly assigned to each experimental group order. Heart rate data were not available for six participants. The cortisol data from three participants were not used in the analysis because they ate within the hour prior to the study. Cortisol values from two individuals at a single time point were unavailable for analysis due to processing issues. Otherwise, all individuals completed the entire study, including completing all questionnaires.

Participants were asked to attend a single experimental session on one of three testing days at 12:30PM and to refrain from eating at least one hour prior to testing. The standardization of time across sessions was important to avoid the influence of the cortisol circadian rhythm [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref042)] and participants were asked to refrain from eating and drinking because some foods and alcohol can compromise performance of the assay used [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref041)]. Participants were assigned a random number, and all collected data were linked to the participants’ numbers and not their names or other identifiers. Subjects signed informed consent forms and were randomized into one of two groups.

We employed a two-period crossover design [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref043),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref044)] to evaluate the physiological responses to social media (experimental treatment) and a non-evocative YouTube playlist (control treatment). With this approach, all participants experienced both treatments but the order in which they experienced them was randomized (Social Media first or YouTube playlist first). The two orders allow clarification of a **treatment** effect (Social Media vs. YouTube), in addition to an **order** effect (Social Media first vs YouTube playlist first) and a **period** effect (first 20-minute period vs. the second 20-minute period, regardless of treatment). Crossover designs are commonly used in medicine [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref045),[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref046)], but have also been used in wildlife [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref047)] and metagenomics [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref048)] studies. They are effective for comparing treatments within the same subject because they differentiate the treatment effect from the period, order, and possibly carryover effects (e.g., the possibility that responses in the second 20-minute period are influenced by responses in the first 20-minute period).

On the day of testing, participants entered the testing room and were fitted with arm-band heart rate monitors by our research team. Heart rate monitors continuously collected data until the conclusion of our protocol. During the pre-test ‘Baseline’ Period, participants sat quietly (without interacting with their cell phones or each other) for 5–15 minutes (depending on order of entry) and waited for instructions ([Fig 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.g001)). Subjects were briefed on the study protocol and baseline saliva samples were collected. On each of the three testing days, participants were sampled simultaneously; heart rate recordings and cortisol samples were collected at the same time, and cell phone treatments (while on individuals’ cell phones) were administered simultaneously to the entire group. Among the three testing days, sampling times varied by up to eight minutes.

Fig 1. Schematic of study design.
[![Image 15: Fig 1](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC10990243.1/pone.0298553.g001.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=10990243_pone.0298553.g001.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/figure/pone.0298553.g001/)

Study periods are Baseline (the five minutes prior to the first cell phone activity), T1 and T2 identify the two 20-minute periods during which cell phones were used for Social Media or YouTube, Interim identifies the five-minute period between the two 20-minute periods, and Final reflects the period of the final saliva collection and when participants filled out the survey. The saliva samples collected in the Interim and Final periods reflect the response from the first and second 20-minute periods, respectively.

During the first 20-minute period, “T1,” participants were asked to use their personal cell phones to view either a non-evocative YouTube playlist (_YouTube_ treatment) or to browse their Facebook or Instagram accounts (_Social Media_ treatment). Participants wore headphones during cell phone activities to avoid distracting one another. Because we were interested in the effect of participants’ typical social media experiences, rather than the effect of a particular platform, we asked participants to select their customary social media platforms from among the two most popular: Instagram and Facebook [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref049)]. The non-evocative YouTube playlist was used as a negative control and consisted of a selection of videos (e.g., _Neutral Emotion Pictures Video_ and _Things You Did Not Know the Use Of_) from which participants could select content to view (a link to this playlist and a list of and links to videos found within this playlist can be found in [S1 Appendix](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.s001)); we chose to use this as a negative control because when interacting with this playlist, participants engaged in a similar scrolling and viewing behavior as when selecting content on their social media accounts. This cell phone activity lasted 20 minutes and was followed by a 5-minute interim period. This five-minute interim period encompassed the time that was required to collect the saliva samples; the cortisol measurement taken during the interim period reflects the cortisol response during the first 20-minute period. Participants did not interact with their cell phones or each other during this interim period.

During the second 20-minute period, “T2,” subjects were again asked to use their personal cell phones for 20 minutes to view either _YouTube_ or _Social Media_; this selection alternated from the subject’s first treatment, so that each subject completed both treatments but in random order. Following this 20-minute cell phone activity, a third saliva sample (“Final”) was collected, after which participants completed an online demographic and psychological survey via google forms (see Psychological measures). Surveys were administered at the end of our data collection to avoid the possibility that the surveys would themselves cause stress and influence our results. We chose 20-minute experimental periods because several studies have shown that salivary cortisol peaks 20 minutes after a psychological stressor [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref050)–[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref052)]. Heart rate monitors were collected from participants after they completed the questionnaires. [Fig 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.g001) provides a schematic of the overall study design, indicating the study periods and the identifying terms used throughout this article.

### Physiological measures

To evaluate subjects’ physiological responses, both heart rate and salivary cortisol levels were measured. Subjects wore Polar OH1 (Polar Electro Oy, Finland) optical heart rate sensors around their upper arm to continuously record heart rate for the duration of the experiment. These sensors utilize photoplethysmography technology to determine heart rate and have a sampling rate of 50Hz.

Using time records, heart rate data were encoded to match the study periods described in [Fig 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.g001). We calculated the average heart rate from the final five minutes prior to T1 and T2 and identified them as the Baseline and Interim periods, respectively. For T1 and T2, we used the average heart rate from the full 20 minutes of each period. Unreported comparisons based on the last five minutes of all periods yielded no change in the results.

Subjects provided saliva samples before the first cell phone treatment and immediately after each of the two treatments. To collect saliva, subjects placed absorbent swabs (SalivaBio Oral Swabs, Salimetrics; State College, PA) in their mouths for 2 minutes and then removed and sealed the swabs in purposely designed tubes. Swabs were centrifuged and the resulting saliva samples (approximately 1ml) were frozen at -20°C for up to one week before analysis. Salivary free cortisol was measured using a commercially available enzyme immunoassay kit (Salivary Cortisol ELISA Kit, Salimetrics) [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref041)].

All samples, standards, and controls were run in duplicate, and the manufacturer’s protocol was followed without modification. A standard curve was run with each assay, as were high and low standards (provided with the kit). Briefly, cortisol in the provided standards and in our unknown samples competed with cortisol conjugated to horseradish peroxidase for binding sites on capture antibodies (bound to the microtiter plate). After an incubation and wash step, tetramethylbenzidine was added and changed color when it reacted with the horseradish peroxidase (conjugated to cortisol). The amount of color change, quantified by a plate reader (Bio-Rad, iMark Microplate Absorbance Reader; Hercules, CA), was inversely proportional to the amount of cortisol present in the unknown samples. Data reduction software provided with the plate reader was used to interpolate our data using a 4-parameter non-linear regression curve fit. The lower limit of sensitivity for this assay was 0.007μg/dl, and the inter-assay variation was 5.6% and 5.4% for high and low controls, respectively. Intra-assay variation ranged from 2.3–5.4%. All indicate acceptable limits of variation. The cortisol antiserum cross-reacts with dexamethasone (19.2%), but all other cross-reactivity values were less than 0.6%. To stabilize the variance, the base 10 logarithm of cortisol was used in data analysis [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref053)].

### Psychological measures

Because psychological factors can influence one’s physiological response [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref054)], we surveyed participants about their social media use, self-esteem, tendency to make social comparisons, and their ongoing stress, using validated and widely used assessments ([Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.t002)). These factors were examined because they could alter the relationship between the physiological stress response and cell phone activities in this study. Assessments were self-reported with personal cell phones via Google Forms, following saliva sampling in the “Final” period (see [Fig 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.g001)), and scale outcomes were calculated as defined by their developers. To avoid the possibility that thoughts of stress prompted by the Perceived Stress Scale could influence responses on other scales, this was the last scale to be administered. Scales are briefly described in [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.t002), and additional details can be found in the [S2 Appendix](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.s002).

Table 2. Validated psychological scales used in our study to quantify psychosocial factors.

| Psychological Scale | Measures: | Reference |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Intensity of Social Media Use (Facebook Intensity Scale; Instagram Intensity Scale) | Participants’ engagement with the platforms with respect to their number of “friends,” daily time engagement, emotional investment, and extent to which one’s daily activities are integrated with the platform | [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref055),[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref056)] |
| Self-Esteem Scale | Feelings of self-worth and self-acceptance | [[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref057)] |
| Social Comparison Scale | Self-perception of social rank, relative attractiveness, and acceptance within one’s social group, as pertains to social media | [[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref056),[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref058)] |

Additional details in the [S2 Appendix](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.s002).

### Statistical analysis

Using 2-group t-tests, we confirmed equality of the two groups (_Social Media then YouTube_ and _YouTube then Social Media_) for age, psychological measures, and baseline measures of heart rate and cortisol. We confirmed our groups were similar in terms of sex and social media preference using chi-square tests. Because we randomly assigned individuals to group order, this assessment was necessary to ensure group equality on these key elements.

We confirmed a lack of carryover from the first 20-minute period to the second following standard protocol [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref043),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref044)]. We fit a repeated measures model in a mixed model framework, incorporating fixed factors of treatment group (order), period, their interaction, and random effect of participant. We then added each potential moderator (sex, age, and the four psychological measures) to the model to examine whether there was a change in the observed relationship between the treatments and physiological stress response; moderators were added independently and were not combined into a single model. We used self-reported sex and discretized age as under 25 years (“digital natives” who have grown up with social media) and 25 years or older. In the event of statistical significance in the 3-way interaction, we used model-based estimates of the outcomes at selected values of the moderator to better understand these interactions. Based on the model results (indicating a significant effect of period), we explicitly tested for a treatment effect on heart rate and cortisol using only the first 20-minute period in a two-group t-test. We adjusted for multiplicity using the false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref060)].

All statistical models used were evaluated for appropriateness with residual plots, including whether there were differences in mean response or variance among the study days. Statistical significance was defined as p (or adjusted p) ≤ 0.05. Linear modeling was completed with SAS 9.4 and all other descriptive statistics and plotting were completed in R version 4.0.2 [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref061)] using the _tidyverse_ library [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref062)] in the RStudio IDE [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref063)].

Men and women were equally likely to use Facebook or Instagram (χ 2 1 = 0.240, p = 0.624), but on average those using Facebook were older than those using Instagram regardless of group (T 36.2 = 4.36, p<0.001; Facebook mean age 33.6 (2.5), Instagram mean age 21.5 (1.2)).

Considering the statistically significant period effect and non-significant interaction between treatment order and period, we directly compared heart rate and cortisol responses between cell phone treatments during T1 only. There were no significant differences in mean heart rate (T 153 = -0.22, p = 0.827) or cortisol (T 106 = 0.40, p = 0.687) between those viewing Social Media and YouTube during the T1 period.

We separately added sex and age to our models examining the effects of order and period (as indicated by a 3-way interaction) and found that neither heart rate nor cortisol responses were moderated by participants’ sex (heart rate p = 0.361, cortisol p = 0.442) or age (heart rate = 0.545, cortisol p = 0.837). Next, we considered the moderating effects of social media platform (Facebook or Instagram) and psychological measures (as described in [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.t002)) on heart rate and cortisol measurements. We found only a single significant 3-way interaction when examining the moderating effect of Intensity of Social Media Use on cortisol (F 2,100 = 3.15, p = 0.047). High Intensity of Social Media use was associated with elevated cortisol at the baseline experimental period among those in the _Social Media then YouTube_ group. As this only affects measurements before the experiment occurs, and doesn’t reflect our experimental conditions, we do not believe it is relevant to our study conclusions and do not discuss it further.

### Data availability statement

Accession numbers and/or DOIs will be made available after acceptance and title and abstract have been accepted by reviewers.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243)Discussion

Because of concerns surrounding the pervasive use of social media, we set out to examine whether social media provokes a physiological stress response. The crossover design of our experiment allowed us to differentiate the effect of our social media treatment from the effect of treatment period, and we found a period effect but no treatment effect. Among those participating in our study, 20 minutes of social media use did not elicit a physiological stress response and instead, the use of smartphones seemed to reduce activity of the sympathetic nervous system and HPA axis. Further, despite evidence of sex and age-specific differences in digital media use and psychological well-being [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref064)], we found no evidence of age or sex modifying the physiological responses to our smartphone treatments. Additionally, neither psychological traits nor habits of social media use modified the physiological responses in our experiment. We were surprised by these findings because a growing body of literature suggests that excessive smartphone use, and social media use in particular, is detrimental to mental and physical health [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref010),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref016),[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref065)]. We expected to find that social media use would trigger a measurable physiological stress response and that this might help explain its contribution to psychiatric and physical morbidities. Instead, our findings seem to lend credence to the suggestion [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref036),[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref037)] that accessing social media (and in the case of our study, YouTube) acts to assuage stress.

Nevertheless, despite the absence of a physiological stress response to our social media treatment, our findings do not preclude the possibility that social media use induces psychological stress as has been frequently posited [[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref066)–[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref068)]. Among studies examining the physiological response to psychological stressors, some have elicited robust physiological responses [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref069)–[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref071)], while other studies fail to find an association [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref026),[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref072)]. These contradictory findings may be explained by variations in the cognitive appraisal of a stressor; some perceptions of stress are more likely to elicit a physiological response than others [[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref070),[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref073),[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref074)]. Specifically, stressors that are appraised as _uncontrollable_, _novel_, _challenging_, and/or _threatening_ are most likely to activate the HPA axis and sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system [[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref073)]. When stressors are appraised in this way, the situation may be perceived as requiring extra resources and thus physiological and behavioral modification are initiated to help provide these resources. In reference to the findings in our study, content viewed for 20 minutes on smartphones may not have been appraised as uncontrollable, novel, challenging, or threatening and thus did not provoke a physiological stress response.

Mobile devices are _controllable_ and are not _novel_. While cell phone alerts solicit attention, users can control the amount and type of information disseminated in their feeds. Further, cell phones have lost their novelty and are ubiquitous in our culture. Perhaps when cell phones were novel their use prompted a physiological response, but more recently this response has become habituated, such that a diminished physiological response occurs with repeated exposure to the same stimulus [[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref075),[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref076)]. Our participants may have been habituated individuals using their cell phones in the manner to which they have become accustomed. Consequently, a physiological stress response was not provoked by our experimental treatment.

When we gave our study instructions, fitted heart rate monitors, and collected saliva samples, we may have inadvertently introduced a sense of novelty and uncontrollability, which has been shown to elicit a physiological stress response [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref077)–[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref079)]. This could explain the relatively higher heart rate during the Baseline and Interim study periods than during the cell phone treatment periods; the sympathetic nervous system seemed to be more active during periods of smartphone abstinence than during periods of smartphone use. Similar findings have been reported by Johnshoy et al. [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref037)] and Rus and Tiemensma [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref036)] who found that social media use on personal devices attenuated the physiological stress response to an acute stressor (Trier Social Stress Test). It may be that contact with smartphones offers a form of social support, even if an individual does not interact with members of one’s social group through social media. Access to the phone itself may be a reassuring comfort in times of uncertainty.

Social media and YouTube may not have been perceived as _challenging_ or _threatening_. While we did not directly survey feelings of challenge or threat, we surmise our social comparison and self-esteem scales offer insight into such emotions. Those who consistently rank themselves as inferior on the social comparison scale may have felt threatened by online interactions with their “friends,” and those who ranked themselves as superior might have felt challenged. Similarly, it can be assumed that those with low self-esteem may have felt more challenged or threatened by social media than those with higher self-esteem. Studies have suggested that threats to the social self (i.e. situations that could lead to rejection of an individual’s self-worth) often result in psychobiological responses, including HPA axis and cardiovascular activation [[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref070),[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10990243#pone.0298553.ref071)]. args.summary:
This scientific study published in PLOS ONE (2024) by Oppenheimer et al. investigated whether social media use elicits a physiological stress response. The study involved 59 participants (aged 13-55) in a crossover design where each subject experienced both 20-minute sessions of social media browsing (Facebook/Instagram) and viewing a non-evocative YouTube playlist. Researchers measured heart rate (autonomic nervous system) and salivary cortisol (HPA axis activity) as biomarkers of stress.

Key findings:
- No significant physiological stress response was detected from social media use compared to the YouTube control.
- A significant period effect was observed: both heart rate and cortisol decreased over the duration of the experiment regardless of treatment type.
- Neither age, sex, social media habits, nor psychological measures (self-esteem, social comparison, perceived stress, social media intensity) moderated the physiological response.
- Heart rate declined an average of 7.3 BPM from baseline to the second treatment period.
- The sympathetic nervous system appeared more active during periods of smartphone abstinence than during smartphone use.

The authors suggest that the controllability, familiarity, and non-threatening nature of social media may explain the absence of a stress response, and that smartphone use may actually act to assuage stress rather than provoke it. However, they note this does not preclude the possibility that social media induces psychological stress, as the cognitive appraisal of stressors influences whether a physiological response occurs.

## Abstract

### Background

Smartphone screen time has risen sharply in recent years. Even though an association between smartphone use and mental health is well documented, it is still unclear whether this is simply a correlation or causality. The aim of this study is to investigate the effects of smartphone screen time reduction on mental health indicators.

### Methods

This non-blinded, parallel randomized controlled trial (RCT) was performed to investigate the impact of a 3-week screen time reduction to ≤ 2 h/d in healthy students on stress (PSQ), well-being (WHO-5), depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), and sleep quality (ISI) at baseline (t0), post-intervention (t1), and at follow-up (t2 = 6 weeks after t1). For the intention to treat analysis, repeated measures ANOVAs and post-hoc tests (for time as well as group differences) were performed and effect sizes were presented as partial eta squared (η 2 = time × group) and group-mean differences.

### Results

In total, 111 out of 125 healthy students (70 females; mean age = 22.68 ± 2.6 years; mean screen time = 276 ± 115.1 min/day) were randomly assigned to intervention—(_n_ = 58; 3 weeks of screen time reduction to ≤ 2 h/day) or control group (_n_ = 53). Although no differences were observed at baseline (t0), significant post-intervention (t1) effects of small to medium size were observed on well-being (η 2 = .053), depressive symptoms (η 2 = .109), sleep quality (η 2 = .048), and stress (η 2 = .085). Significant group differences (_p_ ≤ .05) were found post-intervention (t1) for depressive symptoms (_Mean Difference_ (_MD)_ = 2.11, _Standard Error_ (_SE)_ = 0.63, 95% _Confidence Interval_ (CI) [0.87, 3.36]), sleep quality (_MD_ = 2.59, _SE_ = 0.97, 95% CI [0.66, 4.51]), well-being (_MD_ = -1.54, _SE_ = 0.68, 95% CI [.-2.89, -0.18]), and stress (_MD_ = 6.91, _SE_ = 3.48, 95% CI [0.01, 13.81]). Screen time increased rapidly after the intervention and at follow-up the values were once again approaching the initial level.

### Conclusions

The study highlights mental health improvements through smartphone screen time reduction. Three weeks of screen time reduction showed small to medium effect sizes on depressive symptoms, stress, sleep quality, and well-being. The results suggest a causal relationship, rather than a merely correlative one, between daily smartphone screen time and mental health.

### Trial registration

The study was preregistered on Open Science Framework (trial registration number: A9K76) on November 8, 2023.
