## Background

Smartphones have become an integral part of our everyday lives. Worldwide, 5.6 billion people own a smartphone and almost 5 billion use social media sites. This indicates an increase of over 200 million in the last year alone [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR1 "Kemp S. Digital 2023: Global overview report. In: DataReportal. 2023. 
                  https://datareportal.com/reports/digital-2023-global-overview-report
                  
                . Accessed 18 Dec 2023.")]. Daily smartphone screen time has risen sharply in recent years with an average daily screen time of 3 h and 46 min [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR2 "Moody R. Screen time statistics: Average screen time in US vs. the rest of the world. In: Comparitech. 2023. 
                  https://www.comparitech.com/tv-streaming/screen-time-statistics/
                  
                . Accessed 6 March 2024.")]. In Austria, 38% of adolescents use their phones five or more hours per day [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR3 "Felder-Puig R, Teutsch F, Winkler R. Gesundheit und Gesundheitsverhalten von österreichischen Schülerinnen und Schülern. Ergebnisse des WHO-HBSC-Survey 2021/22. BMSGPK; 2023; 1–107.")].

Intensive smartphone use reflects the high utility of smartphones in modern society. Evidence also suggests positive effects of smartphone use, such as increased social connectedness among social media users [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR4 "Jensen M, George MJ, Russell MR, Odgers CL. Young adolescents’ digital technology use and mental health symptoms: Little evidence of longitudinal or daily linkages. Clin Psychol Sci. 2019. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/2167702619859336
                  
                .")] and providing a platform for exchange among minorized groups [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR5 "Madden M, Calvin A, Hasse A. A double-edged sword: How diverse communities of young people think about the multifaceted relationship between social media and mental health. In: common sense; 2024. 
                  https://www.commonsensemedia.org/sites/default/files/research/report/2024-double-edged-sword-hopelab-report_final-release-for-web-v2.pdf
                  
                "), [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR6 "Berger MN, Taba M, Marino JL, Lim MSC, Skinner SR. Social media use and health and well-being of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer youth: Systematic review. J Med Internet Res. 2022. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2196/38449
                  
                .")]. Furthermore, individuals with mental health issues have reported finding distraction through positive smartphone content beneficial [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR7 "Rideout V, Fox S, Well Being Trust. Digital health practices, social media use, and mental well-being among teens and young adults in the U.S. In: HOPELAB; 2018. 
                  https://digitalcommons.providence.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2092&context=publications
                  
                . Accessed 18 December 2024.")], and improvements in mood have been observed following increased use of entertainment apps [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR8 "Rodman AM, Burns JA, Cotter GK, Ohashi Y-GB, Rich RK, McLaughlin KA. Within-person fluctuations in objective smartphone use and emotional processes during adolescence: An intensive longitudinal study. Affect Sci. 2024; 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s42761-024-00247-z
                  
                .")]. Nevertheless, an increasing number of studies report negative effects associated with intensive smartphone use. A large-scale study (> 1 million adolescents) found that more time on screens is associated with lower psychological well-being [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR9 "Twenge JM, Martin GN, Campbell WK. Decreases in psychological well-being among American adolescents after 2012 and links to screen time during the rise of smartphone technology. Emotion. 2018; 
                  https://doi.org/10.1037/emo0000403
                  
                .")]. Numerous cross-sectional studies discovered that smartphone use was significantly associated with mental health symptoms with a gradually higher prevalence of psychological symptoms with each hour of daily screen time (e.g. [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR10 "Pieh C, Plener PL, Probst T, Dale R, Humer E. Assessment of mental health of high school students during social distancing and remote schooling during the COVID-19 pandemic in Austria. JAMA Netw Open. 2021. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2021.14866
                  
                ."),[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR11 "Humer E, Gächter A, Dale R, Probst T, Pieh C. The association of health behaviors and mental health during COVID-19. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2022. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2022.06.001
                  
                ."),[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR12 "Humer E, Probst T, Wagner-Skacel J, Pieh C. Association of health behaviors with mental health problems in more than 7000 adolescents during COVID-19. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2022. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19159072
                  
                ."),[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR13 "Woo KS, Bong SH, Choi TY, Kim JW. Mental health, smartphone use type, and screen time among adolescents in South Korea. Psychol Res Behav Manag. 2021. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2147/prbm.S324235
                  
                ."),[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR14 "Mayerhofer D, Haider K, Amon M, Gächter A, O’Rourke T, Dale R, Humer E, Probst T, Pieh C. The association between problematic smartphone use and mental health in Austrian adolescents and young adults. Healthcare. 2024. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/healthcare12060600
                  
                .")],). However, these studies as well as the majority of research in this field are cross-sectional [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR15 "Orben A. Teenagers, screens and social media: A narrative review of reviews and key studies. Soc Psychiatry Psychiatr Epidemiol. 2020. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s00127-019-01825-4
                  
                .")] and causal interaction remains unclear. Longitudinal, naturalistic studies observed screen time, mental health, and possible mutual changes over time. A study found that frequent social media use predicted later poor mental health and well-being [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR16 "Russell MV, Gireesh A, Stiglic N, Hudson LD, Goddings A-L, Ward JL, Nicholls DE. Roles of cyberbullying, sleep, and physical activity in mediating the effects of social media use on mental health and wellbeing among young people in England: a secondary analysis of longitudinal data. Lancet Child Adolesc Health. 2019. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/S2352-4642(19)30186-5
                  
                .")]. Given the topic’s relevance, well-founded interventional studies are only sparsely represented. A systematic review found an association between screen time in general and depressive symptoms [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR17 "Tang S, Werner-Seidler A, Torok M, Mackinnon AJ, Christensen H. The relationship between screen time and mental health in young people: A systematic review of longitudinal studies. Clin Psychol Rev. 2021. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2021.102021
                  
                .")]. A large-scale longitudinal study from the UK on more than 12,000 young people found that frequent social media use predicted later poor mental health and well-being [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR16 "Russell MV, Gireesh A, Stiglic N, Hudson LD, Goddings A-L, Ward JL, Nicholls DE. Roles of cyberbullying, sleep, and physical activity in mediating the effects of social media use on mental health and wellbeing among young people in England: a secondary analysis of longitudinal data. Lancet Child Adolesc Health. 2019. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/S2352-4642(19)30186-5
                  
                .")]. Further, a review of 13 reviews found moderately strong evidence for an association between screen time and depressive symptoms [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR18 "Stiglic N, Russell MV. Effects of screentime on the health and well-being of children and adolescents: A systematic review of reviews. BMJ Open. 2019. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-023191
                  
                .")]. A review on the use of mobile phones or wireless devices found limited evidence that such usage may be associated with poorer mental health in children and adolescents [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR19 "Girela-Serrano BM, Spiers ADV, Ruotong L, Gangadia S, Toledano MB, Di Simplicio M. Impact of mobile phones and wireless devices use on children and adolescents’ mental health: A systematic review. Eur Child Adolesc Psychiatry. 2024. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-022-02012-8
                  
                .")]. In addition, the importance of considering the purpose of use is indicated, since smartphone screentime appears to be detrimental to mental health from as little as two hours per day, depending on the purpose of use, and from four hours, regardless of the usage purpose [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR13 "Woo KS, Bong SH, Choi TY, Kim JW. Mental health, smartphone use type, and screen time among adolescents in South Korea. Psychol Res Behav Manag. 2021. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2147/prbm.S324235
                  
                .")].

Despite the relevance of the topic, well-designed interventional studies are only sparsely represented. A systematic review found only 12 randomized clinical trials (RCTs) on digital detox and mental health with a variety of different designs, interventions, sample sizes, or measurements. Even though there were consistent effects for depressive symptoms, the results were otherwise inconsistent [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR20 "Radtke T, Apel T, Schenkel K, Keller J, von Lindern E. Digital detox: An effective solution in the smartphone era? A systematic literature review. Mob Media Commun. 2021. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/20501579211028647
                  
                .")]. Positive effects are also evident for appearance- and weight-esteem after three weeks of reduced social media time [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR21 "Thai H, Davis CG, Mahboob W, Perry S, Adams A, Goldfield GS. Reducing social media use improves appearance and weight esteem in youth with emotional distress. Psychol Pop Media. 2024. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1037/ppm0000460
                  
                .")].

## Methods

The present study aimed to investigate the effect of smartphone screen time reduction on mental health indicators. The primary a priori hypothesis was that mental health would improve after the intervention compared to the control group as well as compared to baseline.

### Registration

The ‘Digital Detox Study’ ([https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/A9K76](https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/A9K76)) followed the CONSORT guidelines for randomized trials [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR22 "Schulz KF, Altman DG, Moher D. CONSORT 2010 statement: Updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomized trials. Ann Intern Med. 2010; 
                  https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-152-11-201006010-00232
                  
                .")]. The protocol was registered on November 8, 2023, at Open Science Framework (OSF) [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR23 "Digital detox study. 
                  https://osf.io/a9k76
                  
                . Accessed 8 Oct 2024.")] prior to enrollment and aligned with the required data set of the World Health Organization’s International Clinical Trials Registry Platform [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR24 "WHO Trial Registration Data Set (Version 1.3.1). 
                  https://www.who.int/clinical-trials-registry-platform/network/who-data-set
                  
                . Accessed 7 March 2024.")]. In addition, the study was retrospectively registered to ClinicalTrials.gov on 19 March 2024 to comply with the criteria of the International Committee of Medical Journal Editor [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR25 "Digital Detox Study: A randomized controlled trial. 
                  https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06353451?cond=digital%20detox&rank=1
                  
                . Accessed 8 Oct 2024.")].

### Hypothesis

The primary hypothesis was that mental health indicators, particularly stress, depressive symptoms, and sleep quality; would improve throughout the intervention compared to the control group as well as to baseline. No hypothesis was stated regarding follow-up effects.

### Study design

The study was promoted via on-site information events in Krems, Austria, social media, and university notices. The inclusion criteria were: healthy students aged 18–29 years, owning a smartphone and using it at least 3 h per day, with no diagnosed or treated mental disorder, and no ongoing psychotherapy or psychopharmacological treatment. Moderately elevated levels in mental health questionnaires were not reasons for exclusion. After enrollment and screening for eligibility (November 10, 2023), participants were randomized to the control or intervention group using the method of simple randomization provided the ESMira app [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR26 "Lewetz D, Stieger S. ESMira. A decentralized open-source application for collecting experience sampling data. Behav Res Methods. 2023; 
                  https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-023-02194-2
                  
                .")], which is based on a random number generator, like a coin toss, ensuring true randomness. They were informed of their group allocation via message in ESMira before the intervention, without prior access to it. Smartphone screen time was assessed weekly for both groups. Following a 10-day baseline phase to monitor the participants’ smartphone screen time and physical activity, mental health indicators were measured at baseline (t0; November 19, 2023), after 3 weeks of intervention (t1; December 12, 2023), and at follow-up (t2; January 21, 2024).

The intervention group received a fitness tracker to track physical activity during baseline and intervention phase.

After baseline (t0), the intervention group reduced smartphone screen time (≤ 2 h/d) for three consecutive weeks, while the control group continued using their smartphones as usual for the entire study duration (parallel design, no blinding). The two-hour limit was selected based on a study involving over 7000 adolescents in Austria, which found a significantly higher incidence of depressive symptoms or stress, with three to four hours of daily smartphone use, while one to two hours of usage showed no difference compared to the control group (< 1 h) [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR12 "Humer E, Probst T, Wagner-Skacel J, Pieh C. Association of health behaviors with mental health problems in more than 7000 adolescents during COVID-19. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2022. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19159072
                  
                .")]. A Korean study also found that smartphone use of two or more hours per day, depending on the type of use, was associated with negative effects on mental health [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR13 "Woo KS, Bong SH, Choi TY, Kim JW. Mental health, smartphone use type, and screen time among adolescents in South Korea. Psychol Res Behav Manag. 2021. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2147/prbm.S324235
                  
                .")]. Screen time limiters were recommended, but not obligatory. After the intervention, no further requirements were imposed on screen time (see Additional file 1: Fig. [A2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#Fig2)). The control group was offered participation in the intervention after follow-up (cross-over), to minimize dropouts and missing items.

### Data collection and randomization

After signing an informed consent form, participants joined the study in the ESMira [[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR27 "Software: ESMira. 
                  https://www.kl.ac.at/de/universitaet/wissenschaftliche-organisationseinheiten/fachbereich-psychologische-methodenlehre-7
                  
                . Accessed 7 March 2024.")] app via QR code. All data collection procedures, including randomization, communication, questionnaire completion, and screenshot uploads were conducted with the app. Randomization of ESMira works autonomously and is impervious to external influences.

### Smartphone screen time

Smartphone screen time was assessed weekly in both groups using the smartphones’ built-in screen time measurements. Each Monday, participants were prompted to upload a screenshot of their screen time from the previous week (Monday to Sunday).

### Mental health indicators

Mental health indicators were evaluated in both groups at baseline (t0), post-intervention (t1), and follow-up (t2). Participants were reminded to complete the questionnaires via push notifications every Sunday.

In addition to the a priori-defined main outcomes (depression, well-being, stress, sleep), additional measures were collected to determine baseline differences between the groups and to detect possible further effects of screen time reduction on mental health.

#### Main outcomes

### Well-being (WHO-5)

The validated German version of the World Health Organization well-being questionnaire (WHO-5) was used to measure well-being with five self-rating items [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR28 "Brähler E, Mühlan H, Albani C, Schmidt S. Teststatistische Prüfung und Normierung der deutschen Versionen des EUROHIS-QOL Lebensqualität-Index und des WHO-5 Wohlbefindens-Index. Diagnostica. 2007. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1026/0012-1924.53.2.83
                  
                ."), [29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR29 "Topp CW, Østergaard SD, Søndergaard S, Bech P. The WHO-5 Well-Being Index: A systematic review of the literature. Psychother Psychosom. 2015. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1159/000376585
                  
                .")]. Scores range from 0 (no well-being) to 25 points (maximal well-being). Cronbach’s alphas were: t0: α = 0.75, t1: α = 0.78, t2: α = 0.82.

### Depressive symptoms (PHQ-9)

Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR30 "Kroenke K, Spitzer RL, Williams JB. The PHQ-9: Validity of a brief depression severity measure. J Gen Intern Med. 2001. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1525-1497.2001.016009606.x
                  
                .")] in the validated German version [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR31 "Löwe B, Spitzer RL, Gräfe K, Kroenke K, Quenter A, Zipfel S, Buchholz C, Witte S, Herzog W. Comparative validity of three screening questionnaires for DSM-IV depressive disorders and physicians’ diagnoses. J Affect Disord. 2004. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-0327(02)00237-9
                  
                .")]. The PHQ-9 contains nine self-rating items on a four-point scale ranging from 0 (“not at all”) to 3 (“nearly every day”), resulting in a total score from 0 to 27. Cronbach’s alphas were: t0: α = 0.76, t1: α = 0.75, t2: α = 0.81.

### Stress (PSQ-20)

Stress was evaluated with the German version [[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR32 "Fliege H, Rose M, Arck P, Levenstein S, Klapp BF. PSQ - Perceived Stress Questionnaire. In: Leibniz Institute for Psychology – Open Test Archive; 2009."), [33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR33 "Fliege H, Rose M, Arck P, Walter OB, Kocalevent R-D, Weber C, Klapp BF. The Perceived Stress Questionnaire (PSQ) Reconsidered: Validation and reference values from different clinical and healthy adult samples. Psychosom Med. 2005. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1097/01.psy.0000151491.80178.78
                  
                .")] of the 20-item short form of the Perceived Stress Questionnaire (PSQ-20) [[34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR34 "Levenstein S, Prantera C, Varvo V, Scribano ML, Berto E, Luzi C, Andreoli A. Development of the perceived stress questionnaire: A new tool for psychosomatic research. J Psychosom Res. 1993. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-3999(93)90120-5
                  
                .")]. Each item is rated from almost never (= 1) to usually (= 4), with a transformed sum score from 0 to 100. Cronbach’s alphas were: t0: α = 0.93, t1: α = 0.93, t2: α = 0.94.

### Sleep quality (ISI)

Sleep quality was measured using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR35 "Morin CM, Belleville G, Bélanger L, Ivers H. The Insomnia Severity Index: Psychometric indicators to detect insomnia cases and evaluate treatment response. Sleep. 2011. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/34.5.601
                  
                ."), [36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR36 "Bastien CH, Vallières A, Morin CM. Validation of the Insomnia Severity Index as an outcome measure for insomnia research. Sleep Med. 2001. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/s1389-9457(00)00065-4
                  
                .")] in its validated German version [[37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR37 "Gerber M, Lang C, Lemola S, Colledge F, Kalak N, Holsboer-Trachsler E, Pühse U, Brand S. Validation of the German version of the Insomnia Severity Index in adolescents, young adults and adult workers: Results from three cross-sectional studies. BMC Psychiatry. 2016. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-016-0876-8
                  
                .")]. The ISI comprises 7 self-reported items, each rated on a scale from 0 to 4, resulting in sum scores from 0 to 28. Cronbach’s alphas were: t0: α = 0.81, t1: α = 0.83, t2: α = 0.87.

#### Additional outcomes

### Problematic smartphone use (SAS-SV)

Problematic smartphone use was measured using the validated German [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR38 "Haug S, Castro RP, Kwon M, Filler A, Kowatsch T, Schaub MP. Smartphone use and smartphone addiction among young people in Switzerland. J Behav Addict. 2015. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1556/2006.4.2015.037
                  
                .")] short version of the Smartphone Addiction Scale (SAS-SV) [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR39 "Kwon M, Kim D-J, Cho H, Yang S. The Smartphone Addiction Scale: Development and validation of a short version for adolescents. PLoS ONE. 2013. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0083558
                  
                .")]. The 10 items address the following content areas: daily-life disturbance, withdrawal, cyberspace-oriented relationship, overuse, and tolerance. Cronbach’s alphas were t0: α = 0.84, t1: α = 0.87, t2: α = 0.89.

### Anxiety symptoms (GAD-7)

The German version [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR40 "Löwe B, Decker O, Müller S, Brähler E, Schellberg D, Herzog W, Herzberg PY. Validation and standardization of the Generalized Anxiety Disorder Screener (GAD-7) in the general population. Med Care. 2008. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1097/MLR.0b013e318160d093
                  
                .")] of the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7 scale (GAD-7) [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR41 "Spitzer RL, Kroenke K, Williams JB, Löwe B. A brief measure for assessing generalized anxiety disorder: The GAD-7. Arch Intern Med. 2006. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1001/archinte.166.10.1092
                  
                .")] was used to measure anxiety symptoms with 7 self-rating items on a four-point scale, from 0 to 3 (maximum score 21). Cronbach’s alphas for anxiety were t0: α = 0.83, t1: α = 0.87, t2: α = 0.87.

### Eating disorder (SCOFF)

We used the validated German version [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR42 "Richter F, Strauss B, Braehler E, Adametz L, Berger U. Screening disordered eating in a representative sample of the German population: Usefulness and psychometric properties of the German SCOFF questionnaire. Eat Behav. 2017. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eatbeh.2016.06.022
                  
                ."), [43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR43 "Richter F, Strauß B, Berger U. Deutschsprachige Kurzskalen zur Erfassung auffälligen Essverhaltens. PPmP-Psychother Psychosom Med Psychol. 2018. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0043-106433
                  
                .")] of the screening tool SCOFF (Sick, Control, One stone, Fat, Food) [[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR44 "Morgan JF, Reid F, Lacey JH. The SCOFF questionnaire: Assessment of a new screening tool for eating disorders. BMJ. 1999. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.319.7223.1467
                  
                .")] to assess relevant symptoms of eating disorders (anorexia and bulimia nervosa). Five items can be answered with “yes” = 1 or “no” = 0. The total score ranges from 0 to 5. A total score of 2 or above indicates disordered eating. Cronbach’s alphas were: t0: α = 0.64, t1: α = 0.37, t2: α = 0.46.

### Body Appreciation (BAS-2)

To examine the respondents’ body image, we used the validated German version [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR45 "Behrend N, Warschburger P. Validation of a German version of the Body Appreciation Scale-2 (BAS-2). Body Image. 2022. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bodyim.2022.01.020
                  
                .")] of the Body Appreciation Scale-2 (BAS-2) [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR46 "Tylka TL, Wood-Barcalow NL. The Body Appreciation Scale-2: Item refinement and psychometric evaluation. Body Image. 2015. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bodyim.2014.09.006
                  
                .")]. The scale is comprised of 10 items, which can be rated from “never” (1) to “always” (5). Higher scores indicate a more positive body appreciation. Cronbach’s alphas were: t0 α = 0.94, t1: α = 0.94, t2: α = 0.95.

### Activity measurement

Physical activity estimates were collected as part of the screening for eligibility (i.e. number of days per week with 60 or more minutes of physical activity per day; see Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#Tab1)). Furthermore, during both the baseline and intervention phase, the intervention group (but not the control group) used fitness trackers (Fitbit Inspire 3) to objectively assess physical activity. The fitness trackers were worn to monitor the potential influence of increased physical activity on mental health outcomes more accurately than self-reported data. Moderate to very high intense physical activity in minutes per day was documented.

**Table 1 Characteristics of the study sample and differences between the intervention and control group**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z/tables/1)

### Incentives

Participants were allowed to keep the fitness tracker after completing the study (value: € 99,-).

### Sample size

Assuming small to medium effects (Cohen’s _d_ = 0.45, power 0.8, significance level < 0.05, icc = 0.05), a minimum of 40 people per group was needed to complete the post-intervention assessment (t1). Considering a drop-out rate of 20%, at least 50 people per group were recruited.

### Statistics

We used the statistic software IBM SPSS Statistics Version 29 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) [[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR47 "IBM Corp. IMB SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 29.0. 2022.")] to analyze the data. χ 2-Test and independent samples t-tests were used to examine differences at baseline regarding age, gender, smartphone screen time, physical activity, and mental health indicators between the control and intervention group.

To examine the effect of reduced smartphone screen time on mental health indicators, repeated measurements ANOVAs (rm-ANOVA) were applied. The primary hypotheses focused on the difference between t0 (baseline) and t1 (post-intervention) in the intervention group and on the difference between control group and intervention group (intention-to-treat analysis). In a secondary analysis, the follow-up time point (t2) was also included (however, no a priori hypothesis was stated). The follow-up was 6 weeks after t1 and 12 weeks after enrollment. Group allocation (control vs. intervention) was the between-group factor. Time was the within-group factor (t0, t1, t2). A subgroup analysis (rm-ANOVA) of those, who strictly adhered to the ≤ 2 h smartphone screen time limit was also performed (per-protocol analysis).

In case of baseline group differences, these variables were added as covariates in the rm-ANOVA. In the original pre-registration, we planned to include physical activity as a covariate. However, since there were no baseline differences between the two groups, we did not include it. If the sphericity assumption was violated, the conservative Greenhouse–Geisser correction was applied. In the post hoc tests, Bonferroni correction was applied to adjust for multiple comparisons. Missing values (missing completely at random; Little’s MCAR-test: χ 2 = 259.38, _df_ = 283, _p_ = 0.840; t0: 2.7%, t1: 5.9%, t2: 13.5%) were dealt with via maximum likelihood estimation. Maximum likelihood estimation utilizes all available information from the observed data, including partially complete cases and it seems more precise than the other estimations, especially under “missing at random” assumption. The parameters are chosen to maximize the likelihood that the assumed model results in the observed data. This contrasts with other methods like listwise deletion (Complete Case Analysis), which only consider fully observed cases. Percentage changes in the main outcomes between baseline and post-intervention were calculated for the intervention group [[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR48 "Hurst H, Bolton J. Assessing the clinical significance of change scores recorded on subjective outcome measures. J Manip Physiol Ther. 2004. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmpt.2003.11.003
                  
                .")]. Effect sizes were presented as partial eta squared (η 2 = time × group) and group-mean differences. The value of η 2 ranges from 0 to 1 and can be interpreted as small- (η 2 ≈ 0.01), medium- (η 2 ≈ 0.06), and large effects (η 2 ≈ 0.14) [[49](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR49 "Cohen J. Statistical power for the behavioral sciences. 2nd ed. New York: Routledge; 1988.")].

### Ethics

The study was conducted according to the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki [[50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR50 "World Medical Association. World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki: Ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects. JAMA. 2013. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2013.281053
                  
                .")] and CONSORT guidelines for non-pharmacological trials [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#ref-CR22 "Schulz KF, Altman DG, Moher D. CONSORT 2010 statement: Updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomized trials. Ann Intern Med. 2010; 
                  https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-152-11-201006010-00232
                  
                .")]. The university’s ethics committee approved the study protocol on October 23, 2023 (number: EK GZ 67/2021–2024). Although the study was preregistered on Open Science Framework (trial registration number: A9K76), some components, such as the randomization procedure or the exclusion criteria, are insufficiently reported there.

## Results

### Study sample

From 125, 111 students (70 females; 22.7 (± 2.6) yrs) were randomly assigned to intervention (_n_ = 58) or control group (_n_ = 53) (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#Fig1)). Two participants were excluded (1 above the age limit, 1 in ongoing treatment) and 12 withdrew after the eligibility screening without giving reasons.

**Fig. 1**

![Image 7: Fig. 1](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12916-025-03944-z/MediaObjects/12916_2025_3944_Fig1_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z/figures/1)

Study flow chart

At baseline, screen time, physical activity (self-reported number of days per week with ≥ 60 min. of physical activity), age, gender, and mental health indicators (except disordered eating) did not differ between the intervention and control group (see Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#Tab1)). On average, participants spent 276.37 (± 115.1) minutes per day on smartphone use and reported exercising on 2.87 (± 1.8) days per week.

### Screen time reduction

Control (268.22 ± 88.90) and intervention group (284.71 ± 133,64) did not differ in screen time at baseline (_t_ = −0.771 (99.89), _p_ = 0.443). During intervention (weeks 3–5), screen time differed significantly between the control and intervention group (see Additional file 2: Figure [A1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#Fig1)) with an average screen time of 129.46 ± 46.32 min./day (intervention group) and 264.19 ± 84.83 min./day (control group) (all _p_-values ≤ 0.001). The intervention group reduced their screen time by 155.25 ± 132.14 min/day. Significant screen time differences between intervention group (225.73 ± 89.06 min/day) and control group (270.42 ± 100.31 min./d (_t_ = 0.351 (109); _p_ = 0.014) only persisted to the first post-intervention week (week 6). From week 7 onwards no differences in screen time were observed.

Although all participants significantly reduced screen time during intervention phase (weeks 3–5), not all participants managed to reduce their screen time to the predetermined time limit. Therefore, an additional subgroup analysis was carried out with those who strictly adhered to the limits (≤ 2 h/d). There was no baseline difference between this subgroup compared to control group as well as to the other part of the intervention group, which did not strictly adhered to the time limit (see Additional file 3: Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#Tab1)).

### Physical activity

Self-stated physical activity at the beginning of the study was reported in both groups as number of days per week with physical activity ≥ 60 min (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#Tab1)). During baseline phase (week 1–2), moderate to vigorous physical activity averaged 43.93 ± 22.90 min./d, objectively measured by a fitness tracker (only in the intervention group, not in the control group). During intervention phase (weeks 3–5), moderate to vigorous physical activity was 42.77 ± 31.78, 47.90 ± 30.44, and 44.05 ± 25.00 min./d. Physical activity did not differ statistically between baseline and intervention phase (all _p_-values > 0.5). Since objective physical activity data were only obtained from the intervention group, no between-group differences could be estimated.

### Mental health indicators

Time × group interactions were observed in the main mental health outcome measures (depressive symptoms, well-being, sleep quality, and stress), showing small to medium effect sizes (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z#Tab2)). Mean differences between the groups at all three time points and associated confidence intervals can be found in Table A4 in Additional file 5.

**Table 2 Outcomes of the rm-ANOVAs for depression, well-being, stress, and sleep**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-025-03944-z/tables/2)

### Baseline and post-intervention for the total sample

#### Main outcomes

Depressive symptoms: A time×group interaction was evident when comparing baseline with post-intervention in depressive symptoms (_F_(1; 109) = 13.358, _p_< 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.109). Post-hoc tests highlighted differences within the intervention group comparing t0 and t1 (_p_< 0.001) and t1 and t2 (_p_ = 0.039). The group comparison at t1 revealed differences between the control and the intervention group (_p_ = 0.001). The mean group difference at t1 was (_MD_ = 2.11; _SE_ = 0.063; 95% CI [0.87, 3.36]; _p_ = 0.001) (further information see Additional file 5: Table A4). Depressive symptoms decreased by 27% from t0 and t1 in the intervention group (within-group effect).

Well-being: There was a time×group interaction when comparing baseline with post-intervention in well-being (_F_(1; 109) = 6.088, _p_ = 0.015 partial η 2 = 0.053), post-hoc test (t0-t1) was significant for the intervention group (_p_< 0.001), and group comparison (control vs. intervention group) was significant at t1 (_p_ = 0.026). The mean group difference at t1 was (_MD_ = −1,54; _SE_ = 0.68; 95% CI [−2.89, −0.18]; p = 0.026) (Additional file 5: Table A4). Well-being increased by 14% from t0 and t1 in the intervention group (within-group effect).

Stress: There was a significant time×group interaction when comparing baseline with post-intervention in stress (_F_(1; 109) = 10.164; _p_ = 0.002, partial η 2 = 0.085), post-hoc test (t0-t1) was significant in the intervention group (_p_< 0.001) as well as from t1 to t2 (_p_ = 0.027), and group comparison was significant at t1 (_p_ = 0.05). args.summary:
This webpage presents a randomized controlled trial (RCT) published in BMC Medicine (February 21, 2025) investigating the causal relationship between smartphone screen time reduction and mental health. The study, conducted with 111 healthy students (70 females; mean age 22.68 years; average baseline screen time 276 minutes/day), randomly assigned participants to an intervention group (3 weeks of screen time reduction to ≤2 hours/day) or a control group (continued usual smartphone use). Mental health indicators were measured at baseline (t0), post-intervention (t1), and at 6-week follow-up (t2).

Key findings: The intervention group significantly reduced screen time to an average of 129.46 minutes/day (vs. 264.19 minutes/day in controls). Significant post-intervention improvements of small to medium effect sizes were observed for depressive symptoms (η²=.109, 27% reduction), well-being (η²=.053, 14% increase), sleep quality (η²=.048), and stress (η²=.085). Significant group differences were found at t1 for depressive symptoms (MD=2.11), sleep quality (MD=2.59), well-being (MD=-1.54), and stress (MD=6.91). However, screen time increased rapidly after the intervention ended, approaching baseline levels by follow-up.

The study concludes that three weeks of smartphone screen time reduction yields small to medium mental health benefits, suggesting a causal rather than merely correlative relationship between daily smartphone screen time and mental health. The trial was preregistered on Open Science Framework (A9K76) and retrospectively registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06353451).

## Highlights

*   •We modified smartphone users' default notification systems. 
*   •We assigned people to control or 3 distinct schedules of batching notifications. 
*   •Batching alerts hourly produced little change compared to control (use as usual). 
*   •Batching notifications 3 times a day reduced stress and increased well-being. 
*   •Completely switching off alerts produced, instead, more anxiety and FoMO. 

## Abstract

Every day, billions of us receive smartphone notifications. Designed to distract, these interruptions capture and monetize our time and attention. Though smartphones are incredibly helpful, their current notification systems impose underappreciated, yet considerable, mental costs; like a slot machine, they exploit our inherent psychological bias for variable rewards. With an app that we developed, we conducted a randomized field experiment (n = 237) to test whether batching notifications—delivering notifications in predictable intervals throughout the day—could improve psychological well-being. Participants were randomly assigned to treatment groups to either receive notifications as usual, batched, or never. Using daily diary surveys, we measured a range of psychological and health outcomes, and through our app system, we collected data on phone use behaviors. Compared to those in the control condition, participants whose notifications were batched three-times-a-day felt more attentive, productive, in a better [mood](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/mood), and in greater control of their phones. Participants in the batched group also reported lower stress, lower productivity, and fewer phone interruptions. In contrast, participants who did not receive notifications at all reaped few of those benefits, but experienced higher levels of anxiety and “fear of missing out” (FoMO). We found that inattention and phone-related [fear of missing out](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/fear-of-missing-out) contributed to these results. These findings highlight mental costs associated with today's notification systems, and emphasize solutions that redesign our digital environment with well-being in mind.

args.summary:
This research article, published in December 2019 in Computers in Human Behavior (Volume 101, pp. 84-94), reports on a randomized field experiment (n=237) investigating whether batching smartphone notifications can improve psychological well-being. The study was conducted by Nicholas Fitz, Kostadin Kushlev, Ranjan Jagannathan, Terrel Lewis, Devang Paliwal, and Dan Ariely.

Using a custom-developed Android app, participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: receiving notifications as usual (control), batched hourly, batched three times a day (morning, midday, evening), or no notifications at all (never). The experiment lasted two weeks, with daily diary surveys measuring a range of psychological and health outcomes, plus phone use behavior data collected via the app.

Key findings:
- Participants whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive, in a better mood, and in greater control of their phones compared to the control group.
- The three-times-a-day batching group also reported lower stress, lower productivity (likely reduced distraction), and fewer phone interruptions.
- The hourly batching condition produced little change compared to control.
- Participants who received no notifications at all reaped few of the benefits experienced by the batched group, and instead experienced higher levels of anxiety and "fear of missing out" (FoMO).
- The effects were mediated by improvements in subjective quality of attention and reductions in phone-related FoMO.

The study is grounded in psychological theory on the costs of task-switching and cognitive load, arguing that current notification systems exploit users' psychological bias for variable rewards (similar to slot machines). The results suggest that redesigning notification systems to deliver alerts in predictable, batched intervals can significantly improve well-being by reducing interruptions and restoring a sense of control.

Written evidence submitted by the Digital Mental Health Group (NDC0008) Call for Evidence on Neuroscience and Digital Childhoods The Digital Mental Health Group is a research group at the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, University of Cambridge. Professor Amy Orben, Principal Investigator of the group, is an internationally recognised leader in research on the relationship between digital technologies and adolescent mental health and wellbeing. Professor Orben directed a Feasibility Study of Methods and Data to Understand the Impact of Smartphones and Social Media on Children and Young People for the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology in 2025 (Orben et al., 2026). She also sits on the Department for Education’s Science Advisory Council. The Digital Mental Health Group’s work broadly focuses on how the digital environment influences young people’s mental health and wellbeing outcomes, with close attention to the mechanisms that underpin such effects. This report was written by Brandon C. Davidson, Dr Luisa Fassi, Ioanna Fokas, Lukas J. Gunschera, Professor Amy Orben and Dr Georgia Turner, in alphabetical order. Executive Summary E1. The current evidence base linking digital device use and brain development is limited, with small and inconsistent associations and heterogeneous methodologies. Findings are mixed (including null results in large cohorts), with some studies reporting associations with differences in overall brain volume, and brain regions related to reward processing and cognitive control. However, no clear causal conclusions can be drawn due to reliance on cross-sectional designs, measurement inconsistencies, and potential confounding factors. E2. A key requirement for progress is moving beyond screen-time-based measures to consider how the affordances of digital media may shape adolescent brain development in more specific ways. We highlight the rewarding design of social media platforms (e.g., ‘likes’) as a key example of such mechanisms. E3. Evidence suggests small, bidirectional associations between digital device use and traits such as attention problems and impulsivity, which are relevant to neurodevelopmental conditions. However, there is minimal evidence for causal links with clinically diagnosed disorders, and most studies focus on symptoms rather than diagnoses. E4. Progress requires multi-method approaches that triangulate evidence across designs (i.e., well-designed observational studies, RCTs etc.). This requires linking large-scale UK longitudinal cohorts to high-quality measures of digital engagement, streamlining research and development processes to keep pace with evolving technologies, and enabling robust social media data access for vetted researchers. 1. What impact do digital devices have on the brain development of children and adolescents? Brain development is influenced by and closely linked to social, behavioural and educational development. Digital devices interact with this broader developmental system, encompassing both neural processes and the myriad environmental and behavioural factors that shape them. As a result, isolating their specific impact on brain development is challenging. Moreover, given the widespread integration of digital devices into children daily lives, identifying their effects at the individual level presents additional methodological difficulties (Bak-Coleman et al., 2025), as digital media now permeates all aspects of this complex system at a global level. For example, digital device use may influence behaviours children and young people engage in, which will in turn change the brain, which might then, in turn, change behaviour. Digital technologies could therefore be both the driver of brain changes and influenced by brain changes. This makes it difficult to understand and establish causal impacts of digital device use on brain development. As such, we should not expect an evidence base that isolates the direct effects of digital device use on brain development; instead, interpretations must carefully account for bidirectional influences and the potential role of unmeasured third variables. In addition, the nature of the exposure of ‘device use’ may implicate different developmental consequences on brain structure. For example, the time spent on digital devices may result in the displacement of core activities known to be important in child and adolescent brain development (i.e., sleep, exercise, socialisation). Alternatively, the types of content exposed to (i.e., long-form vs. short-form, harmful content types compared to pro-social or educational content) and the activities engaged with may result in differential brain development outcomes in specific regions of interest. Below, we narratively review the empirical literature and relevant reviews linking digital media and brain development to elucidate the extent to which the evidence supports a relationship between the two. The question of the physical effects of digital devices in children and adolescents on the brain is not our area of expertise and, as such, this synthesis is not comprehensive with regards to potential outcomes, especially in that area. Digital Device Use and Brain Development A range of reviews have examined the impact of digital device use on children and adolescents’ mental and physical development (see Appendix 1 for a narrative overview of key studies), with some focusing specifically on brain development. A scoping review of 16 cross-sectional neuroimaging studies found that more frequent and prolonged screen time, as well as “problematic” usage behaviours, were associated with reduced activity in brain regions involved in attentional and control networks, alongside increased activity in reward-related regions (Marciano et al., 2021, 2025). Similarly, a review of studies in the general population reported that “excessive” smartphone use was associated with smaller brain volumes, particularly in subcortical regions (Lin et al., 2022). This association was more pronounced in adolescent participants compared to adults. In addition, a review of internet and smartphone “addiction” found associations with impairments in cognitive control, including altered reward processing (e.g., anterior cingulate cortex, insula, amygdala) and executive function (e.g., dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, frontal and parietal regions) in adolescents and young adults (aged 13-25; León Méndez et al., 2024). However, the current evidence base linking excessive digital device use to brain development remains limited. As highlighted by Montag et al. (2023) methodological heterogeneity, defined as substantial differences in study design and procedures, constrains the interpretability and comparability of findings. For example, variability in MRI processing pipelines can substantially influence observed structural differences (Zhou et al., 2022), while inconsistent definitions of “excessive,” “problematic,” or “addictive” digital media use hinder cross-study synthesis. Moreover, the relatively small number of studies included in existing reviews limits the strength of inferences that can be drawn. Further, the lack of longitudinal research precludes causal inference, meaning that whilst there may be a relationship, we cannot infer the causal direction of this association (Wadsley & Ihssen, 2023). Several candidate explanations could account for the associations observed in cross-sectional studies: individuals with pre-existing structural or functional brain differences may engage in greater digital media use; increased digital media use may in turn alter brain development; or a third variable may both increase social media use and directly influence brain development, producing a spurious association. Further evidence comes from a small number of large-scale longitudinal cohort studies examining associations between digital media use and structural brain development and functional organisation, which improve on the small sample sizes of included studies across the above systematic reviews. Using data from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) cohort, which follows children from age 9, Miller et al. (2023) found no evidence of an association between digital screen engagement and functional brain organisation (n=7,890). They also found no evidence that children with higher levels of engagement (n=4,024) exhibited patterns of functional brain organisation associated with maladaptive functioning. Another study examining digital media use and brain development over a longer time period using the ABCD cohort found that whilst individual digital media did not influence cortical or striatal volumes, there was a statistically significant, although small in effect size, association between high social media use and cerebellum volume over time (n=1462; Nivins et al., 2024). A recent study also using the ABCD cohort (n=7614) found that higher average daily social media use was significantly associated with lower total cortical thickness and volume, although there was no association between self-reported “social media addiction” and any identified regions of interest (Nagata et al., 2026). Ultimately, the substantial differences in the results of studies using this cohort limit our ability to make strong conclusions for or against a relationship between digital media use and structural brain development. Digital Affordances A major challenge in evidence provision is that studies and reviews focusing on time spent and ‘excessive’ or ‘problematic/addictive’ use of digital assume that increasing time spent on these devices will result in larger associations with brain development in a dose-response manner. However, the range of action possibilities on digital media, deemed ‘digital affordances’, may limit the extent to which all use can be treated as equivalent. Instead, understanding how digital media relates to brain development requires attention to the specific affordances young people engage with, which may reveal more precise associations. One such example of understanding digital media engagement through an affordances approach is reward learning on social media. Digital platforms use quantifiable social rewards (e.g., ‘likes’) to incentivise posting behaviour, such that receiving more ‘likes’ increases the drive to post more frequently (Turner et al., 2025). Reinforcement learning models formalise this process through mathematical equations, and fitting these models to raw social media behaviour (i.e., posting on Twitter/X or Instagram) demonstrates that these processes successfully capture posting dynamics (Lindström et al., 2021; Turner et al., 2024). Sensitivity to these social media rewards varies across contexts, such as an increase to social media reward sensitivity the COVID-19 pandemic compared to non-pandemic periods, and increases in social reward sensitivity are associated with increased mental health symptoms cross-sectionally (Davidson et al., 2025; Mirea et al., 2024). Adolescents are particularly sensitive to social media feedback, they learn faster from changes in ‘likes’, and fluctuations in ‘likes’ has a stronger influence on adolescent mood (da Silva Pinho et al., 2024). This increased sensitivity to ‘likes’ was associated with individual differences in subcortical–limbic brain volumes in older adolescents (ages 18-24). Further, research in early adolescents (ages 12–13) shows that habitual social media checking is linked to changes in neural sensitivity to social rewards and punishments. At age 12, habitual checkers exhibited lower sensitivity to social anticipation than non-habitual users, particularly in regions such as the amygdala, insula, ventral striatum, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Longitudinally, sensitivity increases in habitual users but decreases in non-habitual users (Maza et al., 2023). The authors of this research postulate that this trajectory reflects a potentially increasing sensitivity to online social rewards and difficulty in inhibitory control, consistent with the affordances account. Gaming and the Brain There is a distinct literature examining the relationship between gaming and brain development. Different teams postulate different associations, with a general consensus emerging that the genre and use patterns of gaming are important in understanding potential associations (Bavelier et al., 2011; Brilliant T. et al., 2019; Kühn et al., 2014; Mohammadi et al., 2020). However, as this is not our area of expertise, we encourage the committee to ensure that focused input on this topic is provided through another expert submission. 2. What are the short, medium and long-term effects on the brain of using digital devices in childhood and adolescence? Due to the lack of long-term evidence in this area – driven partially by the relative newness of many digital devices and technologies – the evidence base focuses largely on the short term (i.e. immediate) and medium term (i.e. weeks, months) effects of using digital devices. a. How does dopamine and any other hormones released by the use of certain devices impact brain development? Dopamine regulates motivation and the brain’s learning response to reward and uncertainty. Therefore, all activities which are potentially pleasurable or uncertain can trigger dopamine release. During adolescence, the dopaminergic system and related striatal regions are implicated in underlying two common features of adolescence: escalation in risk-taking behaviours and increased desire to spend time with and earn the approval of peers (Steinberg, 2008), which may be amplified by digital environments that provide frequent, salient, and variably delivered social rewards. Certain aspects of digital media use may create conditions that have been shown to trigger particularly high amounts of dopamine release, such as high reward availability at uncertain schedules of delivery. For example, one study demonstrated using fMRI that adolescents (aged 13-18) viewing ‘social media posts’ with many ‘likes’ compared to those with fewer ‘likes’ was associated with increased activity in neural regions implicated in reward processing (Sherman et al., 2016). Importantly, however, no study has directly examined dopamine release in response to social media input, nor can we currently assess the extent to which dopamine release influences patterns of digital device use deemed ‘addictive’ or ‘problematic’. This can only be achieved through pharmacological intervention studies that manipulate dopamine release directly. During childhood and adolescence, neural dopamine pathways are undergoing development (Hoops & Flores, 2017). This means adolescence is a particularly sensitive period to dopamine perturbation (Suri et al., 2023). Furthermore, as this development is influenced by pubertal stage, brain responses to dopamine release differ by both sex and age (Walker et al., 2017). Research into the effects of increased dopamine transmission in adolescence has shown that altered dopamine levels in adolescence can significantly influence prefrontal cortex development, and can lead to lasting cognitive changes in adulthood such as reduced behavioural inhibition and altered reward sensitivity (Walker et al., 2017). However, effects depend on the levels of dopamine changes, with lower dopamine doses showing reduced or minimal effects (Areal & Blakely, 2020). As such, dopamine is clearly implicated in adolescent responses to environmental reward and uncertainty, and exposure to dopamine perturbation can have lasting consequences for adolescent brain development. In order to understand the relevance of this discussion to digital media usage, we will first require evidence about the exact quantity of dopamine disturbance caused by different levels or types of screen use, which is currently poorly understood. Only then can we make a judgement regarding the relevance of dopamine to discussions of digital device use. b. Is there evidence of a link between use of digital devices in childhood and adolescence and any neurological and behavioural conditions? Neurodevelopmental conditions are complex disorders that influence the growth and development of the brain, and are commonly associated with behavioural and cognitive differences that arise during childhood (Pallanti & Salerno, 2023). Examples include attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and conduct disorders. Our expertise is on cognitive and behavioural outcomes commonly associated with these conditions, such as attention problems, lower executive functioning, and externalising behaviours. We exclude in our evidence synthesis other neurological conditions, involving brain pathology. Overall, the existing evidence base suggests associations between digital device use and cognitive or behavioural outcomes relevant to neurodevelopmental conditions, but currently does not yet support a causal link with diagnosed conditions (Teague et al., 2026). Meta-analyses report small but statistically significant associations between screen use and externalising problems, including ADHD-related behaviours (Eirich et al., 2022; Nikkelen et al., 2014; Ra et al., 2018). A longitudinal systematic review further suggests that these relationships are bidirectional, highlighting that children with ADHD symptoms appear more vulnerable to developing high digital media use, and high digital media use subsequently predicts later ADHD symptom levels (Thorell et al., 2024). Emerging evidence also points to potential mechanisms underlying these associations. For example, impulsivity appears to mediate the link between screen use and later ADHD symptoms, particularly for social media use (Wallace et al., 2023). Across these studies, associations are typically small and heterogeneous, with outcomes varying by the type of digital media, the outcome, and individual characteristics. We highlight two important caveats. The majority of studies assess symptoms and behavioural traits rather than clinically diagnosed neurodevelopmental conditions. As such, the evidence base primarily reflects associations with subclinical symptom presentations, rather than the development or onset of diagnosable conditions (e.g., ADHD or ASD). This problem extends beyond neurodevelopmental disorders. For example, a systematic review found that although studies examining clinically diagnosed internalising conditions (e.g., anxiety, depression) reported broadly comparable associations to those focusing on symptom measures, only 11% of studies included clinical populations (Fassi et al., 2024). We recommend future studies that aim to consider the relationship between digital media use and neurodevelopment to consider clinical cut-offs, validated questionnaires and clinical diagnoses to better capture neurodevelopmental conditions. Second, although longitudinal studies provide insights into the directionality of associations (such that social media use precedes an increase in symptoms) within individuals over time, they do not fully establish causality. In particular, other factors that change over time, such as shifts in family context, peer relationships, or developmental processes, may influence both digital media use and neurodevelopmental outcomes. As a result of this complex and ever-changing system, it remains difficult to isolate the independent contribution of digital media use (Orben et al., 2026). c. Does the use of digital devices in childhood and adolescence have physical effects that impact the brain – for example, on brain function, the eyes, or elsewhere in the body? As mentioned previously, the question of specific effects of digital device use on brain development is not our area of expertise. Our narrative summary in response to 1) provides an overview of the literature we identified that speaks to this question. 3. How do children and adolescents view the impact of digital devices, and how far are their views taken into account in policy? The views of children and adolescents on the impact of digital devices is not an area of our team’s expertise. As such, we provide an overview of some key studies but encourage evidence provision by other expert groups on this topic, as well as consultation with children and young people themselves. Children and adolescents provide a diverse range of perspectives, both positive and negative, about the use of digital devices and the features it provides. For example, a recent Delphi study (a research method that seeks to reach broad agreement across selected participants on a range of statements), involving adults and adolescents (aged 11–15) showed that a majority of young people agreed on the role of social media in emotional regulation and empowerment, both of which domains did not reach consensus with adults (Hickman Dunne et al., 2026). For example, this includes ideas that “young people use social media as a positive distraction from their personal problems” and that “young people cope with problems through discussion with their friends on social media.” However, the same study also highlighted negative perceptions of social media use which converged across groups, with consensus reached on experiences such as “[worrying] about not being liked by others on social media” and “[becoming] so absorbed in social media that they do not realise how much time has passed.” A current challenge in this space is understanding youth perspectives and experience at scale. One emerging approach uses a novel narrative elicitation method that enables individuals to share brief “micro-narratives” from their lived experiences, regardless of writing ability or background (Skeggs, Mehta, Yap, et al., 2025). In a study of 901 adolescents, this method identified four main types of harm experienced on social media: those arising from others’ behaviour (e.g., cyberbullying, scams), harmful behaviours in young people themselves (e.g., compulsive use, social comparison), exposure to harmful content (e.g., curated or graphic material), and platform-related harms (e.g., algorithmic exposure; Skeggs, Mehta, Katiyar, et al., 2025). Current digital policies and public discourse often emphasise potential risks of child and adolescent screen use, and digital policies may seek to incorporate youth perspectives on the complex benefits and harms they report experiencing. Effective regulation must move beyond aggregate metrics and utilise child and adolescent-centred approaches that consider the needs and rights for both connection and protection of young people. 4. Is there adequate evidence around the impact of digital devices on the development of children and adolescents? No – the evidence base is limited. Current evidence is limited by its reliance on self-report measurement, its cross-sectional nature and the small effect sizes and heterogenous effects observed across the literature (Orben et al., 2026). Digital devices are also often conceptualised and studied as a monolith, with little attention given to the important nuances of digital device type, content type and type of use. In addition, given the ubiquity and implications of digital device use at both individual and societal levels, typical methods to causal evidence provision may not be applicable in isolation (Bak-Coleman et al., 2025). a. Where is more research needed on their impact? To fill current gaps in the evidence base, future research should focus on the longer-term impacts of digital device use in childhood and adolescence. Beyond simply studying cognitive and/or psychological effects, attention should also be given to physical/neurobiological effects of device use. Research should move beyond self-report measures of digital device use towards objective data, facilitated through app-tracking, data donation or mandated data sharing from social media companies. We provide the below recommendations to support an improved research infrastructure in order to facilitate this shift in evidence provision: • Enhancing the quality and scope of digital technology data within large-scale UK observational cohort studies by linking longitudinal data to high quality measures of digital engagement. • Adopt a faster, more streamlined Research and Development process for research on digital harms in order to recognise and address the rapid speed with which digital devices evolve and exert their effects on populations (Orben & Matias, 2025). • Prioritise and enable robust social media data access for vetted researchers to enable public interest research on the harms and benefits on digital device use (Social Platforms Data Access Taskforce, 2026). Access to social media and digital device data currently depends on fragmented and industry controlled mechanisms, limiting the ability of independent researchers, regulators and policymakers to assess how the technology operates in practice (Santini et al., 2026). Moreover, establishing causal links between digital media use and brain development requires moving beyond purely cross-sectional and observational designs. One avenue is through randomised controlled trials (RCTs), an experimental method which evaluates the efficacy of an intervention by randomly assigning participants to a treatment or control group. RCTs are considered the ‘gold-standard’ for causal inference, with bias and confounding minimised through the randomisation procedure and well-designed control groups (Orben et al., 2025). However, the unique context of digital media may limit their utility. Several key assumptions are difficult to satisfy, including violations of the stable unit treatment value assumption, challenges in identifying representative non-user groups, and difficulties disentangling individual- and societal-level effects (Bak-Coleman et al., 2025). Given these limitations, we recommend a triangulation approach to causal inference, combining multiple methods with different underlying assumptions (Bak-Coleman et al., 2025). Although observational and experimental studies may be inconclusive in isolation, convergence with findings across studies can strengthen confidence in results. Further, causal modelling of pre-existing data can advance causal inference when appropriately designed, while qualitative and mixed-methods (e.g., focus groups, interviews, co-design) and ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) offer more adaptable, lower-cost approaches for evolving policy needs, although they less directly address causality (Orben et al., 2025). Appendix 1: Digital Media Use and Outcomes in Children and Adolescents Digital Device Use in Childhood and Adolescence An umbrella review (review of reviews) of the benefits and risks associated with youths’ interactions with electronic screens found small to moderate effects on a range of outcomes (Sanders et al., 2024). In education, results were mixed; screen use was negatively associated with literacy, but this effect was positive when parents watched with children. Concerning health, there was evidence for small associations with depression. Authors reported a high risk of bias in the literature and high heterogeneity. Such findings reflect the difficulty of studying device use in this population, highlighting the importance of considering child-only use as well as child-parent use, the nature of the activity, and the type of device used. A second, more recent review, found that digital media use in children and adolescents was associated with a range of negative developmental outcomes (Teague et al., 2026). Social media was associated with higher depression, behavioural problems, self-injury and substance use, and lower self-perception and academic achievement. Video gaming was linked to greater aggression and externalising behaviour. However, video gaming was also linked to modestly higher attention and executive functioning, reflecting the possible benefits of gaming described below. Other digital media use, including digital device use and messaging/communication media, was associated with depression. This review found associations between social media and positive development were stronger with objective exposure measurement, indicating the presence of a potential negative bias with regards to public perception of digital media use. We underscore the importance of treating childhood and adolescence as a nuanced developmental period, rather than a homogenous block. Effects of digital device use on developmental outcomes likely vary depending on which stage of childhood or adolescence the young person finds themselves in, as has been observed with regards to social media (Orben et al., 2022; Teague et al., 2026). It is unclear whether this is due to biological or social factors, or both. However, we caution against making blanket conclusions on digital device across all of childhood and adolescence, instead supporting a more developmental approach which recognises the plurality of this time-period. Smartphones in Childhood and Adolescence A review on the relationship between smartphone use and academic achievement in children and adolescence showed that increased frequency of smartphone use is linked to reduced academic success (Amez & Baert, 2020). However, these results are heterogeneous with regard to the method of data gathering (objective vs subjective, child-based vs parental report), the measures of academic performance used in the analysis, and the measures of smartphone use adopted (frequency, time spent, content consumed, etc.). This indicates the presence of several moderating factors of the relationship between digital device use and academic attainment. The authors also emphasise that the reported associations cannot be given a causal interpretation, given that they are based on observational, correlational evidence. In our rapid review for this evidence submission, we found no reviews of the literature on the relationship between smartphone use and mental or physical health in children and young people specifically. Given that reviews are considered one of the strongest types of evidence due to their synthesis of results from across the literature, we consider this a key gap to target in future research. Artificial Intelligence in Childhood and Adolescence To our knowledge, there are no reviews of the sparse literature on the effects of artificial intelligence technologies on childhood and adolescence. args.summary:
The Digital Mental Health Group (MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, University of Cambridge) submitted evidence to the UK Parliament's call for evidence on Neuroscience and Digital Childhoods (April 2026). The report addresses the impact of digital devices on children's brain development, short/medium/long-term effects, youth perspectives, and adequacy of current evidence.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Brain Development Impact**: The evidence base linking digital device use to brain development is limited, with small/inconsistent associations and heterogeneous methodologies. Cross-sectional studies show associations between excessive screen time and reduced activity in attentional/control networks, smaller brain volumes (particularly subcortical regions), and altered reward processing. However, large-scale longitudinal studies (ABCD cohort) produce mixed results - some find no association with functional brain organization (n=7,890), while others find small associations with cortical thickness. No clear causal conclusions can be drawn due to cross-sectional designs and confounding factors.

2. **Digital Affordances**: Moving beyond screen-time measures, the report highlights that social media reward mechanisms (e.g., 'likes') may shape adolescent brain development. Adolescents learn faster from 'likes' changes, and this sensitivity is associated with individual differences in subcortical-limbic brain volumes. Habitual social media checking in early adolescents (ages 12-13) is linked to changes in neural sensitivity to social rewards.

3. **Dopamine Effects**: While digital media may trigger dopamine release (e.g., fMRI study showing adolescents viewing posts with many 'likes' had increased reward-related neural activity), no study has directly examined dopamine release from social media. The exact quantity of dopamine disturbance from screen use remains poorly understood.

4. **Neurodevelopmental Conditions**: Small, bidirectional associations exist between digital device use and ADHD-related behaviors, attention problems, and impulsivity. However, most studies assess symptoms rather than clinically diagnosed conditions, and minimal evidence supports causal links with diagnosed disorders.

5. **Youth Perspectives**: Adolescents report both positive and negative experiences. A Delphi study showed youth agreed social media helps with emotional regulation and empowerment, but also reported worries about social acceptance and absorption. A micro-narrative study of 901 adolescents identified four harm types: others' behavior, harmful self-behaviors, exposure to harmful content, and platform-related harms.

6. **Evidence Gaps**: Current evidence is limited by self-report measurement, cross-sectional designs, small effect sizes, and treating digital devices as a monolith. The report recommends: linking UK longitudinal cohorts to objective digital engagement measures, faster R&D processes to keep pace with evolving technologies, and enabling robust social media data access for vetted researchers. A triangulation approach combining multiple methods is recommended over relying solely on RCTs.

7. **Gaming**: The report notes distinct literature on gaming and brain development, with genre and use patterns being important, but defers to other experts on this topic.
