## 1. Introduction

In today’s rapidly digitized and globalized society, education systems around the world are increasingly focused on developing the so-called key competences of the 21st century—among which digital competences, creative thinking, problem-solving and visual–spatial reasoning are particularly important ([European Commission, 2018](#B9-education-16-00947); [OECD, 2019](#B24-education-16-00947)). The European Key Competences Framework and the OECD’s Future of Education and Skills 2030 clearly emphasize the need to align education with the demands of the labor market and technological innovations shaping the modern world ([European Commission, 2018](#B9-education-16-00947); [OECD, 2019](#B24-education-16-00947); [World Economic Forum, 2020](#B33-education-16-00947); [Ferrari, 2013](#B11-education-16-00947)).

In this context, visual–spatial abilities (hereinafter VSAs) take on a new meaning. Once predominantly associated with fields such as engineering and architecture ([Sorby, 2009](#B27-education-16-00947)), today VSA is recognized as the foundation for a wide range of digital and creative skills—including 3D modeling, virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR), computer animation, data visualization, and digital design ([Yue, 2008](#B34-education-16-00947); [Roca-González et al., 2017](#B26-education-16-00947); [Medina Herrera et al., 2024](#B22-education-16-00947); [Tiwari et al., 2024](#B28-education-16-00947)). Within the Digital Competence Framework for Citizens (DigComp), VSAs are key to developing competencies such as digital content creation, visual literacy, and the use of digital tools for communication and learning ([Vuorikari et al., 2016](#B31-education-16-00947)). The World Economic Forum also identifies visual reasoning as one of the skills that will have increasing value in the labor market by 2025 ([World Economic Forum, 2020](#B33-education-16-00947)).

An increasing number of research shows that it is possible to develop VSA in a targeted manner through appropriate teaching programs, especially in digitally rich educational environments ([Medina Herrera et al., 2024](#B22-education-16-00947); [Roca-González et al., 2017](#B26-education-16-00947); [Tiwari et al., 2024](#B28-education-16-00947)). For example, [Medina Herrera et al.](#B22-education-16-00947) ([2024](#B22-education-16-00947)) show that the integration of VR, AR, and 3D printing in the classroom can significantly improve VSA, and thus students’ ability to creatively solve problems in digital contexts. Similarly, Roca-González et al. point out that virtual technologies encourage deeper spatial reasoning, while paralleling the development of transversal skills such as digital competence and creativity.

In addition to their role in the development of specific digital skills, visual–spatial abilities also have a broader significance as a meta-cognitive resource that enables learning transfer—the transfer of learned knowledge and skills into new, different domains of learning and work. The developed VSA enables students to better understand and solve tasks involving spatial organization, logical modeling, abstract visualization, and manipulation of complex information in a variety of contexts ([Tiwari et al., 2024](#B28-education-16-00947); [Hegarty & Waller, 2004](#B15-education-16-00947); [Uttal et al., 2013](#B29-education-16-00947); [Wai et al., 2009](#B32-education-16-00947)).

Research shows that improving VSA can contribute to more successful learning in areas that are not closely related to spatial reasoning at first glance—such as mathematics, physics, chemistry, programming, and even reading and understanding complex texts ([Tiwari et al., 2024](#B28-education-16-00947); [Uttal et al., 2013](#B29-education-16-00947); [Wai et al., 2009](#B32-education-16-00947)). This transfer effect is particularly important in education systems oriented towards the development of transversal competences of the 21st century. As [Uttal et al.](#B29-education-16-00947) ([2013](#B29-education-16-00947)) point out, the development of visual–spatial abilities can contribute to cognitive flexibility—the ability to apply knowledge in a variety of situations—which is key to success in dynamic and interconnected areas of work and learning.

Given these educational and technological trends, there is a growing interest in the application of instructional programs that actively engage spatial reasoning. One such example is the computer animation (CA) course, which directly engages the mechanisms that underlie visual–spatial thinking through work with 2D and 3D geometric transformations, modeling and mental manipulation of spatial objects ([Yue, 2008](#B34-education-16-00947); [Roca-González et al., 2017](#B26-education-16-00947); [Medina Herrera et al., 2024](#B22-education-16-00947); [Tiwari et al., 2024](#B28-education-16-00947); [Martín-Dorta et al., 2008](#B21-education-16-00947); [Ardebili, 2006](#B1-education-16-00947); [Moritz & Youn, 2022](#B23-education-16-00947)).

Accordingly, the aim of this research is to examine whether and to what extent a computer animation course can contribute to the development of visual–spatial abilities of students and thus support the acquisition of a wider range of key competencies needed for learning and working in the 21st century. In particular, the impact of previous experience in working with 3D tools was examined, as well as the effect of the retesting itself.

The study is therefore grounded in the assumption that visual–spatial abilities are trainable cognitive resources that can be systematically developed through active and digitally mediated learning environments ([Castro-Alonso et al., 2024](#B5-education-16-00947); [Medina Herrera et al., 2024](#B22-education-16-00947)).

Existing research on visual–spatial ability development has primarily focused on processes involving virtual reality, CAD systems, and 3D modeling environments, demonstrating their effectiveness in enhancing spatial reasoning and related competencies. However, comparatively less attention has been given to the role of computer animation (CA) courses, as structured pedagogical programs in higher education, particularly in large, quasi-experimental settings.

This study aims to address this gap by examining the impact of a CA course on visual–spatial abilities, with a particular focus on differences related to prior experience and the potential of such programs to support broader competence development. In this way, the study contributes to bridging the gap between cognitive research on spatial abilities and applied educational practices in digitally mediated learning environments.

## 2. Theoretical Framework and Literature Review

### Visual–Spatial Abilities

Visual–spatial abilities (VSAs) represent a base component of human cognition, encompassing the capacity to mentally generate, manipulate, and interpret visual and spatial information. They are integral to a broad range of cognitive processes, including memory, attention, problem-solving, reasoning, and learning flexibility ([Bar-Hen-Schweiger & Henik, 2024](#B2-education-16-00947)). Within contemporary educational and professional contexts, these abilities are increasingly recognized as essential building blocks for 21st-century competencies—notably creativity, problem-solving, digital literacy, and adaptability in digital work environments ([European Commission, 2018](#B9-education-16-00947); [OECD, 2019](#B24-education-16-00947); [European Commission, 2022](#B10-education-16-00947)).

From a theoretical perspective, the development of visual–spatial abilities through a CA course can be interpreted through several complementary learning and cognitive frameworks. First, constructivist and experiential learning theories suggest that knowledge is more effectively acquired when learners actively manipulate and transform representations rather than passively observe them. In the context of computer animation, students continuously engage in spatial transformations, modeling, and problem-solving, which supports active knowledge construction.

Second, from the perspective of cognitive learning theories, spatial reasoning is strengthened through interaction with visual and virtual environments, as learners mentally simulate object movement, rotation, and transformation. Recent research emphasizes that cognition is grounded in sensorimotor interaction and that interactive learning environments can significantly enhance spatial reasoning and engagement ([Castro-Alonso et al., 2024](#B5-education-16-00947); [Chang & Aberash, 2026](#B6-education-16-00947)). This is particularly relevant in digital and immersive contexts, where technologies such as 3D modeling and animation enable rich embodied experiences that support learning and creative thinking ([Lehrman, 2025](#B18-education-16-00947)).

Finally, Cognitive load theory provides an additional explanatory framework, suggesting that structured learning environments can facilitate schema construction and reduce cognitive overload in complex spatial tasks. Recent studies highlight that integrating embodied cognition with cognitive load theory leads to more effective learning in complex digital environments, particularly for novice learners ([Zou et al., 2025](#B35-education-16-00947)). These perspectives collectively support the assumption that visual–spatial abilities can be systematically developed through targeted, technology-enhanced educational interventions ([Medina Herrera et al., 2024](#B22-education-16-00947)).

Visual–spatial intelligence regulates the ability to accurately perceive spatial relationships, perform mental transformations, and reason about objects and their interactions in 2D and 3D space ([Hegarty & Waller, 2004](#B15-education-16-00947); [Maier, 1996](#B20-education-16-00947)). As [Moritz and Youn](#B23-education-16-00947) ([2022](#B23-education-16-00947)) highlight, the ability to mentally visualize and rotate objects has become critical in modern fields such as design and engineering, where mastery of 3D software directly correlates with professional success. This demonstrates how VSAs are transforming from abstract cognitive constructs into applied competencies relevant for thriving in digital domains.

Contemporary frameworks, such as the Key Competences for Lifelong Learning, Digital Competence Framework for Citizens (DigComp) and OECD Future of Education and Skills 2030, explicitly underline the importance of visual–spatial skills. These abilities enable effective navigation of complex digital environments, facilitate visual communication, and support the creation and manipulation of digital content—essential capabilities in fields like CAD design, VR/AR, industrial design, data visualization, and computational animation ([World Economic Forum, 2020](#B33-education-16-00947)).

The structure of visual–spatial abilities is multifaceted. Many studies ([Bar-Hen-Schweiger & Henik, 2024](#B2-education-16-00947), [Kozhevnikov & Hegarty, 2001](#B17-education-16-00947)) suggest that VSA encompasses several interrelated but distinct components, including:

* Mental rotation—the ability to mentally rotate objects in space;
* Spatial visualization—the ability to manipulate and transform visual representations;
* Spatial perception—the ability to accurately judge spatial relationships;
* Perspective taking—the ability to adopt different viewpoints in space.

[Bar-Hen-Schweiger and Henik](#B2-education-16-00947) ([2024](#B2-education-16-00947)) further propose an overarching cognitive factor—mental manipulation—that underlies these components and extends beyond purely spatial processing to encompass broader cognitive flexibility.

Recent research also demonstrates the importance of advanced, logically valid spatial ability tests in virtual environments, such as the ASVT-V used by [Moritz and Youn](#B23-education-16-00947) ([2022](#B23-education-16-00947)), which successfully captured domain-specific improvements in spatial visualization in fashion design education. This aligns with the broader trend of integrating virtual and immersive technologies to foster VSA ([Medina Herrera et al., 2024](#B22-education-16-00947); [Roca-González et al., 2017](#B26-education-16-00947); [Tiwari et al., 2024](#B28-education-16-00947)).

Importantly, the development of VSA has been shown to facilitate learning transfer—the ability to apply acquired knowledge and skills across different contexts and disciplines ([Tiwari et al., 2024](#B28-education-16-00947); [Hegarty & Waller, 2004](#B15-education-16-00947); [Wai et al., 2009](#B32-education-16-00947)). Enhanced VSA supports flexible thinking and enables learners to approach unfamiliar problems through improved spatial reasoning and visualization strategies. For example, [Uttal et al.](#B29-education-16-00947) ([2013](#B29-education-16-00947)) and [Wai et al.](#B32-education-16-00947) ([2009](#B32-education-16-00947)) demonstrate that strengthening VSA contributes to improved outcomes in domains such as STEM education, architecture, and even verbal reasoning, indicating that spatial training can produce broad cognitive benefits that extend beyond its immediate domain of application.

In empirical educational research, the Purdue Spatial Visualization Test (PSVT) ([Guay, 1977b](#B13-education-16-00947)) remains a widely used instrument for assessing VSA. The PSVT includes three subtests—Views, Developments, and Rotations—designed to measure core spatial visualization skills. While the original PSVT utilized isometric projections ([Appendix A](#app1-education-16-00947), [Figure A1](#fig_body_display_education-16-00947-f0A1), [Figure A2](#fig_body_display_education-16-00947-f0A2) and [Figure A3](#fig_body_display_education-16-00947-f0A3)), subsequent revisions ([Branoff, 2000](#B4-education-16-00947); [Yue, 2008](#B34-education-16-00947)) incorporated trimetric projections and more realistic 3D representations to enhance logical validity and better reflect the cognitive demands of modern digital tasks ([Appendix A](#app1-education-16-00947), [Figure A4](#fig_body_display_education-16-00947-f0A4), [Figure A5](#fig_body_display_education-16-00947-f0A5) and [Figure A6](#fig_body_display_education-16-00947-f0A6)).

Despite certain limitations (e.g., ambiguity in 2D interpretations), PSVT continues to provide a reliable and valid measure of spatial abilities, particularly within STEM disciplines ([Maeda & Yoon, 2013](#B19-education-16-00947)). Performance on the PSVT correlates strongly with success in tasks requiring spatial reasoning and visualization, such as CAD modeling, engineering drawing, and 3D animation ([Moritz & Youn, 2022](#B23-education-16-00947)).

In the context of this study, visual–spatial abilities are conceptualized as both a cognitive foundation and as a set of applied competencies crucial for effective performance in digital and creative domains. Moreover, fostering VSA can provide a powerful mechanism for promoting learning transfer, helping learners generalize and adapt cognitive strategies across varied academic and professional tasks ([Tiwari et al., 2024](#B28-education-16-00947); [Uttal et al., 2013](#B29-education-16-00947); [Wai et al., 2009](#B32-education-16-00947)). The integration of computer animation courses with spatial ability development offers a promising direction for fostering these skills in higher education. By engaging students in activities involving 2D and 3D transformations, modeling, and mental manipulation of spatial objects, such courses can directly enhance VSA and contribute to the broader development of 21st-century competencies ([Medina Herrera et al., 2024](#B22-education-16-00947); [Roca-González et al., 2017](#B26-education-16-00947); [Tiwari et al., 2024](#B28-education-16-00947)).

As [Moritz and Youn](#B23-education-16-00947) ([2022](#B23-education-16-00947)) demonstrated, domain-specific training in fields such as fashion design leads to measurable improvements in spatial visualization, supporting the idea that VSA can be deliberately created through targeted educational interventions. Similarly, [Bar-Hen-Schweiger and Henik](#B2-education-16-00947) ([2024](#B2-education-16-00947)) emphasize that fostering VSA is not only beneficial for spatial cognition “per se” but also for enhancing general cognitive flexibility and problem-solving capacity, both of which are critical for enabling effective learning transfer across diverse contexts.

In sum, visual–spatial abilities are emerging as a vital cognitive resource for navigating and contributing to the increasingly visual and interactive digital landscape of the 21st century. Their development through educational interventions, such as computer animation courses, holds significant potential not only for providing learners with specialized technical skills but also for fostering transferable cognitive competencies essential for lifelong learning and professional adaptability.

## 3. Methodology

### 3.1. Research Participants

Students of the Information Technology study program of the Technical Faculty in Zrenjanin participated in the research. A total of 346 students were enrolled, divided into two groups: experimental and control. The survey was conducted during the winter semesters of 2022/2023, 2023/2024 and 2024/2025.

A computer animation (CA) course was chosen as the educational strategy because it naturally integrates activities that foster the development of visual–spatial reasoning (VSA), which is a key component of transversal competencies in contemporary 21st-century education frameworks—including digital creativity, problem-solving, and design thinking ([European Commission, 2018](#B9-education-16-00947); [OECD, 2019](#B24-education-16-00947); [Roca-González et al., 2017](#B26-education-16-00947)).

The experimental group consisted of students who attended a computer animation course during year IV and voluntarily wanted to participate and who met one basic condition: to be studying CA for the “first” time (i.e., did not renew the year). Besides this, there were no additional conditions for this group selection. This provided a very diverse sample (men, women, singles, married, young, older, etc.).

The experimental group included 231 students. Of these, 154 were full-time students whose study costs are covered by the government and whose classes are organized on weekdays—hereinafter GB (budget group). The other 77 were part-time self-financing students—hereinafter GS (self-funded group). For this group, classes are organized only on weekends. The demographics of the participants are shown in the following tables and graphs.

Regarding the gender structure of the respondents, the majority of students at this faculty are male. The gender structure in the GB group was 36 women/118 men, while in the GS group, there were 28 women/49 men. In total, there were 64 women/167 men in the experimental group ([Table 1](#table_body_display_education-16-00947-t001)).

**Table 1.**
Gender distribution of sample.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

The age of the students ranged from 21 to 34 years, and the average age was 21 years, which is the most commonly registered value. The mean age of full-time students was 21.88 years, while that of self-financing students was 23.39 years ([Table 2](#table_body_display_education-16-00947-t002)).

**Table 2.**
Age distribution of sample.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

The control group consisted of second-year students of Engineering Management (115 students), who had no contact with the CA course. Their average age was 20.53 years, and the most common age was 20 years. The gender ratio was 24.36% women and 75.64% men.

### 3.2. Research Instruments

A survey questionnaire and the Purdue Spatial Visualization Test (PSVT) were used ([Guay, 1977b](#B13-education-16-00947)). Before taking the PSVT, students filled out a short questionnaire with two questions, with the aim of gaining additional insight into their visual–spatial abilities.

* The first question concerned self-assessment of the ability to mentally manipulate three-dimensional objects and orientation in three-dimensional (real or virtual) environments. The answers were given on a 5-point scale: 1—“Very difficult”, 2—“Difficult”, 3—“Medium”, 4—“Easy”, 5—“Very easy”.
* The second question was related to previous experience working with 3D design software, with four offered answers: N—“No experience”, P—“Poor”, M—“Medium”, S—“Significant”.

In addition to the survey, the respondents solved only the PSWT subtests Rotations and Views (PSWT-R and PSWT-V), since these areas are most related to the topics covered in the computer animation course.

PSVT was chosen as a measurement instrument because it is widely used in educational research and is specifically intended to evaluate progress in visual–spatial ability after the educational process ([Yue, 2008](#B34-education-16-00947); [Guay, 1977b](#B13-education-16-00947); [Martín-Dorta et al., 2008](#B21-education-16-00947); [Kaplan et al., 2021](#B16-education-16-00947)).

In this study, an adapted version of the PSVT was used, developed in accordance with modern examples from the literature ([Yue, 2008](#B34-education-16-00947); [Branoff, 2000](#B4-education-16-00947)), including a high-resolution visual representation and the possibility of standardized online testing.

The translation and adaptation of the test for Serbian students were carried out through the process of bilingual translation and cross-validation, with the verification of understanding and clarity of instructional and test items. Translation was tested in a pilot group of 30 students, where no significant influence of language factors on performance was observed, which allows valid use of the test in a domestic context.

Unlike PSVT, other tests, such as MRT or MCT, focus on tasks such as “mental bending”, which were not directly represented in the teaching activities of the CA course and were not used in this research.

PSVT-R and PSVT-V together contain a total of 60 questions (30 questions in each subtest). To make the test as accessible as possible, an online version of the test was used.

The recommended time to complete each test was 20 min (about 40 s per question), with no way to go back to the previous questions.

### 3.3. Organization of the Study

The research was conducted in two phases of testing:

* The first test was conducted at the beginning of the semester for both groups.
* The second test was carried out:

  ▪
  :   In the 15th week of the semester (end of semester).

  ▪
  :   For the control group, in the 6th week of the semester.

As part of the research, three cases were analyzed:

* Case 1: Determining whether there is an increase in VSA after attending a CA course. A paired t-test was used for this analysis, which compared the results before and after the PSWT test in:

  ▪
  :   The entire experimental group.

  ▪
  :   The GB subgroup.

  ▪
  :   The GS subgroup.

Pearson’s correlation analysis between initial test results and individual progress was also conducted.

* Case 2: Checking if only repeating the PSVT (without attending a CA course) leads to an improvement in scores. A paired t-test was applied to the results of the control group (pre-test and post-test) to assess the effect of the test repetition itself.
* Case 3: Comparative analysis of the results of the PSWT pre-test and post-test in the experimental group, depending on the previous level of experience in working with 3D software. The aim was to determine whether previous experience has an impact on the level of progress in the development of VSA. A correlation analysis was performed for each category of experience.

The same group of students consisted of test takers who took both the pre-test and the post-test. Students who did not participate in the post-test were not included in the further analysis.

All participants were familiar with the objectives of the research and gave their voluntary consent to participate. Participation was voluntary, and students could withdraw at any time.

During the semester, students from the experimental group attended the computer animation course under standard conditions, without additional interventions or special treatment.

## 4. Research Results

### 4.1. Self-Assessment of VSA and Previous Experience with 3D Software

When asked about coping with a 3D environment, the majority of students in the experimental group estimated that they possessed an intermediate level of visual–spatial ability (VSA) (58%), while 23% rated their abilities as “easy”. The lowest number of respondents indicated the following options: “very difficult” (8%), “difficult” (5%) and “very easy” (8%).

A question about previous experience in using 3D design software yielded the expected results. The majority of students (43%) had no previous experience, 29% had poor, 18% had secondary, while only 10% reported significant experience.

In the control group, only 5% of students reported moderate experience with 3D software, 16% poor, and as many as 79% had no previous experience.

When it comes to navigating the 3D environment, 46% said “medium”, 34% “easy”, while the rest chose: “very difficult” (7%), “difficult” (5%) and “very easy” (8%).

### 4.2. Case 1: Effect of Computer Animation Course on VSA

#### 4.2.1. Results by the Entire Experimental Group

[Table 3](#table_body_display_education-16-00947-t003)a–c shows the results of the paired t-test for the entire experimental group. The null hypothesis was that there was no difference between the mean values before and after the course.

**Table 3.**
(a) Results of a paired T-test of all sampled students—Paired Sample Statistics. (b) Results of a paired T-test of all sampled students—Paired Sample Correlations. (c) Results of a paired T-test of all sampled students—Paired Sample Correlations Test.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

The results show that the average score on the PSVT increased from 35.85 to 42.93. by +7.08 points (t = 14.37, p < 0.05).

This represents a statistically significant difference between the results before and after the course.

#### 4.2.2. Results by Subgroups

[Table 4](#table_body_display_education-16-00947-t004)a–c shows the results for full-time and [Table 5](#table_body_display_education-16-00947-t005)a–c shows the results for self-funded students.

**Table 4.**
(a) Results of a paired T-test of full-time students—Paired Sample Statistics. (b) Results of a paired T-test of full-time students—Paired Sample Correlations. (c) Results of a paired T-test of full-time students—Paired Samples Test.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

**Table 5.**
(a) Results of a paired T-test of self-financing students—Paired Sample Statistics. (b) Results of a paired T-test of self-financing students—Paired Sample Correlations. (c) Results of a paired T-test of self-financing students—Paired Samples Test.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

* Full-time students (GB): an increase of +8.95 points (t = 15.19, p < 0.05).
* Self-funded students (GS): increase of +2.21 points (t = 5.06, p < 0.05).

Greater progress in full-time students may be associated with more intensive engagement during the course, including more classes and continuous work.

#### 4.2.3. Correlation Analysis

Correlation between the initial level of VSA (pre-test) and the progress after the course (personal progress score—PPS) is shown in [Table 6](#table_body_display_education-16-00947-t006):

**Table 6.**
Correlation between the initial level and the newly acquired level of VSA.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

* Whole group: r = 0.324;
* GB group: r = 0.318;
* GS group: r = 0.297.

The obtained weak correlation indicates that the baseline level of VSA did not have a decisive impact on the progress achieved during the course.

### 4.3. Case 2: Effect of Retesting Itself

In order to determine if an increase in scores could only occur due to retaking the test, a paired T-test was applied to the control group ([Table 7](#table_body_display_education-16-00947-t007)a–c).

**Table 7.**
(a) Results of a paired T-test of control group students—Paired Sample Statistics. (b) Results of a paired T-test of control group students—Paired Sample Correlations. (c) Results of a paired T-test of control group students—Paired Samples Test.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

The result shows an increase of +1.76 points (t = 4.50, p < 0.05).

Although a statistically significant increase was observed, its intensity was significantly lower compared to the experimental group (+7.08 points), suggesting that participation in the CA course was the main factor in the improvement of VSA.

### 4.4. Case 3: The Impact of Previous Experience with 3D Software

[Table 8](#table_body_display_education-16-00947-t008) shows the results of a comparative analysis of progress in VSA depending on previous experience with 3D software:

**Table 8.**
Results of comparative analysis.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

* No previous experience (N): +9.44 points;
* Poor experience (P): +7.28 points;
* Medium experience (M): +3.44 points;
* Significant experience (S): +3.00 points.

The highest improvement was recorded in students with no previous experience, while students with greater previous experience made less relative progress.

#### Correlation Analysis

Correlation between pre-test and post-test scores ([Table 9](#table_body_display_education-16-00947-t009)) by previous experience groups was analyzed:

**Table 9.**
Results of correlation between pre-test and post-test scores.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

* No experience (N): r = 0.396;
* Poor (P): r = 0.401;
* Medium (M): r = 0.427;
* Significant (S): r = 0.465.

The growth of correlation in line with the increase in previous experience indicates a ceiling effect—in more experienced students, progress in VSA was limited due to the high initial level of ability.

### 4.5. Summary Conclusion of [Section 4](#sec4-education-16-00947)

The results indicate that attending the CA course significantly contributed to the development of students’ visual–spatial abilities. Progress was more pronounced among students with no prior experience with 3D software, indicating the potential of this type of educational intervention to improve VSA and reduce the gap in initial competencies.

### 4.6. Limitations of Research

When interpreting the results, the following limitations of the study should be taken into consideration:

* Self-sampling: Participation in the course and in the research was voluntary, which may lead to over-participation by more motivated students.
* Self-assessment of previous experience: Previous experience with 3D software was assessed through a self-assessment, which may be subject to subjective errors and different assessment standards.
* Possible influences of external factors: Level of engagement during the course, individual motivation, and previous exposure to similar activities were not controlled for and could have affected the variability of results.

## 5. Discussion: Visual–Spatial Ability as a Foundation for 21st-Century Competencies

Visual–spatial ability (VSA) is becoming increasingly important with the rapid development and integration of emerging technologies such as computer graphics, computer animation, data visualization, virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR), and supercomputing. Consequently, enhancing VSA may support the development of competencies relevant for digital and creative careers, and for meeting the demands of the modern labor market ([European Commission, 2018](#B9-education-16-00947); [OECD, 2019](#B24-education-16-00947); [Roca-González et al., 2017](#B26-education-16-00947)).

International frameworks such as ([OECD, 2019](#B24-education-16-00947)) and ([European Commission, 2018](#B9-education-16-00947)) emphasize the importance of transversal competencies—among which visual reasoning, digital content creation, and problem-solving in virtual environments rely heavily on well-developed visual–spatial abilities.

Therefore, exploring whether and how these cognitive abilities can be developed through targeted educational interventions is of great pedagogical relevance.

This study investigated whether participation in a Computer Animation (CA) course can contribute to improving VSA, and whether any observed increases could be attributed to test repetition effects. The results demonstrate that attending the CA course had a significant positive impact on VSA, as evidenced by the paired t-test results, which showed a statistically significant difference between pre-test and post-test mean scores.

From a theoretical perspective, these findings can be interpreted through the lens of embodied cognition and cognitive load theory. The observed improvements suggest that active engagement with 3D environments, such as those present in computer animation courses, enables learners to develop spatial reasoning through simulated interaction with virtual objects, supporting embodied learning processes ([Castro-Alonso et al., 2024](#B5-education-16-00947); [Lehrman, 2025](#B18-education-16-00947)).

Furthermore, the greater gains observed among students without prior experience may be explained by the interaction between embodied learning and cognitive load mechanisms, where structured activities reduce cognitive overload and facilitate schema construction in complex spatial tasks ([Zou et al., 2025](#B35-education-16-00947)). This aligns with recent findings showing that embodied and technology-enhanced learning environments significantly improve spatial reasoning, working memory, and engagement ([Chang & Aberash, 2026](#B6-education-16-00947)).

Similar findings have been reported in numerous studies emphasizing the role of CAD, computer animation, and 3D modeling courses in improving spatial visualization abilities ([Sorby, 2009](#B27-education-16-00947); [Yue, 2008](#B34-education-16-00947); [Rajeb et al., 2025](#B25-education-16-00947); [Martín-Dorta et al., 2008](#B21-education-16-00947); [Doloritos Mico et al., 2025](#B8-education-16-00947)).

The positive effect of active engagement with 3D technologies on VSA observed in this study is consistent with the findings of [Medina Herrera et al.](#B22-education-16-00947) ([2024](#B22-education-16-00947)), who reported a 25% increase in VSA through VR- and AR-enhanced instruction. Furthermore, the observed gains in VSA align with broader trends reported by [Roca-González et al.](#B26-education-16-00947) ([2017](#B26-education-16-00947)), who demonstrate that immersive 3D virtual environments can effectively support the development of VSA and related competencies crucial for the digital era ([Roca-González et al., 2017](#B26-education-16-00947)).

An interesting pattern emerged when analyzing results by subgroup: although both full-time and self-financing students improved, the full-time students exhibited greater gains. This is likely attributable to their more consistent involvement with the CA course—they attended more frequent and longer sessions, which aligns with the well-established principle that both qualitative and quantitative aspects of instructional design contribute to learning outcomes ([Sorby, 2009](#B27-education-16-00947)). [Ardebili](#B1-education-16-00947) ([2006](#B1-education-16-00947)) similarly found that the intensity and duration of 3D modeling courses significantly affect the degree of improvement in spatial abilities.

The analysis also revealed a weak correlation between initial VSA levels and subsequent gains. Several factors could contribute to this: individual differences in motivation, engagement, and even misinterpretation of certain test elements (e.g., color, texture, lighting cues in 3D representations). Moreover, external factors such as fatigue, interest level, and personal circumstances could have influenced performance gains.

This is an open-access research article published in *Education Sciences* (MDPI, 2026, Volume 16, Issue 6, 947) authored by Marjana Pardanjac, Snežana Vitomir Jokić, Biljana Radulović, Ivana Berković, Eleonora Brtka, and Nadežda Ljubojev from the Technical Faculty "Mihajlo Pupin," University of Novi Sad, Serbia.

**Purpose:** The study examines whether participation in a Computer Animation (CA) course can enhance visual–spatial abilities (VSAs), thereby supporting the development of 21st-century competencies such as digital literacy, creative problem-solving, and interaction with virtual/3D environments.

**Methodology:** A total of 346 students participated—231 in the experimental group (attending the CA course) and 115 in the control group. The Purdue Spatial Visualization Test (PSVT) was used to assess VSA before and after the course. The experimental group was further divided into full-time (budget) students (GB, n=154) and part-time self-financing students (GS, n=77). The study ran over three winter semesters (2022/2023, 2023/2024, 2024/2025). Three cases were analyzed: (1) impact of CA course participation, (2) test–retest effects, and (3) role of prior 3D software experience.

**Key Results:**
- The experimental group showed a statistically significant VSA improvement of +7.08 points (t=14.37, p<0.05).
- Full-time students (GB) improved by +8.95 points, while part-time self-financing students (GS) improved by +2.21 points, suggesting that more intensive course attendance leads to greater progress.
- The control group showed minimal gains of +1.76 points, confirming that course participation—not test repetition—drove improvements.
- Students with no prior 3D software experience showed the greatest improvement (+9.44 points), followed by poor (+7.28), medium (+3.44), and significant (+3.00) experience groups, indicating a "ceiling effect" for more experienced students.
- A weak correlation between initial VSA level and progress (r≈0.3) suggests baseline ability did not decisively impact gains.

**Conclusion:** Computer Animation courses can effectively support the development of visual–spatial abilities, which are foundational for digital and creative 21st-century competencies. The study bridges cognitive research on spatial abilities with applied educational practices in digitally mediated learning environments.

**Limitations:** Self-sampling, self-assessment of prior experience, and uncontrolled external factors (motivation, engagement) were noted as limitations.

FEATURE The Importance of Identifying Spatial Skills in Talented Students Jonathan Wai, PhD1 and Joni M. Lakin, PhD2 Abstract: Students’ talent and potential cannot be served until they are recognized by schools or caregivers.
While the ﬁeld of gifted education has had success in identifying many students with talents in reading and mathematics, those with spatial talents are often overlooked. This article reviews how we might identify spatial talent using traditional tests as well as observations during planned activities. Identifying spatial talent is an area in need of further research and assessment development.
Keywords: assessment, identiﬁcation, talent development, spatial talent, science, technology, engineering, mathematics T his article explores the why and how of identifying or recognizing the spatial talents of students through advanced education, gifted and talented education, and similar services, and then provides some suggestions on what to do after identiﬁcation. While there is debate in the ﬁeld about the term “gifted” and the value of formal identiﬁcation processes, and around which tests should be used (Gentry, 2022; Meyer & Plucker, 2022), we believe there is substantial value in a process that is objective and standardized (simply meaning everyone takes the same test in the same way) that gives every student an opportunity to demonstrate potential and have their talent more fully developed (Subotnik et al., 2011). Well-developed standardized tests measure developed aptitudes that matter and operate in the real world no matter what they are labeled, and removing the use of these tests simply means that other, typically more subjective identiﬁcation processes with less robust evidence in support of their use, will ﬁll the gap. Of course, which tools to use in the identiﬁcation process depends on the student and the program services.
Identiﬁcation is also a practical issue. The 2020-2021 State of the States in Gifted Education (Rinn et al., 2022) reports that 41 out of 52 U.S. states and territories who responded to the survey had a state deﬁnition of giftedness and reported that they were required to identify students in alignment with that deﬁnition. While most states leave the exact identiﬁcation process to the districts, there are 10 with mandated processes and other states that constrain the options available for identiﬁcation. Thus, identiﬁcation is largely a local issue, and ﬂexibility in meeting state policies comes down to district, school, and ultimately individual coordinator priorities and interpretations of the policy. The changing of policy is quite challenging—and in many cases there is the risk that changing the policy at all may remove legislative support for gifted education given how often the area is under attack. The Marland Report—a document providing the foundation for many state policies—did mention the importance of spatial reasoning talents (Wai et al., 2022), but in many cases, perhaps due to the fact that almost all currently used tests focus solely on math and verbal reasoning, spatial talents remain neglected (Lubinski, 2010).

“ INCORPORATING GIS ACROSS THE CURRICULUM CAN NOT ONLY ENGAGE THE SPATIALLY TALENTED STUDENTS, BUT POTENTIALLY NURTURE THOSE SKILLS IN OTHER STUDENTS.” 178 GIFTED CHILD TODAY July 2024 In this article, we describe the evidence speciﬁcally for identifying spatial talents so that these talents can be more fully developed.
Why Identify Spatial Talents?
The core purpose of identifying students with any kind of talent is to match that talent with developmentally appropriate educational or other programming (Assouline et al., 2015; Lubinski & Benbow, 2000; Subotnik et al., 2011). A common misconception of those who work outside gifted education is that students with academic gifts will naturally perform well in all areas of academic performance. This is rarely the case. Lohman et al. (2008) found that only one-third of the highest performing (stanine 9 - top 4%) students had a ﬂat proﬁle with no signiﬁcant strength or weakness across the three batteries of CogAT (verbal, quantitative, or nonverbal).
The vast majority of students had a relative weakness in one or more domains.
VanTassel-Baska et al. (2007) demonstrated the importance of considering domain scores when identifying academic potential among students from low-income families. Students from low-income backgrounds that participated in their study were much more likely to have one area of cognitive strength rather than uniformly high ability across all of the domains of the tests. In a three-year follow-up, these students’ achievement scores were highest in the same domain where they had high ability scores previously.
What this means is that students have wide individual differences in their skill proﬁles, which are not just limited to math, verbal, and spatial reasoning (Lubinski & Benbow, 2000). The broader structure of abilities (Caroll, 1993) illustrates a wider set of established reasoning aptitudes that should also be considered. And no matter what we label these talents or whether we identify them or not, they will still operate in the real world (and most certainly will matter for each individual).
Longitudinal studies of talent search data similarly demonstrate that areas of strength in youth are associated with the domain of expertise as adults (Makel et al., 2016; Park et al., 2007). Spatial aptitude is incredibly important for a wide range of occupations in a variety of STEM ﬁelds and the visual arts (Uttal & Cohen, 2012; Wai et al., 2009), and even when it comes to patents and other innovations (Kell et al., 2013).
Why Use Tests?
The purpose of using standardized tests to identify potential talent is simply because this means everyone takes the same test in the same way (Koretz, 2009). This provides one reasonably objective indicator to help assess a student’s strengths (and weaknesses) so that the appropriate developmental curriculum in speciﬁc domains can be matched reliably and validly. The reason you’d use a thermometer to measure temperature rather than feeling someone’s forehead is simply because the thermometer will give you more accurate readings. This is no different when it comes to objective versus subjective measures (Sackett et al., 2008). This does not rule out using subjective indicators or various checklist procedures or nominations. An objective standardized test may most fruitfully be used in conjunction with a wide variety of indicators to make a broader, more holistically informed decision about student placement in services and programs. Ideally, as development unfolds, repeated assessments will be administered to allow students more pathways into gifted services. Early identiﬁcation—and continued identiﬁcation—can also help underserved students be more readily matched to challenging learning environments that can then accelerate or ratchet up their achievement so that they are able to compete at the state and national levels on their way to college or careers (Wai & Worrell, 2020).
Do Existing Tests Measure Spatial Talent?
In the established structure of cognitive aptitudes or “three-stratum theory” (Carroll, 1993), there is general reasoning at the top stratum due to what is known as the positive manifold, or the observation that all cognitive tests are positively correlated. Beyond general reasoning, broad abilities like ﬂuid reasoning reﬂect the ability to solve novel and complex problems while crystallized ability is most aligned to academic achievement, or the result of formal learning experiences. Within ﬂuid reasoning, there are three speciﬁc factors alignined to quantitative, verbal, and reasoning with abstract concepts. Visualization, though potentially part of ﬂuid reasoning, is also present as another broad factor in this model (Carroll, 1993).
Analyses of reasoning tests, particularly the radex approach of modeling task complexity, consistently yield math, verbal, and spatial factors (Johnson & Bouchard, 2007; Lubinski, 2004; Lubinski & Benbow, 2000). For the purposes of this brief review, we note that based on this empirically well-established hierarchical model of abilities, spatial reasoning is a core neglected and well measured construct distinct from math and verbal reasoning (Lohman, 1999).
Math and verbal reasoning are almost uniformly measured by nearly all educational standardized tests. This is true for the NWEA MAP tests, the NAEP, PISA, or the SAT, ACT, and the GRE. The Dental Admissions Test, however, still has a spatial reasoning measure, most likely due to the fact that 3D spatial reasoning is so fundamental to performance in this profession. Snow (1999) made the insightful observation that the tests are often a reﬂection of 179 vol. 47 n no. 3 GIFTED CHILD TODAY the structure or content of schools as they are currently composed. Schools value mathematical and verbal symbol systems and reasoning within those systems—and much of school is set up for students with these strengths. And it turns out that students with spatial reasoning strengths often face greater challenges when it comes to behavioral issues and academic underachievement (Lakin & Wai, 2020). In fact, we’re missing millions of students with spatial reasoning strengths when it comes to academic assessment systems, including G/T identiﬁcation systems (we calculate roughly 2 to 3 million missed based on current U.S. K-12 numbers). And because spatial reasoning is less correlated with socioeconomic status (SES) than math or verbal reasoning, more underserved youths from lower income backgrounds would be selected for G/T or other talent development programs using tests that incorporate spatial reasoning (Wai & Worrell, 2015).
As with other areas of reasoning and achievement, spatial reasoning has a few distinct factors that represent different kinds of skills within the spatial category. There are numerous tests that were designed to measure each, primarily for research purposes (Eliot & Smith, 1983).
Based on our review of the literature, two types of spatial reasoning—spatial visualization and mental rotation— are especially important for understanding individual differences and have been shown to consistently correlate to academic performance in mathematics, science, or other STEM ﬁelds.
Spatial visualization involves the ability to encode detailed visual information and reason using those visual representations. A good example of this kind of reasoning is the object assembly task (Ivie & Embretson, 2010), which asks examinees to look at a set of shapes and determine which of the response options can be created from those shapes (similar to providing Tangram pieces and asking the examinee what shapes can be made from those pieces; see Figure 1). This task involves noticing ﬁne distinctions in the size or angle of the shapes in order to rule out other response options. Another interesting test of visualization skills is embedded ﬁgures, which asks examinees to identify the presence of a target shape within a larger, more complex ﬁgure (see Figure 2). Gilligan et al. (2019) used this test format for a study with students ages 6 to 10.
Mental rotation involves the ability to imagine rotating 2- and 3-dimensional objects in space. By far the most used assessment of this skill is the Purdue Spatial Visualization Test-Rotations (Yoon, 2011), in which examinees determine how one abstract ﬁgure has been rotated and then imagine how another abstract ﬁgure could be rotated in the same way. A simpliﬁed example of this kind of question is shown in Figure 3. For younger children, 2D objects may provide enough challenge, such as the 2D rotation task (Figure 4) where examinees are asked if two objects are the same or different apart from their 2D rotation (based on Gilligan et al., 2019).

180 GIFTED CHILD TODAY July 2024 Current tests used in gifted education identiﬁcation, such as nonverbal reasoning tests, are often assumed to be measuring spatial reasoning, but in fact, they do not do that well, if at all in most cases (Lohman, 2005).
This is because spatial reasoning is related most closely to 3D mental rotation, which most nonverbal tests actually do not capture. Nonverbal tests, particularly those based on matrices may provide some measure of visualization skills, but also a large degree of general reasoning skills (Lohman, 1999). A nonverbal test will often minimize the demand on students’ visual imagination, such as avoiding overly complex folds (especially hidden, layered folds) on a paper folding task. Or a matrix reasoning item may be solved by visual patterns but does not draw on ﬁne distinctions of shape and orientation. Spatial skills are more strongly invoked when students have to make detailed comparisons of size, angle, or other visual features as well as when they are required to imagine rotating or otherwise transforming an object in their mind’s eye while problem solving. Clinical assessments like the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children have separate tests for ﬂuid reasoning (which includes matrix reasoning) and visuospatial reasoning that load onto distinct factors (Canivez et al., 2020). The UK’s Cognitive Abilities Test (CAT) also has separate nonverbal and spatial batteries. The spatial score is a slightly better predictor of math and science scores than the nonverbal score (GL Education, 2020).
How Might Parents, Teachers, or Schools Identify Spatial Talent?
Spatial reasoning skills exist on a continuum (and a normal or bell shaped distribution) just like math and verbal reasoning. This means that spatial talent will vary widely among students. Though all reasoning capacities are developed, unlike other areas of reasoning, spatial reasoning has been shown to grow more with experience (Uttal et al., 2013). Here we brieﬂy discuss ways that various stakeholders might consider better identifying spatial talent in their local contexts.
Norm-Referenced Tests One of the only norm-referenced tests of spatial talent for K-12 schools is the Spatial Test Battery developed by Johns Hopkins’ Center for Talented Youth (Stumpf et al., 2013), which is only available through their testing services and is designed for middle and junior high school students. Vocational assessments for adults also include spatial tests, such as the assembling objects format on the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (ASVAB; Defense Manpower Data Center, 2006).
Other Tests Without Norms Other tests are freely available, but do not provide normative information or interpretation of scores. For an informal process, these may be sufﬁcient. Some available tools include the Spatial Reasoning Instrument, which was made freely available and is designed for students ages 11-13 (Ramful et al., 2017). The full instrument and scoring key are available at https://serc.edu.au/spatial-reasoning-instrument/. The scoring key distinguishes items measuring spatial visualization, rotation, and perspective skills.
Another freely available test that is widely used, but provides just one highly challenging format, is the Purdue Spatial Visualization Test (Yoon, 2011). It is better for assessing spatial skills among high school students. For practitioners or teachers interested in digging into the academic literature, Okamoto et al. (2015) provide a nice overview of tests used by researchers with young children; the full tests may be available elsewhere.

181 vol. 47 n no. 3 GIFTED CHILD TODAY Rating Scales/Observation Tools The Teachers’ Observations of Potential in Students (TOPS), which is part of the larger U-PLUS ∼STARS program (Coleman, 2016), offers one of the only published tools to include spatial abilities. The TOPS is designed to capture teacher observations during high-level learning activities for elementary students (Stambaugh & Chandler, 2021). Teachers could use the indicators of spatial talent on their own or possibly with other educators as “look fors” in the classroom. The TOPS includes these indicators: - Has a good sense of direction.
- Figures out why and how things work.
- Takes objects apart and reassembles with speed and accuracy.
- Creates interesting shapes and patterns.
- Creates three-dimensional structures.
Some cautions on this tool include a lack of evidence for the speciﬁc types of skills associated with spatial ability. The tool includes several indicators based on the association of spatial skills with a “kinesthetic” learning style or type of intelligence. Both of these theories lack empirical support but continue to permeate educational practice (Brown, 2023; Pashler et al., 2008; Rousseau, 2021).
Teacher or Parent Observations Students’ spatial talents could also be observed when engaging in various types of problem solving. The curriculum guide by Hollett and Cassalia (2022) offers many cross-curricular examples of spatial thinking for grades 3-5, especially the activities related to visualizing, perspectives, dimensions, and math-related structure concepts. Hawes et al. (2015) provide examples for younger children including construction play, puzzles, drawing tasks, and paper folding. Any of these kinds of activities could be used alongside an observation tool like TOPS to document observations of students’ relative skills in spatial thinking.
What Should we do After Identifying Spatially Talented Students?
As we mentioned earlier, the purpose of identifying talent is to help match that talent with appropriate educational or other programming. So, think about existing programs (e.g., robotics, engineering, visual data science; see Coxon, 2013 for a variety of options for spatial programming) that are already provided in local schools or in extracurricular activities. The strongest evidence to date regarding the impact of interventions or training relates to spatial training interventions on improving spatial reasoning itself (e.g., Lowrie et al., 2018; Sorby, 2009; Sorby et al., 2018). Sorby’s work focuses on building spatial thinking skills through lessons on engineering drafting, including different types of perspective drawing as well as using computer-aided design (CAD) tools. Spatially talented students may also excel in geospatial tasks, including using geographic information system (GIS) tools. Alibrandi and Goldstein (2015) reviewed curriculum for middle school that connects geospatial thinking to social studies as well as science, English Language Arts, and math. Incorporating GIS across the curriculum can not only engage spatially talented students, but potentially nurture those skills in other students.
The research on the causal impact of spatial training programs on later outcomes, such as STEM career choice, is still underexplored, but this is true for much of gifted education programming (Wai & Benbow, 2021). While this research is important and needs to be done, we take the general view from the gifted education research community that challenging educational programs are useful and important for talent development (e.g., Assouline et al., 2015; Subotnik et al., 2011). Just as students who are in third grade but reading at the eighth grade level might be provided books at the eighth grade level, so should programming also be accelerated and matched to the skills of spatially gifted students. Some spatial curricula and interventions that might be useful are Moss et al. (2016), a guide on spatial activities that develop early mathematical thinking. Robinson et al.
(2018) link spatial and engineering through a tinkering curriculum, which relates to the popular idea of makerspaces as STEM learning venues. Flick and Lakin (this issue) explore a wide range of activities that can be integrated into an existing curriculum.
Differentiation on ability proﬁles or cognitive strengths is not the same as the recommendations that might be associated with learning styles (Lohman, 2005).
Instead of aligning instruction to students’ cognitive strengths, teachers should ﬁnd ways to use those strengths to build up all areas of students’ academic development (Callahan et al., 2022; VanTassel-Baska et al., 2007).
Students may also beneﬁt from instruction that emphasizes communication in their weaker areas. Many people think that students who have spatial strengths should be taught using more ﬁgures and pictures.
However, we know that these students are actually better at imagining shapes and relationships, so they beneﬁt less from ﬁgures. The visuals will actually be more useful to students with verbal strengths because they are less facile with visualizing! For students with spatial strengths, consider strategies that scaffold their learning from language, such as a graphic organizer that helps students follow a lecture or breakdown a textbook chapter. These 182 GIFTED CHILD TODAY July 2024 students may generate their own visual heuristics in math computation. This should be encouraged but also connected to traditional math concepts and representations.
Allow these students to exhibit and stretch their talents. They may show remarkable talent for 3D design and printing, so teachers can use their products as examples for others or they may need more challenging activities than other students. They may also create innovative visuals or representations of their learning, such as creating a detailed timeline of events based on a social studies unit. These products can inspire other students and spark creative collaborations among students with different strengths.
Conclusion At this time, the options for assessing spatial talents are limited, but not impracticable. Using low-stakes tests and observations, teachers can begin to identify and serve spatial talents in the classroom right away. As awareness of spatial reasoning grows, we hope that norm-referenced, high-quality assessments will become available to incorporate into formal gifted identiﬁcation processes, as required by many districts and states. We hope that gifted coordinators will consider including spatial reasoning into their identiﬁcation processes to help identify a larger pool of underserved talent, many from impoverished backgrounds.

args.summary:
This article by Drs. Jonathan Wai and Joni M. Lakin (published in Gifted Child Today, July 2024) argues that spatial talents in students are systematically overlooked in gifted education, which traditionally focuses on math and verbal reasoning. The authors advocate for identifying spatial talent through standardized tests and observations to better match students with appropriate educational programming, particularly in STEM fields.

Key points include:
- Most students have uneven cognitive profiles; only one-third of top-performing students show flat profiles across verbal, quantitative, and nonverbal domains.
- Spatial reasoning is less correlated with socioeconomic status than math or verbal reasoning, meaning incorporating spatial tests could help identify more underserved students.
- Existing standardized educational tests (e.g., SAT, ACT, NAEP, MAP) largely neglect spatial reasoning, though the Dental Admissions Test and the UK's CAT4 include spatial batteries.
- Two key spatial skill types are spatial visualization (e.g., object assembly, embedded figures) and mental rotation (e.g., Purdue Spatial Visualization Test).
- Nonverbal reasoning tests (e.g., matrix reasoning) are often mistakenly assumed to measure spatial reasoning but do not capture 3D mental rotation effectively.
- Available identification tools include: the Johns Hopkins Spatial Test Battery (norm-referenced, for middle school), the free Spatial Reasoning Instrument (ages 11-13), the Purdue Spatial Visualization Test, and the TOPS observation tool (Teachers' Observations of Potential in Students).
- After identification, spatially talented students should be matched with programming such as robotics, engineering, GIS tools, CAD, and spatial training interventions (e.g., Sorby's work).
- The authors estimate roughly 2-3 million U.S. K-12 students with spatial strengths are missed by current identification systems.
- The article was developed under grant #R305A210428 from the U.S. Department of Education's Institute of Education Sciences.

RESEARCH STARTER

# Digital native

A "digital native" refers to individuals born during or after the information age, particularly those from the late twentieth century into the twenty-first century. There is also discussion about first-generation digital natives, who experienced the internet's early days, versus second-generation digital natives, who have been exposed to advanced technology like smartphones from infancy. Understanding these dynamics is crucial as society adapts to the ongoing digital transformation.

## Full Article

A digital native is someone who was born during or after the information age, a period of emerging digital technology. The term “digital native” most commonly refers to those born at the end of the twentieth century and into the twenty-first century. Digital natives began interacting with digital technology at a young age and are unfamiliar with life without tools such as the [Internet](/research-starters/social-sciences-and-humanities/internet-aesthetic), cell phones, and computers. Digital natives (often identified as [millennials](/research-starters/social-sciences-and-humanities/millennial-generation), Generation Y, and Generation Z) stand in contrast to digital immigrants, who were born before the prevalence of digital technology and had to adopt it later in life.

### Overview

The term “digital native” was coined by writer Marc Prensky in 2001 in an article for the journal *On the Horizon* about an emerging issue in education; he also created the term “digital immigrant” in the same article. In the article, he was writing about the changing nature of teaching—students have grown up around digital technology, while their teachers did not—and how it is affecting the educational system. He argued that the discontinuity has changed how students think critically and process information, which has widened the gap between them and their teachers, who must adapt to the new environment. Prensky further noted that digital immigrants often retain an “accent” that blends outdated language and behavior, highlighting their struggle to reconcile the new and the old.

The primary trait of digital natives is the ability to receive information rapidly, often through parallel processes and [multitasking](/research-starters/computer-science/multitasking-computing), taking on many things at once. Digital natives, who became used to these skills through their formative years, have entirely different frameworks for learning from those of the digital immigrants who are their teachers. This can be as simple as a student being able to read and watch television at the same time or a much wider divide related to communication, networking, and connectivity in instruction. Another related issue is the disconnect between the attention of natives and the methodology of immigrants.

Beyond education, the concept of digital natives has become, in the broader sense, related to demographic and generational differences. The differences between the two groups—occasionally referred to as “analog versus digital”—are increasingly important as technology development continues to accelerate. Digital natives adapt to new technology almost instinctively, utilizing prior experience to intuit how to use something new; digital immigrants often struggle to keep up and often fail when they attempt to apply more traditional styles of thinking to new contexts.

The gap between digital natives and digital immigrants, known as the [digital divide](/research-starters/political-science/digital-divide), has further implications when examined on a global scale. Poverty in developing nations is a potent example of this gap between the connected and disconnected, making it clear that it is not just a generational concern and instead runs the risk of being an ever-widening issue. The concept of digital natives is not without some controversy, however, with some critics noting that learning the use of digital technology is more simply a matter of access and cultural capital.

In their 2015 book, *The New Digital Natives: Cutting the Chord*, Dylan Seychell and Alexiei Dingli draw a distinction between first-generation digital natives and second-generation digital natives (2DNs). First-generation digital natives grew up before the advent of smartphones, tablets, social networking, and widespread Wi-Fi and laptop use. Their web access started only when they were able to use a mouse or read, unlike their children, the 2DNs, many of whom first accessed the web via touchscreens as toddlers.

Research showed that the “digital native” concept was largely a myth—youth technology exposure did not automatically build critical digital skills, with computer and information literacy declining despite higher Information and Communications Technology (ICT) use. Generation Alpha, the generation born from the early 2010s onward, emerged as the first “Artificial Intelligence (AI)-native” generation, interacting with generative AI from early childhood. Scholars then preferred terms like “digital navigators.” Marc Prensky later reframed ideas toward AI-enhanced “third millennials” before his 2025 death.

args.summary:
This research starter article defines a "digital native" as someone born during or after the information age (late 20th century onward), who grew up surrounded by digital technology like the Internet, cell phones, and computers. The term was coined by Marc Prensky in 2001 to highlight the educational divide between digital natives (millennials, Gen Y, Gen Z) and "digital immigrants" (those who adopted technology later in life). Key characteristics of digital natives include rapid information processing, multitasking, and intuitive adaptation to new technology, while digital immigrants often retain an "accent" of outdated language and behavior.

The article discusses broader implications beyond education, including the global digital divide (especially in developing nations), and criticism that technology proficiency is more about access and cultural capital than age. It distinguishes between first-generation digital natives (who accessed the web via mouse/keyboard) and second-generation digital natives (2DNs, who used touchscreens as toddlers). Later research challenged the "digital native" concept as largely a myth, finding that technology exposure alone does not build critical digital skills. Generation Alpha (born early 2010s onward) is described as the first "AI-native" generation, and scholars have since preferred terms like "digital navigators." Marc Prensky later reframed ideas toward AI-enhanced "third millennials" before his death in 2025.
