# Future of Jobs: Why Cognitive Skills Will Shape the Careers of Tomorrow

[![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/81871329103545560200c31ecc512702dc7266da508b2aab8a2a3702473109ff?s=44&d=mm&r=g)](https://blog.cognifit.com/author/cognifit/ "Posts by CogniFit")   [CogniFit](https://blog.cognifit.com/author/cognifit/)  on 12/01/2025

*Your child won’t grow into the same world you did. Their future will unfold in an era shaped by AI, automation and rapid economic change – a reality where tools, jobs, and expectations shift faster than any curriculum can keep up with. The only advantage that endures is the human mind: its capacity to think, adapt, and learn in real time. And in a world where roles evolve overnight, cognitive skills are becoming one of the strongest predictors of future readiness.*

![](https://blog.cognifit.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/CogniFit271125.jpg)

**Future-Ready Thinking Starts in Childhood*. Image by Freepik*

If you are raising or teaching children today, you are preparing them for a world that will not resemble the one you entered as an adult. By 2030, their jobs, skills, and daily tools will be shaped by forces moving faster than any previous generation has experienced. They are growing up in an age defined by artificial intelligence, demographic upheavals, economic uncertainty, and global restructuring – all happening at once. And even as future careers continue to shift, the World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 emphasises a stable insight: [cognitive skills](https://www.cognifit.com/cognitive-skills) will determine how well young people navigate the changes ahead.

Analytical thinking, creativity, resilience, flexibility, agility – these are not buzzwords. They are the core capabilities that employers across 55 global economies say will determine who thrives in the next decade. As millions of jobs disappear and millions more emerge, cognitive skills will act as the anchor that helps the next generation adapt, learn, and reinvent themselves repeatedly.

This article explores the findings of the Future of Jobs Report 2025, explains why cognitive skills are becoming the foundation of the future workforce, and highlights how platforms like [CogniFit](https://www.cognifit.com/) can help individuals strengthen these abilities in a world where continuous learning is no longer optional.

## **A Global Workforce Under Transformation**

According to the [Future of Jobs Report 2025](https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/), global labour markets are undergoing one of the most significant transformations in modern history. Between 2025 and 2030, structural labour-market change is expected to affect 22 percent of all existing jobs. Employers anticipate about 170 million new jobs created and 92 million displaced, resulting in a net gain of 78 million roles worldwide. These changes are driven by multiple overlapping forces – technological advancements, economic pressures, demographic shifts, climate-related transitions, and rising geopolitical tensions. The report emphasises that no region or sector will remain untouched.

Yet despite the rapid advancement of AI and automation, the report highlights an important distinction: technology itself is not the primary barrier companies face. The real obstacle is the widening skills gap. Drawing on data from more than 1,000 companies, the report notes that the shortage of qualified talent remains the most serious barrier to business transformation today: nearly 40 percent of the skills required on the job are expected to change, and 63 percent of employers already identify skills gaps as the key challenge ahead. This gap is deepening as industries evolve, underscoring a global need for workers who think critically, solve unpredictable problems, learn quickly, collaborate effectively, and adapt to continuous change.

## **Cognitive Skills at the Heart of Future Employment**

One of the most important insights from the report is the rising value of cognitive and human-centric skills. Even as AI becomes deeply embedded in workplaces, **analytical thinking** remains the single most essential core skill for 2025 and beyond. It is followed closely by:

* creative thinking;
* leadership and social influence;
* resilience, flexibility, and agility.

The report’s list of fastest-growing skills by 2030 reinforces this trend. Alongside AI and big data, networks and cybersecurity, and technological literacy, **cognitive and social-emotional abilities dominate the list**:

These skills are not tied to a single industry. They define what workers in all sectors will need to navigate environments where tools change rapidly, workflows evolve, and economic structures shift.

The message is consistent across the report: **technology skills are necessary, but human cognition will remain irreplaceable.**

## **Job Creation: Where the Opportunities Will Be**

The report highlights the duality of employment growth. Some of the most significant increases in absolute terms will occur in essential and frontline roles, while others will expand in technology, education, and care. For example, agricultural roles alone are expected to grow by 35 million jobs by 2030 due to changes in global food systems and demographic pressure. Education and healthcare roles are also rising as populations age and youth populations expand worldwide.

At the same time, roles most exposed to automation – primarily routine, clerical, and transactional tasks – are projected to decline as AI, robotics and digital platforms continue to advance.

This divergence illustrates why cognitive skills matter across all job categories. Nearly every growing role, whether technical, essential, or human-centered, now depends on capabilities AI cannot fully replicate. Employers increasingly value workers who can interpret complex situations, exercise sound judgment, adapt to unfamiliar challenges, empathize with others, and solve problems creatively. These cognitive abilities form the foundation of long-term employability, allowing individuals to shift across industries, learn new tools, and stay relevant as work continues to evolve.

## **Why Cognitive Skills Matter Across All Job Categories**

Automation is reshaping the tasks people perform, shifting human work toward what requires deeper [thinking](https://blog.cognifit.com/what-is-nonlinear-thinking-and-when-to-use-it/). Analytical reasoning enables workers to interpret information, solve novel problems, and make decisions in uncertain environments. Creative thinking supports innovation in both technical and human-centered roles. Resilience and flexibility help workers cope with new technologies, shifting expectations, and economic volatility.

Whether someone becomes a nurse, a renewable-energy engineer, a software developer, a teacher, or a logistics manager, these cognitive abilities underpin success in every profession.

For young people entering the workforce, these skills form the foundation of every career transition they will make.  For adults already in their careers, **cognitive agility determines how effectively they can adapt, retrain, and stay relevant.**

## **Upskilling and Reskilling: A Global Priority**

One of the clearest messages from the Future of Jobs Report 2025 is the scale of training required over the next decade. According to the report, if the global workforce were represented by 100 people, 59 would need reskilling or upskilling by 2030 – and 11 of them are unlikely to receive the training they need. This gap places more than 120 million workers at medium-term risk of redundancy.

As AI accelerates and job structures continue to shift, employers are intensifying their focus on developing adaptable, cognitively strong workforces able to learn new tools and navigate evolving environments.

## **Demographic Shifts and the Rising Demand for Cognitive Skills**

Demographic change is reshaping global labour demand. Aging populations increase the need for healthcare workers, while expanding youth populations in other regions drive demand for teachers and educators.

These pressures amplify the importance of cognitive and interpersonal skills – such as motivation, teaching, mentoring, talent management, and social influence. As workplaces become more complex, the ability to communicate effectively, adapt to different learning needs, and operate within diverse environments becomes increasingly essential.

Cognitive abilities form the foundation of these capacities. They influence how individuals process information, respond to changing demands, and manage complex social or educational situations.

In this landscape, digital tools that support cognitive assessment and structured cognitive training can be particularly valuable. CogniFit provides dedicated platforms for different professional settings – an [educational platform](https://www.cognifit.com/educational-technology) that allows teachers and institutions to work with students on cognitive development, and a [health-professional platform](https://www.cognifit.com/medical-platform) designed to help clinicians monitor and assess cognitive profiles in their patients. These tools offer structured ways to understand cognitive strengths and challenges, supporting professionals as they navigate the growing demands created by demographic shifts.

## **Why Cognitive Skills Training Should Begin Early**

The pace of technological and economic change means that cognitive development is no longer just a developmental milestone – it is a **strategic advantage**.

Children who build strong [reasoning](https://www.cognifit.com/executive-functions), [memory](https://www.cognifit.com/memory), [attention,](https://www.cognifit.com/attention) and cognitive [flexibility](https://www.cognifit.com/science/shifting) early in life have an easier time learning new technologies, adjusting to change, and acquiring new skills later on. The report emphasises curiosity and lifelong learning as essential qualities for future workers.

Developing cognitive capabilities early helps build the foundation for continuous learning and long-term adaptability.

## **The Role of CogniFit in the Future Skills Landscape**

Platforms like CogniFit, which specialise in cognitive assessment and brain-training programs, align closely with the skills highlighted in the Future of Jobs Report.

CogniFit provides tools that help individuals understand their cognitive strengths and challenges, and offers training programs that support:

* Reasoning;

* Processing speed;
* Planning and others (more than 23 cognitive abilities in total).

[For families](https://www.cognifit.com/family-platform) thinking about the future of their children, CogniFit offers an accessible way to begin strengthening mental agility early. For adults, it provides opportunities to reinforce cognitive foundations that support career adaptability and continuous learning.

To explore cognitive assessment and training options, visit [**www.cognifit.com**](http://www.cognifit.com).

## **A Changing World Demands a New Approach to Learning**

Workforce transformation isn’t coming someday in the future – it’s happening right now. Technology is accelerating, populations are shifting, and industries are being reshaped by forces that move faster than any of us can fully track.

In a world like this, cognitive abilities become the closest thing to solid ground. They help us learn new tools, adapt to unfamiliar situations, stay resilient under pressure, think creatively when routines stop working, and make thoughtful decisions when the world feels unpredictable.

In the years ahead, the people who thrive will be those who can adjust quickly, stay curious, and continue learning long after their formal education ends. That’s why cognitive fitness is no longer just a personal advantage – it’s becoming one of the most practical foundations for navigating a changing world with confidence.

# Study shows habitual checking of social media may impact young adolescents’ brain development

The study provides some of the first findings about social media's possible consequences on the development of adolescent brains.

By the College of Arts and Sciences, Tuesday, January 3rd, 2023

![People on their cellphones looking at social media.](https://www.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/hero_socialmedia-1200x675.jpg)

In one of the first long-term studies on adolescent neural development and technology use, researchers at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill report adolescents’ habitual checking of social media is linked with subsequent changes in how their brains respond to the world around them.

The study, published today in JAMA Pediatrics, reveals that adolescents’ brains may become more sensitive when anticipating social rewards and punishments over time with increased social media usage. 

“The findings suggest that children who grow up checking social media more often are becoming hypersensitive to feedback from their peers,” said Eva Telzer, a professor in UNC-Chapel Hill’s psychology and neuroscience department and a corresponding author. 

Researchers tracked 169 students recruited from public middle schools in rural North Carolina over three years. At the beginning of the study, participants reported how often they checked three popular social media platforms — Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat. Their answers ranged from less than once to more than 20 times a day. Participants underwent yearly brain imaging sessions while completing the social incentive delay task, which measures brain activity when anticipating social feedback from peers. 

“While this increased sensitivity to social feedback may promote future compulsive social media use, it could also reflect a possible adaptive behavior that will allow teens to navigate an increasingly digital world,” says Maria Maza, a doctoral student in psychology and one of the study’s two lead authors. 

Social media platforms deliver a constant and unpredictable stream of social feedback in the form of likes, comments, notifications and messages. 

“These social inputs are frequent, inconsistent and often rewarding, making them especially powerful reinforcers that can condition users to check social media repeatedly,” said Kara Fox, co-lead author of the study and a doctoral student in psychology.  

Other studies have shown that 78% of 13- to 17-year-olds report checking their mobile devices at least hourly; 35% of teens report using at least one of the top five social media platforms almost constantly. The study findings suggest that checking social media repeatedly among young teens ages 12 to 13 may be associated with changes in how their brains develop over a three-year period. The brains of adolescents who checked social media often – more than 15 times per day, became more sensitive to social feedback.

“Most adolescents begin using technology and social media at one of the most important periods for brain development during our lifetime,” said co-author Mitch Prinstein, who also serves as the chief science officer for the American Psychological Association. “Our research demonstrates that checking behaviors on social media could have long-standing and important consequences for adolescents’ neural development, which is critical for parents and policy-makers to consider when understanding the benefits and potential harms associated with teen technology use.”

Additional authors include Seh-Joo Kwon, a doctoral student in the department of psychology and neuroscience, and Jessica Flannery, a previous postdoctoral fellow in the department of psychology and neuroscience. 

The research was supported by funding from the National Institutes of Health and the Winston Family Foundation through its [Winston National Center on Technology Use, Brain and Psychological Development](http://www.teensandtech.org/ "http://www.teensandtech.org/") established at UNC-Chapel Hill.

args.summary:
A study published in JAMA Pediatrics on January 3, 2023, by researchers at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill provides some of the first long-term findings on how habitual social media checking impacts adolescent brain development. The study tracked 169 middle school students from rural North Carolina over three years, examining their social media checking habits (Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat) and conducting yearly brain imaging sessions using the social incentive delay task to measure brain activity when anticipating social feedback.

Key findings: Adolescents who habitually checked social media (more than 15 times per day) showed increased neural sensitivity to social rewards and punishments over time, potentially making them hypersensitive to peer feedback. The study was led by Eva Telzer (professor of psychology and neuroscience), Maria Maza and Kara Fox (doctoral students and co-lead authors), and Mitch Prinstein (co-author and chief science officer for the American Psychological Association). The research was funded by the National Institutes of Health and the Winston Family Foundation.

# Long-term impact of digital media on brain development in children

* [Samson Nivins](#auth-Samson-Nivins-Aff1)[1](#Aff1),
* [Bruno Sauce](#auth-Bruno-Sauce-Aff2)[2](#Aff2),
* [Magnus Liebherr](#auth-Magnus-Liebherr-Aff3)[3](#Aff3),

[Save article](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y/save-research?_csrf=6F3TIwnRlaT2zB8eGUNdpjoW_kbqJV13)

* 74k Accesses
* 33 Citations
* 121 Altmetric
* [Metrics details](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y/metrics)

## Abstract

Digital media (DM) takes an increasingly large part of children’s time, yet the long-term effect on brain development remains unclear. We investigated how individual effects of DM use (i.e., using social media, playing video games, or watching television/videos) on the development of the cortex (i.e., global cortical surface area), striatum, and cerebellum in children over 4 years, accounting for both socioeconomic status and genetic predisposition. We used a prospective, multicentre, longitudinal cohort of children from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development Study, aged 9.9 years when entering the study, and who were followed for 4 years. Annually, children reported their DM usage through the Youth Screen Time Survey and underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging scans every 2 years. Quadratic-mixed effect modelling was used to investigate the relationship between individual DM usage and brain development. We found that individual DM usage did not alter the development of cortex or striatum volumes. However, high social media usage was associated with a statistically significant change in the developmental trajectory of cerebellum volumes, and the accumulated effect of high-vs-low social media users on cerebellum volumes over 4 years was only β = − 0.03, which was considered insignificant. Nevertheless, the developmental trend for heavy social media users was accelerated at later time points. This calls for further studies and longer follow-ups on the impact of social media on brain development.

## Introduction

Children are increasingly engaged with digital media (DM) more than ever before. For example, in the U.S., children aged 8–12 years, on average, spend 4 h and 44 min daily on DM for entertainment purposes[1](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR1 "Media, C. S. The common sense census: Media use by tweens and teens, 2019. Accessed June, 2022."), in addition to its use during school and homework. This rise in usage has sparked concerns among parents, caregivers, and policymakers regarding its potential adverse effects on the developing brains of children. However, research in this domain remains inconclusive and somewhat contradictory.

Concerning the DM's impact on cognitive outcomes, prior studies have reported both beneficial and detrimental associations[2](#ref-CR2 "Lissak, G. Adverse physiological and psychological effects of screen time on children and adolescents: Literature review and case study. Environ. Res. 164, 149–157. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envres.2018.01.015
                  
                 (2018)."),[3](#ref-CR3 "Kostyrka-Allchorne, K., Cooper, N. R. & Simpson, A. The relationship between television exposure and children’s cognition and behaviour: A systematic review. Dev. Rev. 44, 19–58. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dr.2016.12.002
                  
                 (2017)."),[4](#ref-CR4 "Sauce, B., Liebherr, M., Judd, N. & Klingberg, T. The impact of digital media on children’s intelligence while controlling for genetic differences in cognition and socioeconomic background. Sci. Rep. 12(1), 7720–7720. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-11341-2
                  
                 (2022)."),[5](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR5 "Thorell, L. B., Burén, J., Ström Wiman, J., Sandberg, D. & Nutley, S. B. Longitudinal associations between digital media use and ADHD symptoms in children and adolescents: A systematic literature review. Eur. Child Adolesc. Psychiatry. 1–24
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-022-02130-3
                  
                 (2022)."). Similarly, a recent review on brain development simply noted that DM's effects can be both positive and negative[6](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR6 "Wu, D., Dong, X., Liu, D. & Li, H. How early digital experience shapes young brains during 0–12 years: A scoping review. Early Educ. Dev. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/10409289.2023.2278117
                  
                 (2023)."). This inconsistency in findings can be attributed to several factors. First, the general term ‘digital media’ encompasses a wide range of activities, each potentially influencing development in distinct ways or even exerting contrasting effects. Therefore, it is crucial to differentiate between various digital activities, such as playing video games, watching television/videos, and using social media. Second, the age of the participants is a significant factor. For example, research by Orben et al. in 2022 showed that social media use could negatively affect psychological well-being during particular developmental stages, with these stages occurring at different times for boys and girls[7](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR7 "Orben, A., Przybylski, A. K., Blakemore, S. J. & Kievit, R. A. Windows of developmental sensitivity to social media. Nat. Commun. 13(1), 1649. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29296-3
                  
                 (2022)."). In another study, Soares et al. found that boys who spent more time watching television or playing video games at 11 years old, and more time using computers at 11 and 15 years old, showed improved working memory performance at 22 years old[8](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR8 "Soares, P. S. M., de Oliveira, P. D., Wehrmeister, F. C., Menezes, A. M. B. & Gonçalves, H. Screen time and working memory in adolescents: A longitudinal study. J. Psychiatr. Res. 137, 266–272. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpsychires.2021.02.066
                  
                 (2021)."). However, this association was not observed in girls. Third, and perhaps most critical, is the conflation of evidence from cross-sectional and longitudinal studies in reviews. Cross-sectional studies can identify correlations but cannot establish causality. Whereas longitudinal studies may even yield opposite results. For example, a longitudinal study using structural equation modeling has found a negative correlation between time spent playing video games and intelligence[4](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR4 "Sauce, B., Liebherr, M., Judd, N. & Klingberg, T. The impact of digital media on children’s intelligence while controlling for genetic differences in cognition and socioeconomic background. Sci. Rep. 12(1), 7720–7720. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-11341-2
                  
                 (2022)."). However, when controlling for baseline cognition and other background variables, the longitudinal analysis revealed that playing video games positively influenced changes in intelligence (β = 0.17). The initial negative correlation between video gaming and cognitive performance was interpreted as resulting from self-selection.

Longitudinal research on the effect of DM and brain development in children remains limited. A series of studies on a cohort of Japanese children observed that watching television increased grey matter volume in frontal areas[9](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR9 "Takeuchi, H. et al. The impact of television viewing on brain structures: Cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses. Cereb. Cortex. 25(5), 1188–1197. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bht315
                  
                 (2015)."), playing video games increased mean diffusivity in the white matter[10](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR10 "Takeuchi, H. et al. Impact of videogame play on the brain’s microstructural properties: Cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses. Mol. Psychiatry 21(12), 1781–1789. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/mp.2015.193
                  
                 (2016)."), and internet usage decreased grey matter volume in extensive brain regions[11](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR11 "Takeuchi, H. et al. Impact of frequency of internet use on development of brain structures and verbal intelligence: Longitudinal analyses. Hum. Brain Mapp. 39(11), 4471–4479. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1002/hbm.24286
                  
                 (2018)."). Although informative, this is a single cohort of less than 300 individuals, which varied widely in age, between ages 6 to 18. Brain development during this period is nonlinear, which was not accounted for in the statistical modeling. In 2023, Miller et al. assessed the impact of DM on functional connectivity over 2 years in a cohort of over 4000 children[12](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR12 "Miller, J., Mills, K. L., Vuorre, M., Orben, A. & Przybylski, A. K. Impact of digital screen media activity on functional brain organization in late childhood: Evidence from the ABCD study. Cortex 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cortex.2023.09.009
                  
                 (2023)."). They reported no effects exceeding a size of 0.2, the predetermined threshold for significance.

The ongoing debate over what constitutes a meaningful effect size continues without consensus in psychology and neuroscience. This issue is particularly relevant in large-scale studies like the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, where statistical significance may not equate to a meaningful effect for the individual[13](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR13 "Dick, A. S. et al. Meaningful associations in the adolescent brain cognitive development study. Neuroimage 239, 118262. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2021.118262
                  
                 (2021)."). The traditional criteria by Cohen, which categorizes effect sizes of 0.2 as small and 0.5 as medium, were arbitrary from the outset, with Cohen himself acknowledging the lack of solid evidence for these benchmarks[14](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR14 "Funder, D. C. & Ozer, D. J. Evaluating effect size in psychological research: Sense and nonsense. Adv. Methods Pract. Psychol. Sci. 2(2), 156–168 (2019)."). Funder and Ozer propose that effect sizes must be contextualized, and propose as guidelines that an r-value of 0.05 indicates a very small effect and 0.1 a small effect. The frequency of an event may also be crucial, as repeated events can accumulate effects over time, according to Abelson[15](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR15 "Abelson, R. P. A variance explanation paradox: When a little is a lot. Psychol. Bull. 97(1), 129–133. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.97.1.129
                  
                 (1985).").

Furthermore, when interpreting effect sizes, it is essential to consider additional factors. Even a small effect can have significant implications if it influences various aspects of an individual's life or interacts positively with other variables. Habituation or counteractive responses might mitigate an effect's impact[16](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR16 "Anvari, F. et al. Not all effects are indispensable: Psychological science requires verifiable lines of reasoning for whether an effect matters. Perspect. Psychol. Sci. 18(2), 503–507. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/17456916221091565
                  
                 (2023)."). In our analysis, we regard an annual effect size of 0.05 as meaningful. This threshold is deemed appropriate, considering the cumulative influence of DM and the potential for an effect on a general ability like attention to significantly impact schooling and everyday life.

Our study aimed to investigate the individual effects of DM usage on structural brain development in children aged 9.9 years at baseline (T0) over 4 years, adjusted for age, sex, SES, scanner sites, and genetic predisposition. We selected global cortical surface area (CSA) as the main outcome measure since previous studies have shown a strong relationship between global CSA and intelligence across different age groups[17](#ref-CR17 "Schnack, H. G. et al. Changes in thickness and surface area of the human cortex and their relationship with intelligence. Cereb. Cortex 25(6), 1608–1617. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bht357
                  
                 (2015)."),[18](#ref-CR18 "Skranes, J. et al. Cortical surface area and IQ in very-low-birth-weight (VLBW) young adults. Cortex. 49(8), 2264–2271. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cortex.2013.06.001
                  
                 (2013)."),[19](#ref-CR19 "Walhovd, K. B. et al. Neurodevelopmental origins of lifespan changes in brain and cognition. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 113(33), 9357–9362. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1524259113
                  
                 (2016)."),[20](#ref-CR20 "Fjell, A. M. et al. High-expanding cortical regions in human development and evolution are related to higher intellectual abilities. Cereb. Cortex. 25(1), 26–34. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bht201
                  
                 (2013)."),[21](#ref-CR21 "Williams, C. M., Peyre, H. & Ramus, F. Brain volumes, thicknesses, and surface areas as mediators of genetic factors and childhood adversity on intelligence. Cereb. Cortex. 33(10), 5885–5895. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bhac468
                  
                 (2022)."),[22](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR22 "Vuoksimaa, E. et al. The genetic association between neocortical volume and general cognitive ability is driven by global surface area rather than thickness. Cereb. Cortex. 25(8), 2127–2137. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bhu018
                  
                 (2015)."). Moreover, we used cortical surface area rather than cortical thickness because studies have consistently reported an association of environmental variables, such as SES, on cortical surface area rather than on cortical thickness[23](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR23 "Judd, N. et al. Cognitive and brain development is independently influenced by socioeconomic status and polygenic scores for educational attainment. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 117(22), 12411–12418. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2001228117
                  
                 (2020).").

We further investigated the individual brain structures, i.e., the volumes of the striatum and cerebellum, which have been implicated in cross-sectional studies of DM usage[24](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR24 "Kühn, S., Gallinat, J. & Mascherek, A. Effects of computer gaming on cognition, brain structure, and function: A critical reflection on existing literature. Dialogues Clin. Neurosci. 21(3), 319–330. 
                  https://doi.org/10.31887/DCNS.2019.21.3/skuehn
                  
                 (2019)."),[25](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR25 "Pujol, J. et al. Video gaming in school children: How much is enough?. Ann. Neurol. 80(3), 424–433. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1002/ana.24745
                  
                 (2016)."). In general, global CSA tends to increase during this period of childhood a part of normal development with a peak age at 11 years of age[26](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR26 "Bethlehem, R. A. I. et al. Brain charts for the human lifespan. Nature 604(7906), 525–533. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04554-y
                  
                 (2022)."). Building upon our prior research findings[4](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR4 "Sauce, B., Liebherr, M., Judd, N. & Klingberg, T. The impact of digital media on children’s intelligence while controlling for genetic differences in cognition and socioeconomic background. Sci. Rep. 12(1), 7720–7720. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-11341-2
                  
                 (2022)."), we hypothesized that DM usage, particularly playing video games, would be associated with an increase in global CSA. Since DM usage differs between sexes[27](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR27 "Bagot, K. S. et al. Youth screen use in the ABCD® study. Dev. Cogn. Neurosci. 57, 101150. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2022.101150
                  
                 (2022)."), we will study the effect of sex on these relationships.

## Results

### Baseline characteristics

Of the 11,875 children from the ABCD study cohort, 6469 children (age, mean (SD) = 9.9 (0.6) years; boys, n (%) = 3369 (52.1%)) fulfilled our inclusion criteria and were included at the T0 visit (i.e., 9–11 years of age). Of these, 4610 children (age = 12.0 (0.7) years; boys = 2487 (53.9%)) were included at the T2 (i.e., 2 years later) visit, and 1697 children (age = 13.4 (0.6) years; boys = 949 (55.9%)) were included at the T4 (i.e., 4 years later) visit. 1462 children had usable data for all three-time points.

The estimated time spent by these children on DM types at T0 was 0.5 h/day for using social media, 0.9 h/day for playing video games, and 2.1 h/day for watching television/videos (Table [1](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Tab1)).

**Table 1 Descriptive characteristics of the sample.**

Compared to the T0 visit, the estimated time spent using DM types significantly increased over 4 years in the overall cohort and in boys and girls (Table [1](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Tab1)). ### Normal brain developmental trajectory

Overall development followed an inverted U-shaped developmental trend for global CSA, striatum and cerebellum volumes between mid-childhood and early adolescence, i.e., age-related increase during mid-childhood and subsequently decrease during early adolescence. According to the fitted model, the global CSA, striatum, and cerebellum volumes peaked at 10.6, 10.9, and 15.4 years, respectively (Fig. [1](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Fig1)a).

### Interaction of DM usage and time on brain development

There were multiple interactions between the average DM usage and both linear and quadratic effects of time on brain development (Table [2](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Tab2)). Only the significant interactions that survived Bonferroni corrections (p < 0.003) will be discussed below.

### Social media usage

We found a significant interaction between average social media usage and both linear and quadratic effects of time (i.e., average social media usage x time and average social media usage x time2, respectively) with cerebellum volume. Here, we observed a positive association of social media usage and time with cerebellum volumes for a linear term (β = 0.02) but a negative association of social media usage and time with cerebellum volumes for a quadratic term (β = − 0.02) (Table [2](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Tab2)). The consequence of these effects is illustrated in (Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Fig3)a,c); there is a slight difference in trajectory, which results in an earlier decline and lower volume at the last time-point.

There was no significant interaction between social media usage and time with other brain regions studied (i.e., global CSA and striatum volumes) (Table [2](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Tab2)).

### Playing video games

In contrast to social media usage on brain development, we observed a significant positive interaction between average time spent playing video games and a quadratic effect of time (but not linear) with cerebellum volume (β = 0.01) (Table [2](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Tab2)). This resulted in a trajectory with continued increase throughout the study period and a larger cerebellar volume at the last time-point (Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Fig3)b,d).

There was no significant interaction between playing video games and time in other brain regions studied (i.e., global CSA and striatum volumes) (Table [2](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Tab2)).

### Watching television/videos

There was no significant interaction between watching television and time with any of the brain regions studied (i.e., global CSA, volumes of cerebellum and striatum) (Table [2](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Tab2)).

There were no significant three-way interactions between any DM usage, time, and sex with the brain structures studied. Therefore, we did not carry out separate analyses for boys and girls (eTable [4](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#MOESM1)).

### Additional analysis

In investigating whether DM estimates preceded changes in cerebellum volume, we observed a negative trend for high social media users with changes in cerebellum volumes (β = − 0.01; p = 0.10). Conversely, there was a significant positive association for high video game users with changes in cerebellum volumes (β = 0.02; p =  < 0.001) (eTable [5](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#MOESM1)).

We then investigated whether social media usage at T0 could predict total changes in cerebellum volumes (T4–T0) and found that social media usage at T0 was not associated with changes in cerebellum volumes (β = − 0.03; p = 0.16) (eTable [6](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#MOESM1)). The estimate (β = − 0.03) thus represents the overall effect size of social media usage over a 4-year study period.

Furthermore, after excluding time spent on video chatting or texting from social media usage, we still found that the direction of the observed effects between average social media usage on cerebellum volumes remained significant, with the same effect size (β = − 0.02; p = 0.002).

### Sensitivity analyses

When we excluded children who were born preterm, had low birth weight (< 2500 g), or had ADHD diagnosis, 3979 children fulfilled the criteria for eligibility, and the findings of the average social media usage or playing video games and cerebellum volumes remained significant (eTable [7](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#MOESM1)).

Further, our analysis was confined to children with MRI data available across all three visits (n = 1462), and despite this restriction, the observed effects between average social media usage or playing video games and cerebellum volumes remained significant (eTable [8](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#MOESM1)).

## Discussion

In this large prospective cohort study, we studied the long-term effects of DM usage on the development of the cortex, striatum, and cerebellum across three time points spanning between mid-childhood to adolescence, in children aged 9 to 11 years. Despite our initial hypothesis, we found that DM usage did not significantly alter the development of the global CSA or striatum volume. However, children who devote more time to playing video games had a weak increase in cerebellum volume during the critical developmental window of development (β = 0.01), while those who spent more time using social media had a subtle decrease in cerebellum volume (β = − 0.02). These associations persisted in subsequent analysis, even when factors such as preterm birth, lower birth weight, or those with ADHD diagnosis, were excluded, underscoring the robustness of our findings. And these associations also did not differ between the sexes. However, the effect size observed for this association was smaller than our predefined threshold of 0.05. Moreover, in analysing the accumulated differences in cerebellum volumes over 4 years were also very small, which is likely not of relevance to the individual. Nevertheless, this difference was accelerated during the last year (Fig. [2](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#Fig2)). Thus, it is relevant to conduct further research to analyse the long-term effects of social media on brain development.

The term “social media” consists of a broad spectrum of digital tools associated with social interaction, including social networking sites, text messaging applications, and video chatting. Previous studies examining the association between social media use and functional or neural outcomes in both children and adolescents have often either combined all these digital tools under the umbrella term “social media use”[4](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR4 "Sauce, B., Liebherr, M., Judd, N. & Klingberg, T. L., Vuorre, M., Orben, A. & Przybylski, A. K. Impact of digital screen media activity on functional brain organization in late childhood: Evidence from the ABCD study. Cortex 169, 290–308. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cortex.2023.09.009
                  
                 (2023)."),[30](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR30 "Mougharbel, F. et al. Heavy social media use and psychological distress among adolescents: The moderating role of sex, age, and parental support. Front. Public Health 11, 1190390.

We specifically included activities related to social media platforms and studied their singular long-term effect on cerebellum development. Even in this refined analysis, we still observed a persistent weak negative effect of social media usage on cerebellum volumes.

If the negative developmental trend for the cerebellum persists, it might be of significant concern, particularly considering that adolescence serves as the period when many psychiatric disorders have their onset[31](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR31 "Solmi, M. et al. The cerebellum is sensitive to environmental exposures both prenatally, as demonstrated by studies of maternal alcohol, maternal diabetes, hypoxia, and postnatal glucocorticoid exposure[38](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR38 "Limperopoulos, C. et al. The transition from childhood to adolescence represents a critical developmental phase characterized by hormonal and physiological changes, including myelination, strengthening of synapses, and selective pruning of neurons and connections. Social media users often contend with constant distractions, which can significantly impact their behavior, leading to inattention symptoms[43](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR43 "Samson Nivins, M. A. M. & Klingberg, T. Screen time use and longitudinal effects on ADHD symptoms in children. PsyArXiv2024.").                   https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eclinm.2018.12.005
                  
                 (2018)."), among adolescents. Based on these observations, one might speculate that a distinct window of susceptibility to emotion and frequent shifts in task stimuli might be key contributing factors to the observed decrease in cerebellum volumes. At the neuronal level, this could reflect the acceleration of the natural process of synaptic pruning and changes in myelination among high social media users, which would then appear as a decrease in cerebellum volume at a later time point.

Consistent with prior research[46](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR46 "Giedd, J. N. et al. Brain development during childhood and adolescence: A longitudinal MRI study. Nat. Neurosci. 2(10), 861–863 (1999)."),[47](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR47 "Lenroot, R. K. et al. Sexual dimorphism of brain developmental trajectories during childhood and adolescence. Neuroimage 36(4), 1065–1073. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2007.03.053
                  
                 (2007)."), we observed an inverted U-shaped trajectory in the development of the cortex during mid-childhood and adolescence, with girls reaching their peak earlier than boys. Synaptic density in human frontal cortex-developmental changes and effects of aging. Brain Res. 163(2), 195–205 (1979)."),[49](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR49 "Yakovlev, P. I., Lecours, A.-R., Minkowski, A. & Davis, F. Regional development of the brain in early life. 3–70. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1136/adc.43.229.388
                  
                 (University of Michigan, F. A. Davis Company, 1967)."). T. Errant gardeners: Glial-cell-dependent synaptic pruning and neurodevelopmental disorders. Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 18(11), 658–670. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn.2017.110
                  
                 (2017)."). During these stages of development, environmental exposure might guide selective synapse elimination in adolescence[51](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR51 "Kleim, J. A., Lussnig, E., Schwarz, E. R., Comery, T. A. & Greenough, W. T. Synaptogenesis and Fos expression in the motor cortex of the adult rat after motor skill learning. J. Neurosci. 16(14), 4529–4535 (1996)."),[52](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR52 "Bourgeois, J.-P., Jastreboff, P. J. & Rakic, P. Synaptogenesis in visual cortex of normal and preterm monkeys: Evidence for intrinsic regulation of synaptic overproduction. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 86(11), 4297–4301 (1989)."). Supporting this notion, we found that children from lower SES quartiles exhibited smaller global CSA across development compared to their peers.

Although this is a longitudinal study with a large number of participants, the study has some notable limitations. First, this is an observational study, and therefore, we cannot establish causal inference. However, we adjusted for most of the covariates such as age, sex, SES, and genetics. Additionally, to mitigate selection bias, we ensured the inclusion of only one child per family. Second, the estimated time spent on various DM types was self-reported, introducing potential recall or accuracy bias. Nevertheless, it should be noted that studies have reported high test and retest reliability of self-reported behaviors among adolescents[53](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR53 "Brener, N. D., Billy, J. O. & Grady, W. R. Assessment of factors affecting the validity of self-reported health-risk behavior among adolescents: Evidence from the scientific literature. J. Adolesc. Health 33(6), 436–457 (2003)."). Third, the survey questionnaire utilized to capture DM usage from T2 visits onwards was modified compared with T0 or T1 visits in response to technological advancements and the heightened usage of DM among adolescents. However, we harmonized the survey questionnaires from the T2 visit onwards to maintain consistency with the earlier visits. Fourth, the response measure for the survey questionnaire in both T0 and T1 visits was set between ‘0 and 4+ hours’; this is one of the major drawbacks of the ABCD questionnaire. For example, a child who spent four hours engaged in video games or using social media would receive the same score as a child who spent 12 h, despite the significant difference in their exposure. Fifth, the ABCD questionnaire failed to capture information regarding the timing of DM usage, either during the day or night, thus impeding the exploration of the potential effects of bedtime DM usage on brain development. Finally, the survey questionnaires used in this study failed to capture any information regarding the genre of video games. Given that different activities and actions of video gaming may exert distinct impacts on brain development.

In summary, DM usage, particularly playing video games, does not alter cortical brain development during the 4-year window, but social media usage is weakly associated with a decrease in cerebellum volumes, a trend that was accelerated at later time-points. These findings should be continued by longer follow-up, and more detailed documentation of DM usage, but is a cause for concern regarding the usage of social media in children and adolescents.

## Methods

### Participants

The neuroimaging and behavioral data used in this study were obtained from the ABCD Study (data release 5.0; <https://abcdstudy.org/>; <https://doi.org/10.15154/1523041>), a longitudinal cohort of 11,875 children born between 2005 and 2009. These children were enrolled at ages 9–11 years from 21 research sites across the U.S. between 2016 and 2018[54](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR54 "Casey, B. J. et al. The adolescent brain cognitive development (ABCD) study: Imaging acquisition across 21 sites. Dev. Cogn. Neurosci. 08(32), 43–54. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2018.03.001
                  
                 (2018)."), with the intention of following them for a period of at least 10 years. This recruitment cohort closely matches the sociodemographic composition of the US population of 9–11-year-old children. Most of the children were enrolled through local elementary and charter schools at each data-collection site. A smaller portion was recruited through community outreach and word-of-mouth referrals outside of the school setting. Twins were identified and recruited from birth registries[55](/articles/s41598-024-63566-y#ref-CR55 "Feldstein Ewing, S. W. et al. Approaching retention within the ABCD Study. Dev. Cogn. This is a scientific article published in Scientific Reports (volume 14, article 13030, 2024) investigating the long-term impact of digital media on brain development in children. The study used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, a prospective, multicentre, longitudinal cohort of children aged approximately 9.9 years at baseline, followed for 4 years.

**Key Findings:**
- Digital media usage did not significantly alter the development of the global cortical surface area (CSA) or striatum volumes.
- High social media usage was associated with a statistically significant but small change in the developmental trajectory of cerebellum volumes (accumulated effect over 4 years: β = -0.03, considered insignificant).
- Playing video games was associated with a weak increase in cerebellum volume (β = 0.01).
- Watching television/videos showed no significant interactions with any brain regions studied.
- The developmental trend for heavy social media users was accelerated at later time points, warranting further study.

**Methodology:**
- 6,469 children at baseline (T0), with 4,610 at T2 (2 years) and 1,697 at T4 (4 years); 1,462 had data for all three time points.
- Children reported DM usage annually through the Youth Screen Time Survey; brain MRI scans were conducted every 2 years.
- Quadratic-mixed effect modelling was used, adjusting for age, sex, SES, scanner sites, and genetic predisposition (polygenic scores).
- The study differentiated between three types of digital media: social media, video games, and television/videos.

**Normal Brain Development:**
- Global CSA, striatum, and cerebellum volumes followed an inverted U-shaped developmental trajectory, peaking at 10.6, 10.9, and 15.4 years, respectively.
- Girls reached peak brain development earlier than boys.
- Children from lower SES backgrounds had smaller global CSA and cerebellum volumes with earlier maturation.

**Discussion:**
The authors note that while the effect sizes were smaller than their predefined threshold of 0.05, the accelerated negative trend for social media users at later time points calls for further research with longer follow-ups. The cerebellum is sensitive to environmental exposures and is implicated in psychiatric disorders. The study is observational and cannot establish causality, but controlled for multiple covariates including genetics.

# Summary: Social Media is Harming Adolescents at a Population Level

This chapter from the World Happiness Report 2026, authored by Jonathan Haidt and Zachary Rausch (NYU), argues that social media is causing direct and indirect harm to adolescents at a scale large enough to affect population-level mental health trends. The authors address two core questions: the "product safety question" (is social media safe for adolescents?) and the "historical trends question" (did social media contribute to the post-2010 rise in adolescent mental illness?).

The authors present **seven lines of evidence** organized in a legal-style framework:

**Testimony (Lines 1-3):**
1. **What victims say**: Surveys of Gen Z show high levels of regret. 34% of US teens wish Instagram didn't exist, 47% regret TikTok, and 50% regret X. 58% of college students would prefer a world without Instagram. UK surveys find 62% of youth believe social media does more harm than good for under-16s. Internal Meta research found 1 in 3 teen girls said Instagram worsened body image issues, and 37% of teen girls reported seeing posts that made them feel worse about their bodies.
2. **What witnesses say**: 44% of US parents identify social media as the single most negative influence on teen mental health. 42% of US principals believe smartphones/social media are major causes of deteriorating student mental health. 84% of US educators say social media contributes to student mental health issues. Meta's own research found 81% of clinicians say social media exacerbates anxiety disorders.
3. **What company documents reveal**: Internal TikTok documents acknowledge "compulsive usage correlates with a slew of negative mental health effects." TikTok executives stated the product "has baked into it compulsive use." Snapchat internally acknowledged ~10,000 monthly sextortion reports. Meta's founding president Sean Parker admitted they "understood this consciously. And we did it anyway." Meta employees described Instagram as "a drug" and themselves as "pushers."

**Academic Research (Lines 4-7):**
4. **Cross-sectional studies**: Heavy social media users (5+ hours/day) are about 2 times more likely to meet criteria for depression. A 2022 meta-analysis found depression odds increase by 13% for every additional hour of daily social media use. The risk elevation from heavy social media use is comparable to sleep deprivation and greater than poverty.
5. **Longitudinal studies**: Studies cited as "null" actually show significant associations when examining adolescent girls, heavy use, and internalizing disorders (anxiety/depression).
6. **Social media reduction experiments**: (Summarized as showing benefits from reducing use)
7. **Natural experiments**: (Summarized as showing causal evidence of harm)

The authors argue that the preponderance of evidence justifies policy action, and the cost of incorrectly concluding social media is unsafe (waiting until age 16 for accounts) is far lower than the cost of inaction (condemning millions to higher mental illness, self-harm, and victimization).
</summary>

This is a scholarly article from *Memory & Cognition* titled "Digital amnesia: The aftermath of a screenshot" by Sophia P. Fabrizio, Rebecca Lurie, and Deanne L. Westerman (published August 3, 2026). The study investigates the "digital capture effect"—the finding that memory is worse for photographed or screenshotted information compared to merely viewed information. The authors conducted seven preregistered experiments with 892 undergraduate participants.

**Background:** The photo-taking impairment effect has been well-documented, showing that taking photos or screenshots impairs recognition and recall memory. Three mechanisms are proposed: (1) divided attention (the capture task splits cognitive resources), (2) cognitive offloading (relying on an external store reduces encoding effort), and (3) attentional disengagement (the act of capture triggers general inattention). Screenshots are particularly associated with the goal of offloading.

**Key Findings:**
- Screenshotting led to pronounced memory costs with no consistent compensatory benefits across four measures.
- No improved source memory for screenshotted images (Experiment 2).
- No improved performance on modular arithmetic problems after screenshotting (Experiment 3).
- No enhanced memory for subsequently presented items after screenshotting (Experiments 4-5).
- A modest recall boost for a second block of art was found only under very specific conditions with lenient scoring.
- The findings suggest screenshotting imposes considerable memory costs without offering compensatory benefits, contrary to predictions from cognitive offloading theory.

**Conclusion:** The digital capture effect is robust, and the study found no evidence that screenshotting frees cognitive resources to benefit other tasks, working against the idea that automatic offloading compensates for memory impairment.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: What Is the Google Effect on Memory? | Neurosity ---
URL: https://neurosity.co/guides/google-effect-on-memory

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by AJ Keller, CEO of Neurosity (February 2026), explores the "Google Effect" — the brain's tendency to forget information it knows can be easily found online, treating search engines as external memory storage. 

**Key Findings & Research:**
- First documented in a 2011 study by psychologist Betsy Sparrow at Columbia University, published in *Science*. Participants who believed information would be saved to a computer remembered significantly less than those who believed it would be erased. Participants showed better memory for where information was stored than for the information itself.
- The Google Effect builds on "transactive memory" (Daniel Wegner, 1980s) — the brain's natural system of dividing memory labor with trusted partners. The internet is now the ultimate transactive memory partner.
- Adrian Ward (University of Texas, 2017) found that merely having a smartphone nearby reduces cognitive capacity, even when turned off.
- Matthew Fisher (Yale, 2015) found that searching online inflates people's belief in their own knowledge (source monitoring failure). Even unhelpful searches increased self-assessed knowledge.

**Neuroscientific Evidence (EEG):**
- The P300 component (a brain voltage deflection occurring ~300ms after encountering information) is smaller when people expect information to be externally saved — the brain invests less electrical energy in encoding.
- Theta oscillations (4-8 Hz) decrease when information is expected to be externally available, suggesting the hippocampus throttles encoding effort.
- When information is externally available, the brain shows increased prefrontal activation for meta-memory (tracking where to find things) while weakening the archive function (remembering the things themselves).

**Key Concerns:**
1. **Scale Problem** — Unlike human transactive memory partners (limited to ~150 people via Dunbar's number), the internet has no limit, enabling outsourcing across all domains.
2. **Depth Problem** — Digital retrieval is frictionless, requiring less processing time and emotional context, leading to weaker long-term memory traces.
3. **Confidence Problem** — Searching blurs the line between "I found this" and "I know this."
4. **Knowledge Scaffold Problem** — Deep encoding builds interconnected knowledge structures that support synthesis, analogy, creative connection, and critical evaluation. If the Google Effect short-circuits initial encoding, downstream consolidation and integration may never occur.

**Practical Recommendations:**
- Make encoding effortful for important knowledge (handwrite notes, test yourself, explain concepts to others).
- Distinguish between searchable facts and structural knowledge (only the latter supports genuine thinking).
- Use retrieval practice before reaching for a phone.
- Be aware of the confidence inflation effect after searching.

The article concludes that the deepest implication is about the nature of knowing — choosing what to remember is choosing what to think with, and in a real sense, who you are.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a meta-analysis research article published in Frontiers in Psychology (November 19, 2025) by Yamin Shen from East China Normal University, examining the effects of attentional distractions on reading comprehension in digital environments. The study synthesized 32 empirical studies (124 experiments) published between 2000-2025.

**Key Findings:**
- Overall effect: Hedges' g = -0.6411, indicating a moderate-to-strong negative effect of attentional interference on reading comprehension in online environments.
- Significant heterogeneity was found (I² = 88.3%), justifying subgroup analyses.

**Moderators with Significant Effects:**
- **Research design**: Between-group studies showed stronger negative effects (g = -0.81) than within-group designs (g = -0.32), with p = 0.015.
- **Interference type**: TV (g = -0.82) and music (g = -0.82) were most detrimental; interruption (g = -0.21) was least harmful. However, the overall moderating effect was not statistically significant (p = 0.076).
- **Age**: College students experienced greater negative effects (g = -0.72) compared to younger students (g = -0.20 to -0.27), though the overall moderation was not significant at p < 0.05 (p = 0.105).

**Non-Significant Moderators**: Individual consciousness/effort, time control, text type, reading device, and publication year did not significantly moderate the effect.

**Methodology**: The meta-analysis employed a mixed-effects model, used Hedges' g as the effect size measure, and included comprehensive literature searches across major databases (Web of Science, Scopus, APA PsycInfo, etc.). A funnel plot indicated no substantial publication bias.

**Conclusions**: Attentional interference in digital environments consistently impairs reading comprehension. The study supports cognitive load theory and recommends minimizing distractions (especially background music and videos), designing interactive online platforms that promote focus, using eye-tracking tools to monitor attention, and implementing tailored interventions to help students develop self-regulation strategies.

--- SOURCE 1: JMIR mHealth and uHealth - Promoting Self-Regulated Social Media Use on Smartphones With a Mobile Intervention App (Wellspent): Randomized Controlled Trial ---
URL: https://mhealth.jmir.org/2026/1/e56824

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in JMIR Mhealth Uhealth (Vol 14, 2026), evaluates the effectiveness of the Wellspent app, a customizable mobile intervention designed to promote self-regulated social media use. In a 3-week randomized controlled trial involving 70 iPhone users (mean age 26.2, 67% female), participants were assigned to either an intervention group (n=35) that received personalized full-screen reminders with the option to quit or continue social media use after exceeding self-defined time limits, or a control group (n=35).

**Key Findings:**
- The intervention group showed a significant reduction in daily screen time on their most problematic app by approximately 29 minutes (estimate=−29.35, SE 6.84, 95% CI −42.79 to −15.99; P<.001).
- A significant decrease in perceived problematic smartphone use was observed (estimate=−0.46, SE 0.18, 95% CI −0.80 to −0.11; P=.01).
- No significant reduction in problematic social media use or increase in self-efficacy was found.

**Intervention Features:** The Wellspent app incorporates behavior change techniques including goal setting, prompts/cues, feedback on behavior, self-monitoring, and substitution of behavior. Users can define daily time limits, customize reminder frequency and tone, select alternative activities, and set "Danger Zones" for vulnerable time windows. The app preserves user autonomy by allowing them to choose whether to quit or continue after each prompt.

**Background:** The study addresses the problem of problematic social media use, which has been linked to reduced well-being, impulse control difficulties, depression, loneliness, and stress. Existing digital self-control tools often lack customization and rely on restrictive mechanisms that undermine user autonomy. Wellspent aims to fill this gap by combining evidence-based behavior change techniques with flexible, user-driven customization.

**Conclusions:** The Wellspent app demonstrated short-term efficacy in reducing problematic smartphone use and screen time. By allowing users to tailor interventions to their personal goals, the app shows promise as a self-directed tool to support healthier digital habits. The trial was registered at the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00031767).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: The Impact of Smartphone Use on Brain Function in Adolescence: A Scoping Review ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2036-7503/18/2/43

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scoping review published in *Pediatric Reports* (2026, Vol. 18, Issue 2, Article 43) by Marks et al. from Augusta University, examining the impact of smartphone use on adolescent brain function. The review followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines and included 104 articles from 37 countries, with data collected from PubMed, CINAHL, and PsychInfo databases (search conducted February 2025, filtering for articles published 2022–2025 in English). The mean age of participants across studies was 13.91 years. Thematic analysis revealed five key themes:

1. **Psychological Disturbances** (n=52): The most prevalent theme. Subthemes included depression/sadness/suicidality (30 articles), anxiety/stress (27 articles), mental well-being/quality of life (17 articles), loneliness (5 articles), and body image distortion/disordered eating/self-esteem (5 articles). Problematic smartphone use (PSU) was strongly linked to depressive symptoms, and smartphone overdependence was associated with poorer academic outcomes and emotional functioning. Suicide plans and ideation were higher among adolescents with higher screen time, particularly males.

2. **Sleep** (n=43): Subthemes included sleep quality (25 articles), sleep duration/disturbances (22 articles), sleep onset (17 articles), daytime functioning (4 articles), and social jetlag (4 articles). Smartphone overdependence correlated with insufficient sleep, poor sleep quality, delayed sleep onset (up to 52 minutes later), and increased daytime sleepiness. Social media use before bed was particularly detrimental. Adolescent girls were more likely to suffer poor sleep quality.

3. **Socioemotional Functioning** (n=23): Subthemes included emotional regulation, social connectedness/emotional support, and social participation. Smartphones were used for emotional regulation, with mixed effects—some apps improved emotional regulation skills, but general/entertainment use led to difficulty managing emotions. Adolescents using devices for socializing and gaming over 3 hours daily reported higher anger levels and impulsivity.

4. **Executive Function** (n=14): A smaller but notable theme.

5. **Sensory Processing** (n=1): The least represented theme.

The review concludes that smartphones have a variety of primarily negative effects on adolescent brain function, and further research is warranted to determine causal relationships. The study can inform the general population about how smartphone usage affects adolescent brain functioning.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Digital Media, Cognition, and Brain Development in Adolescence ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-69362-5_4

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access academic chapter from the "Handbook of Children and Screens" (Springer, 2024) titled "Digital Media, Cognition, and Brain Development in Adolescence," authored by Marciano, Dubicka, Magis-Weinberg, Morese, Viswanath, Weber, and others. The chapter reviews the relationship between adolescent digital media use, cognitive development, and brain structure/function.

**Key Background:** Nearly half of US adolescents report being constantly online. Almost 1 in 4 adolescents show symptoms of problematic digital media use. Adolescence is characterized by a developmental mismatch: the socioemotional/reward system matures earlier than the cognitive control system (prefrontal cortex), making adolescents highly sensitive to rewards, social feedback, and peer influence. This makes digital media particularly gratifying.

**Brain Correlates:** Prolonged or problematic digital media use is associated with reduced functional and structural connectivity in top-down cognitive control networks (default mode network, central executive network) and increased activation in reward regions (striatum, VTA). The ABCD study (4,277 youths) found that frequent screen exposure correlated with greater maturation of visual/sensory brain areas and links to externalizing symptomatology. Social media use has been shown to activate the same neural reward systems as receiving money.

**Cognitive Effects:** Screen time exceeding 2 hours/day, combined with insufficient sleep and physical activity, is negatively associated with global cognition and academic performance. However, effects are generally negligible-to-small in the general population. Daily digital media use is associated with increased inattention symptoms on the same day.

**Key Limitations:** Most studies are cross-sectional, based on self-reports, and focus on general screen time rather than specific activities or content. Mental health conditions are rarely examined as potential underlying drivers. The term "problematic media use" is preferred over "addictive."

**Recommendations:** Future research should use longitudinal designs, trace data, validated cognitive assessments, and focus on causality. Personalized approaches to digital resilience are recommended over generic screen time limits. Policymakers should compel tech companies to share data and regulate inappropriate content. Educators should promote digital literacy and resilience. More research is needed on vulnerable populations (LGBTQIA+, Global South, low-income, mental health conditions) and positive uses of digital media for learning.
</summary>

This is a scholarly article by David C. Geary published in *Intelligence & Cognitive Abilities* (Vol. 1, Issue 2, 2025, published January 12, 2026) that proposes an evolutionary framework for studying human cognition. The article applies Tinbergen's (1963) four questions—how cognition evolved, what it is for, how it works, and how it develops—to organize research on human cognitive abilities, with a focus on fluid intelligence and two key brain networks: the frontoparietal network (FPN) and the default mode network (DMN).

The article argues that human cognitive evolution was driven primarily by within-species social competition (a "within-species arms race") rather than ecological pressures. As humans achieved ecological dominance through tool technologies and cooking, within-species competition for resource control became the primary selective force. This is supported by evidence that climate change alone cannot explain hominin brain expansion, and by historical population genetic studies showing repeated population replacements and boom-bust cycles.

The DMN, which is disproportionately larger in humans than in other primates, supports self-referential mental models, mental time travel, creative cognition, and social cognition—competencies that would have provided competitive advantages. The FPN supports working memory, controlled problem-solving, and fluid intelligence. The article details how these networks interact, with the salience network orchestrating switching between them during problem-solving.

The article also discusses modern implications: fluid abilities predict academic learning and work performance, and higher cognitive abilities are linked to higher social status, which historically reduced mortality risks. Disruptions to these networks (e.g., in schizophrenia) are associated with social and occupational difficulties. The article provides a multidimensional framework for future empirical studies integrating evolutionary pressures, brain mechanisms, cognitive processes, and developmental trajectories.

--- SOURCE 14: Frontiers | Rethinking perception and cognition in the digital environment ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cognition/articles/10.3389/fcogn.2023.1266404/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a conceptual analysis article published in Frontiers in Cognition on December 1, 2023, authored by Atanas Kirjakovski from the International Balkan University, North Macedonia. The article explores how the digital environment differs from physical and social environments and examines its potential impacts on human cognition and perception.

**Properties of the Digital Environment:** The digital environment is characterized as dynamic, symbolic, immaterial, hyperconnected, hypersocial, spatiotemporally uniform, automated, multifunctional, and personalized. Unlike the physical environment, which changes slowly, the digital environment is fast-paced and constantly recreated. People spend 6-7 hours daily online (nearly half their waking life), with 5.16 billion people (65% of the world population) online. Digital technology compresses time and space, making physical distances trivial.

**Cognitive Effects:** The article reviews several cognitive impacts of digital technology:
- Reading: Printed text offers 10%-30% faster reading and better comprehension compared to screens. Digital text introduces hyperlinking, nonlinearity, and behaviors like scanning and superficial browsing.
- Memory: Digital technology leads to "cognitive offloading" and externalization of memory. The "Google effect" shows people remember less content but better recall where to find information. Taking photos impairs memory for objects by about 14%. Smartphones create an illusion of knowledge, inflating cognitive self-esteem by ~10% compared to laptop searches.
- Attention: Digital devices constantly capture attention; smartphones deplete cognitive capacity even when merely present. Internet addiction correlates with ADHD, especially in young people.
- Multitasking: Heavy media multitaskers show larger task-switching costs, greater distractibility, and differences in brain structure (reduced gray matter in anterior cingulate cortex, greater density in left superior parietal cortex).

**Perceptual Effects:** The article discusses potential perceptual changes:
- Video game players show enhanced orientation sensitivity (the "oblique effect" may be strengthened by digital content), improved radial motion processing, better visual acuity, and enhanced contrast sensitivity.
- Experience-dependent neuroplasticity: Pokémon players in childhood show reorganized ventral temporal cortex attuned to digital creatures even in adulthood. Touchscreen users show differences in somatosensory cortex activity.
- Digital mediation of social interactions may diminish mirror neuron system responses, affecting understanding of others' emotions and intentions.
- The "Proteus effect" shows online avatars change how people disclose information and interpret social distances.

**Future Directions:** The article hypothesizes that visual perception may adapt to 2D scenes, favor monocular cues, and shift thresholds toward discrete digital intensities. Cognition may see increased externalization and offloading, altered sustained attention due to automation, and adaptations favoring searchability over memorization. The author cautions that many findings are preliminary and correlational, and more longitudinal research is needed.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: Digital Device Usage and Childhood Cognitive Development: Exploring Effects on Cognitive Abilities ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9067/11/11/1299

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review article titled "Digital Device Usage and Childhood Cognitive Development: Exploring Effects on Cognitive Abilities," published in *Children* (2024, Vol. 11, Issue 11, 1299) by Clemente-Suárez et al. The review explores the complex relationship between digital device usage and cognitive development in childhood, incorporating over 157 peer-reviewed studies published between 2001 and 2024.

**Methodology:** The authors conducted a comprehensive literature search across PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, using MeSH-compliant keywords. From an initial pool of over 2,158 articles, strict exclusion criteria were applied, resulting in 157 studies included in the final review.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Neurophysiological Foundations:** Digital device interaction influences neural plasticity through neurotransmitter regulation (dopamine, glutamate) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). While this can enhance cognitive functions like visual-spatial skills, prolonged screen-based multitasking can overload cognitive capacity, reducing attention spans and executive function efficiency.

2. **Psychological Impact:** Using cognitive load theory, the review notes that digital devices can exceed the brain's processing abilities, particularly in young children. The environment of "continuous partial attention" can impair sustained attention and deep processing capabilities.

3. **Developmental Considerations:** Drawing on Piaget's and Vygotsky's theories, the review emphasizes that digital devices can replace essential hands-on learning and face-to-face social interactions. 4. **Positive Effects of Digital Devices:**
   - **Visuospatial Skills:** Video games, AR, and VR can enhance spatial navigation, hand-eye coordination, and visual processing abilities.

   - **Memory, Creativity, and Social Cognition:** Multiplayer games encourage teamwork, strategic thinking, and cooperative problem-solving.

The review concludes that the impact of digital devices on cognitive development is dual-edged, depending on context, content, and duration of use. It provides actionable recommendations for parents, educators, and policymakers to promote balanced integration of digital tools in childhood learning environments.
